title: Annotated Chronicle of the Life of Master Hanshan
excerpt: Recorded by Fushan, attendant of the Narayana Cave of the Eastern Sea; annotated by Fuzheng, a disciple of the Kaiyuan Prefectural Office in Wu-Yue

inline.s: Recorded by Fushan, attendant of the Narayana Cave of the Eastern Sea
Annotated by Fuzheng, a disciple of the Kaiyuan Prefectural Office in Wu-Yue

blocks.text: The Imperial Eulogy of Emperor Chongzhen on the Venerable Master Hanshan's Portrait

inline.s: How venerable this elder Master, and what manner of conduct was his! He propped up the Dharma-gate and became its pillar and beam. He bore the hammer and tongs of the Son of Heaven, and stood as a model for Buddhas and patriarchs.
Inscribed by the imperial brush of Zhu Youjian, the seventeenth-generation sovereign (with the imperial seal, reverently offered in the Court of the Nine-Lotus Bodhisattva within the palace).

blocks.text: A Eulogy on the Portrait of the Venerable Kang Senghui, with a Preface, Sent to Master Hanshan

inline.s: The monk Zhenke (Zibai)

The Three Kingdoms were a gathering of heroes, and likewise a gathering of weapons; for compassion and prajñā there was no place to enter in. But our Patriarch Kang, on a single staff, floated across the river; thrice he invoked the Tathagata, and his two eyes wept blood. He let the relic fall into the vase, whose radiance blazed through the six directions and whose grace endured through endless ages. At that time the lord and ministers of Wu were all shaken to the heart and changed in countenance; seeking principle from the event, they knew that the Buddha existed and no longer doubted. The six perfections were translated, and the gate of anapana opened; without distinction of black or white, all attained the pure Dharma-eye. Those who through meditation entered into the subtle were beyond counting, and all were first guided on their way by our Patriarch.

Now Master Hanshan Deqing, banished to the malarial sea for spreading the Dharma, was skilled in the samādhi of the compassionate mind and brought spring back to withered bones. The layman Shenghua, stirred by his reputation and filled with admiration, specially painted the Patriarch's image and sent it to Caoxi, to serve as the Master's guiding influence.

Alas! From the Tang through the Song, the flesh-Buddha manifested at Caoxi, and those who drank of Caoxi and attained the Way were not wanting in any generation. Of late Caoxi has run dry, and the jade grove stands desolate; yet through Master Han's banishment a stirring tide arose and Caoxi was revived. Our Patriarch Kang's emanated body opens its skull-eyes, beyond all comparison to the sands of the Ganges — how could one with a deliberating mind fathom the depth of its merit!
The Daoist Daguan, who knew not how to hold the helm against the wind but only how to push the boat downstream, offered this eulogy, saying:

When Patriarch Kang came to Wu, Master Qing was banished to Yue. O master of the skull — your vajra eye blazes. The sorrow of the malarial sea pierces the bone and startles the soul; in his exile the Master only felt the more the sovereign's bright grace.

At Caoxi the poison of the worm-cup slays all who drink it; the Master drank it, and dissolved every miasma. With his fingers he gathered up the relics — the greed of Patriarch Kang. But such greed was never for himself; how could this heart feel shame?

For spreading the Dharma he incurred guilt, his life as thin as a single thread; across a thousand li of malarial peaks his straw sandals trod everywhere. His road to the thunder-place was steep and high, the hurricane raging; his bowl and vase were swept off alone, yet his eloquent tongue shone clearly.

In southern Yue the demons clap their hands in broad daylight. If my heart is empty, the Bodhisattva's influence is there; but should one respond with a busy heart, it is the folly of Patriarch Kang — carrying ceremonial caps into Yue; who would not doubt it?

At the parting by the stone, the liver and diaphragm ran cold; Ding Sheng blew upon the fire and painted Patriarch Kang's image. From the image the mind is gained; the mind gone, the nature is dark and still; the great function is without constancy — the bell is heard with the eyes.
Roots and dust, host and guest; gathering and releasing, dream and waking; palm upraised to hold the jeweled pagoda on the peak of Mount Lao.
(Master Da, borrowing the eulogy on Patriarch Kang's image to praise Patriarch Han, gave it an even truer meaning. The inscribed image is kept at the Dharma-Cloud Temple on Wuru Peak.)

blocks.text: Patriarch Han's Own Inscription on the Portrait in the Caoxi Image-Hall, as He Approached the End

inline.s: Majestic and imposing, clear and serene; he builds no walls about his heart, and has no forbidding brink. His spirit covers heaven and earth, his eyes prop up the Milky Way. Cast down to the present gate of affairs, he yet never departs from the far shore of the Sound of Majesty.

Whether as a layman or a monk, the shoulder never leaves the carrying-pole. If he is not a servant boy of Buddhas and patriarchs, then he is a petty vendor at the enlightenment fair. Had he not entered the great red furnace, who would have known him for a man of iron? Only when Maitreya is born below will this weighty case be settled.
(The authentic work is at Hanshan Temple, Caoxi.)

blocks.text: A Eulogy on the True Countenance of the Dharma-Patriarch Elder Han

inline.s: The monk Zhixu (spiritual Dharma-descendant)

Of noble countenance and abundant spirit, with firm courage and great might; in emptiness-samādhi his spirit was composed, and the light first cleared. His grief was for the Dharma-gate; what reckoning had he for fortune or harm? Like a flash of lightning, a peal of thunder — a Deshan, a Linji.

Secretly he used, and silently he moved, within the bound of the round sea. Those who knew him said he was a single hand upholding the sky; those who did not, said he was a hero covering the age. Who would think that he must dwell between neither-Chan-nor-doctrine, and both-doctrine-and-Chan, and at last not drift away with the current of the times?
(Master Xu, styled Suhua, was at the very time hearing the profound meaning of the Surangama at the abbot's quarters at Kangju when Fuzheng completed the Annotated Chronicle.)

blocks.text: A Eulogy on the Portrait of the Master, Hanshan

inline.s: (The refuge disciple Fuzheng) Tan Zhenmo (Sao'an)

O our Master the Great Monk, the flesh-patriarch Hanshan: in Yan he was the towering teacher of Cishou; in Yue, the heir-patriarch of Caoxi. The flesh-body stands firm, the palm-leaf scriptures burn with light. The Chan practitioners who have emerged in recent times — how could they match even a ten-thousandth of him? Yet he was a sun and moon with both feet: such radiance is incomparable, but a single eye in the dust and wind, dark and hard to open. Unless his whole course were made manifest, who would know the heavens and earth embraced within him? The lord of Haiyu's inscription on Wuru Peak could not escape hearsay in its telling; the disciples of the Purple Bamboo who passed on his revival still lacked personal attendance and intimacy. Perfumed with sandalwood from head to foot, once parted from the stupa, what inscription remains? The chronicle being completed, it accords with his true biography. The paths beyond the sea are steep, yet word of the far-off wanderer flew without feet; the miracle of Meiling was carved by the disciple Sao after offering incense. I humbly read the Record of the Mirror of the Source by the Chan Master Yongming Zhijue, which says: 'Awakening the mind to become a patriarch is handed down by the sages of old.' Hence the First Patriarch Bodhidharma says: 'Clearly understanding the Chan school of the Buddha-mind, without the slightest error, when practice and understanding correspond, one is called a patriarch.' Again there is a verse: 'He does not see evil and so conceive aversion, nor see the good and so strive with zeal; he does not abandon the foolish to draw near the wise, nor cast away delusion to grasp enlightenment. He passes beyond measure upon the great Way, exceeds all bounds in penetrating the Buddha-mind; he does not tread the same track as the ordinary or the sage — transcendent, he is called a patriarch.' When Fuzheng obtained these words, they exactly corroborate in sequence the meaning of this Master having been honored as a patriarch at Baolin, and likewise tally with Master Da's eulogy on the flesh-patriarch of Caoxi. I therefore presume to name him: the Caoxi-Reviving, Flesh-Body, Heir-Patriarch, Great Monk and Master Hanshan. With reverence I offer this eulogy on his portrait:

A Buddha manifest, a patriarch manifest; of the true line, of the true teaching. He received the robe of Caoxi, and wrote the radiance of the Lankavatara. The Dragon Gate and the Sea Seal, the wonderful gate of Qingliang. Through eons of kalpas the flesh-body came, arriving twice in this one place.
In the eighth year of the Shunzhi reign of the Great Qing, the cyclical year Ximao, on the third day of the third month, the Annotated Chronicle was completed; Fuzheng respectfully records this.

blocks.text: Inscription on Master Hanshan's Six-Verse Handscroll

inline.s: In the eleventh year of the Republic, the cyclical year Renxu, Li Guosong requested an inscription on the Master's Six-Verse handscroll, whereupon I wrote this, and it was then included in the Collected Writings. I now append it here to express my reverence. Recorded by the monk Yinguang, with joined palms.

Master Hanshan was a great power manifesting himself. His merit in spreading the Dharma was deep, yet the envious slandered him. He was exiled to guard Guangzhou, as a means of averting calamity. Fortunately there were great officials who looked upon him with a special eye.

He spread the Dharma at Caoxi and continued the severed life of wisdom. He taught the Dharma according to circumstances, and great abuses vanished. Protecting the country and the people, his merit towered above the civil precedent; after his passing his body remained unspoiled and unchanged.

Guangdong and Jiangxi contended, yet he returned to the bank of Caoxi. The Sixth and the Seventh Patriarchs are honored in the proverb of the age. He magnified the Buddha-sun, serving as rampart and moat for the Dharma; his writings were vast and shone brightly as sun and moon.

The Great Canon circulated, but alas only a small portion of his works; much was lost, though now and then it appears. The exquisite verses of the Six Odes, whose brushwork is firm and vigorous and whose meaning is surpassing — the more one reads them, the more they glow.

For over three hundred years, happily, they have suffered no loss. A true son of the Buddha obtained them from a Shanghai shop; wishing to display the great enterprise, he made a handscroll and begged Guang for an inscription, to manifest the Dharma model.
So I have set forth a brief outline, hoping that later scholars may see and hear.

blocks.text: Preface to the Printing and Circulation of the Annotated Chronicle of Master Hanshan

inline.s: (In the twenty-third year of the Republic, the cyclical year Jiaxu, on an auspicious day of the first month, it was sent to print.)

Mencius said: 'In poverty one perfects oneself alone; in success one perfects the whole world.' This speaks of worldly dharma. But in terms of the Buddha-Dharma, success can indeed perfect the whole world, and poverty can likewise perfect it. Strictly observing the precepts, earnestly upholding the human relations, leading others by his own example, he caused all men to look upon one another and do good. When their joyful longing arose, he then showed them the principle and fact of the threefold cause and effect and the six realms of transmigration; that the mind is originally Buddha, and that through Buddha-recitation one may be reborn — this is the causal condition one may personally realize. Who that has a mind would not gladly follow? Hence the eminent monks of old, wherever they went, gathered many to take refuge. Compared with the teaching of kingly governance, its benefit was the deeper. At the end of the Ming, the imperial law was not upheld, and the great ministers had no authority; those who wielded power were ignorant eunuchs. The wicked leaned on their power to do wrong, and the cautious had no wisdom to devise remedies; so the people were distressed and the state imperiled, beyond saving. Hanshan, Zibai, Lianchi, and Miaofeng all arose in the world at this very time; how great were their secret aid to the way of governance and their unseen shelter of the people's livelihood! Hanshan, slandered for spreading the Dharma, was exiled to Guangzhou; his rescue of the people of Yue and prolonging of the state's life were deep and far-reaching. Had Hanshan not been exiled to Guangzhou, the people of that city would long since have taken to desperate measures and become a worry to the state. The withdrawal of the tax-boats, the pacifying of civil unrest, and the great affair of reconciling Qinzhou were all settled by a single conversation. Who but one who came forth by vow to save the people from flood and fire could have done it? The laymen Ye Yufu and others established a Zhanshan Temple at Qingdao, on the very ground where Hanshan was slandered for spreading the Dharma. Mindful of Hanshan's mighty virtue, they had the Annotated Chronicle printed, so that later readers might be stirred to rise.
Respectfully composed by the ever-ashamed monk Shi Yinguang.

blocks.text: The Annotated True Record of the Self-Narrated Chronicle of the Elder Hanshan, First Volume

inline.s: Recorded by Fushan, attendant at the Nārāyaṇa Cave of the Eastern Sea
Expounded and annotated by the disciple Fuzheng of the Kaiyuan Prefecture of Wu-Yue
The twenty-fifth year of the Jiajing era, the cyclical year Bingwu, in the reign of Emperor Shizong, the Solemn Emperor of the Ming

I am a man of Quanjiao County in Jinling, of the Cai clan. My father was named Yan Gao, my mother of the Hong clan; through life she loved to honor Guanyin, the Great Knight. At first she dreamed that the Great Knight came in through the gate leading a young boy; my mother received him and embraced him, and so conceived. When the time came to give birth, the child came forth wrapped in a white afterbirth. That year, on the twelfth day of the tenth month, at the hour of dawn, in the cyclical hour Jichou, I was born. (The father, once; the mother, once.)

His disciple Zhanyu Guanheng, in his Account of the Great Master Han, Restorer of Caoxi, says: the Master was named Deqing, styled Cheng-yin, and bore the style-name Hanshan. When his mother was delivered, he came forth wrapped in a white afterbirth; when the garment was taken off and washed, the bath-water smelled of rare perfume. After he left home at the Bao’en Temple, one day before the relic pagoda he met a Brahmin monk, who said: “This young master will one day turn the great Dharma-wheel; his mouth is like the upturned moon, that is, the Buddha’s own mouth.” Again, in the cloister of that temple he met a man who said: “The Emperor Yao had brows of eight colors, and you, sir, have brows of five colors; you carry the charge of the Three Teachings.” Later, at Mount Wutai, as he was passing the Great Pagoda Court and was then a dhuta ascetic, he met a monk of very stately bearing, who took the Master by the hand and said: “You, sir, are a great being come again; all the hair of your head is of dark blue-black, and hereafter you will surely carry out great Buddha-affairs.”
O
Fuzheng observes:

The chronological biography records that in the forty-second year of Wanli, the cyclical year Jiayin, in the eleventh month, there came a disciple, the Zhanyu of Wuxin, to pay his respects. In the Master’s Dream-Journey Collection there is a Dharma-talk shown to the Chan man Zhanyu Heng. It says in brief: Zhanyu first relied upon the Great Master Kongyin of Wutai and listened to the study of the scriptures and treatises. After a long time he swept all of that away and single-mindedly raised one thought, earnestly investigating the matter of his own portion. He wandered ten thousand li to the south, and passing Caoxi he called upon the old man and asked for the benefit of instruction. The old man showed him the one road of turning the body about; he assented, bowed, and took his leave, and went to dwell at Mount Nanyue. Before long the old man too arrived. The Chan man, being ill, went to Baoqing to seek a physician, and the old man sighed that in the Chan gate a true student of birth and death is the hardest thing to find. On the first day of the third month of the cyclical year Bingchen, at midnight amid wind and rain, suddenly the Chan man came, braving the rain and plunging through the mud. When the old man saw that his sickness was healed he was greatly delighted. And because he again burned incense and asked for instruction, the old man especially showed him that the sickness of the body being healed, he must by no means be invaded by the sickness of Chan. The ancients said: to renounce feeling is easy, to renounce the dharma is hard. The Chan man renounced the body, that is, renounced feeling; he renounced views, that is, renounced the dharma. With feeling and dharma both forgotten, is he not a man of the great unhindered liberation? This instruction ran to some thousand words. In the Collection there is little that wins his approval, and one may count it on the fingers; rightly there should be a work of restoration. What is to be regretted is that the account is a whole ledger of errors and corruptions, easily misleading later students. For the two visits and requests fell within one and the same time, and he followed the Master for few days. Later he never saw the autobiographical chronological biography, and so what he heard is told differently — a matter of no small consequence. Here I take the chronological biography as the master text, consulting it to supplement one or two especially close and out-of-the-way anecdotes and sayings heard otherwise in the account. Thus the whole story of the hermit of Mount Pan is of deep benefit. Other matters, rambling and unfounded, I have cut away entirely. On the whole, the malady of Chan lies in rushing toward the school of Chan and shunning the teachings. Such people do not understand that the Patriarch Han and the Sixth Patriarch were alike masters of both Chan and the teachings, alike manifest a flesh-body at Caoxi, and alike are without a robe and bowl handed down to a single heir. His Dharma-grandson Suhua Zhixu — who had the cause of first framing the resolve for awakening, and of being received in a dream — was in his generation a man in whom Chan and the teachings were one. He composed Eulogies on the Eighteen Patriarchs and ended them with the Patriarch Han. The Eighteen Patriarchs are precisely those patriarchs who do not transmit the robe and bowl. The one account of the Patriarch Han, abridging Zhanyu’s biography, accords exactly with the chronological biography, and must be counted a loyal partisan’s contribution.
O
The Buddha and patriarch in the flesh, a model for the world, was already so in the mother’s womb. The surpassing cause accumulated through kalpas is no small matter.
The twenty-sixth year, the cyclical year Dingwei

When I was one year old, a wind-disease came upon me and I nearly died. My mother prayed to the Great Knight and vowed to give me up to leave home, and I was registered under the name of the Longevity Temple of the county; hence my milk-name was changed to Heshang. (The mother, a second time.)

Fuzheng recites: the milk-name Great Beauty was in the end perfectly fulfilled. One must know that the Dharma-name Deqing came from the venerable Xilin, and was given at the time of leaving home; the chronicle does not record it. Nor does it record the name his father gave him before it was changed.
The twenty-seventh year, the cyclical year Wushen
When I was three I often sat alone and did not care to play with other children. My grandfather used to say: “This child is like a wooden post.” (The grandfather, once.)
Fuzheng observes: in the end he became exactly this post; his grandfather may be called one who had the eye.
The twenty-eighth year, the cyclical year Jiyou; the twenty-ninth year, Gengxu; the thirtieth year, Xinhai; the thirty-first year, Renzi

When I was seven my uncle cherished me dearly. My mother then sent me to the village school. One day my uncle died and was laid out on the bed. When I came home my mother put me off, saying: “Your uncle is asleep; call him awake.” I called several times, and my aunt, pierced with grief, wept and cried: “O Heaven, where has he gone?” I was astonished and puzzled, and asked my mother: “Uncle’s body is here — where else has he gone?” My mother said: “Your uncle is dead.” I said: “Where do the dead go?” And thereupon I was deeply puzzled. Before long my second aunt bore a son, and when my mother went to look at him I went along. Seeing the infant to be so very small, I asked my mother: “How did this child get into my aunt’s belly?” My mother gave me a slap and said: “Silly child, how did you get into your own mother’s belly?” And again I was deeply puzzled. From this the doubt of dying here and being born there could not be loosed from my heart. (The mother, a third time; the uncle, the aunt, and the younger brother, once each.)

Fuzheng observes: how did this seven-year-old child come by this bone-piercing, marrow-piercing crisis of birth and death? Mother and child, face to face, questioning and answering so great a mass of doubt — a most marvelous single case. The manifest body of Maya, and a brand-new pair of tongs and hammer forging Buddhas and tempering patriarchs: the foremost great public case.
The thirty-second year, the cyclical year Guichou

When I was eight I studied and boarded with relatives across the river. My mother warned me that I was not to come home, but only once a month. One day I came home and, clinging to my mother, would not go back. My mother was angry, whipped me, and drove me to the riverbank, where I would not board the boat. In her anger she seized the topknot of my hair and threw me into the river, and without a backward look went home. Just then my grandmother saw it, urgently called for help and had me pulled out, and sent me home. My mother said: “If this worthless child is not to be drowned, what is the use of keeping him?” And again she beat me and drove me off, with not the least thought of keeping me. At that time I privately thought my mother’s heart hard, and from then on I did not think of home. My mother often wept across the river, and my grandmother scolded her. My mother said: “One must indeed cut off his affection, only then can he study.” (The grandmother, once; the mother, a fourth time.)

Fuzheng, reading to this point, wept so that tears and mucus poured down at every word and every sentence. Whoever reads it without weeping is no human being. Joining his palms he praised, saying: “How kind, how compassionate, how good, how faithful! It being so, how could she not cast away her son, how could he not scrape off his flesh to repay his mother?”
The thirty-third year, the cyclical year Jiayin

When I was nine I studied in the temple, and hearing monks recite the Guanyin Sutra, which can save the world from suffering, I was greatly delighted, and so asked the monks for its text, read it in secret, and could at once recite it. My mother honored Guanyin, the Great Knight, and whenever she burned incense and made obeisance I would always follow her. One day I said to my mother: “Guanyin Bodhisattva has a sutra of one scroll.” My mother said: “I did not know.” I at once recited it through for my mother. My mother was overjoyed and said: “Where did you get this? The sound of your recitation is just like an old monk’s.” (The mother, a fifth time.)

Qian Muzhai (Qian Qianyi) composed the Pagoda Inscription for the Great Master Hanshan of the Five Milk Peaks of Mount Lu in the Great Ming. It says: the Master at nine could recite the Universal Gateway Chapter, which is the Guanyin Sutra named in the chronicle. In the Tianqi era, the cyclical year Dingmao, Chen Dixiang of Nanhai and Fushan, a disciple of the Five Milk Peaks, entrusted his conduct-record to Muzhai for a pagoda inscription. Of the business of restoring Caoxi he seems to have heard a little from Xiao Xuanpu, styled Yunjü, of Xuanhua. But of the eastern journey the beginning and end are not detailed, and it differs utterly from the chronological biography. Now that the flesh-body is at Caoxi, the pagoda inscription of the Five Milk Peaks is truly lost; what may be gleaned from it is a bare tenth.
O

Fuzheng, reading this, understood that to take the examinations and win a name, to serve as a magistrate or minister, one need not trouble to study truly. But to gain right views and become a Buddha or patriarch, there is no one who has not begun from truly studying. Thus this one scroll of the Guanyin Sutra, which in early years he could recite from memory, came about entirely through study. And by reciting it once for his mother he could repay his mother for having beaten and driven him off.
The thirty-fourth year, the cyclical year Yimao

When I was ten my mother pressed me very hard at my lessons, and I suffered under it. So I asked my mother: “What is study for?” My mother said: “To be an official.” I said: “What sort of official?” My mother said: “You begin from the bottom, and with ability you may rise to be prime minister.” I said: “And having become prime minister, what then?” My mother said: “Then you are dismissed.” I said: “A pity to toil a whole life and in the end be dismissed; what use is it? I think one should be something that is never dismissed.” My mother said: “A worthless child like you could only be a board-and-bundle monk.” I said: “What is a board-and-bundle monk? What good is that?” My mother said: “A monk is a son of the Buddha, who walks the whole world, free and at ease, with offerings wherever he goes.” I said: “That is exactly the thing to be.” My mother said: “I fear only that you have not the blessing for it.” I said: “Why does it need blessing?” My mother said: “In this world the top scholar is always to be had; but one who leaves home and becomes a Buddha or patriarch — is he always to be had?” I said: “If I have this blessing, I fear my mother cannot let me go.” My mother said: “If you have this blessing, I can indeed let you go.” I secretly took note of it. (The mother, a sixth time.)

Fuzheng sighs deeply; tsk, tsk. Mother and son in their reunion spoke the speech of the unborn. How clear her instruction, how broad her pointing, how tight the point of the exchange, how swiftly he took it up. At ten, in Jinling, his mother let go the son’s flesh-body. At seventy-eight, at Caoxi, the son’s flesh-body repaid his mother. A cause of the very highest order, a very marvel.
The thirty-fifth year, the cyclical year Bingchen

When I was eleven, I happened to see several traveling monks coming with a gourd and rain-hat slung over their shoulders. I asked my mother: 'What kind of people are these?' She said: 'They are wandering monks.' Inwardly I was pleased and watched them. The monks arrived, set down their loads against a tree, and asked after her and begged alms. My mother said: 'Please sit,' and quickly made tea and prepared a meal of alms, with great respect. When the meal was done, the monks rose, took up their loads, and raised one hand in thanks; my mother quickly avoided it, saying: 'Do not thank us.' The monks went straight off. I said: 'How rude the monks are, not to thank us for the meal.' My mother said: 'If they thanked us, there would be no blessing.' Inwardly I said: 'This is what makes a monk lofty,' and I pondered it earnestly. Thereupon I formed the resolve to leave the home life, but I was troubled that there was no convenient path. (Seen a seventh time by the mother.)

Fuzheng observes: suddenly offering a meal to monks, with not a trace left behind — such a great case; even the case of Zhaozhou testing the old woman at Taishan is no match for it. People know the merit of feeding monks to be a worldly blessing, but this mother and son rather attested the blessing of the Two-Footed Honored One.
O
The above closes the household case.
The thirty-sixth year, the cyclical year Dingsi

When I was twelve, living as I did I took no pleasure in the world, and when my father betrothed a wife for me I at once stopped it. One day I heard a monk from the capital say that the Venerable Xilin of the Bao'en Temple was a man of great virtue, and my heart at once longed to go to him. I told my father, who would not consent; I told my mother, who said: 'In raising a son one follows his will; only see that he accomplishes [his aim],' and so she sent me. That year, in the tenth month, I went to the temple, and the Grandmaster at first sight said, rejoicing: 'This child has an uncommon bone and spirit; if he were to be just a worldly monk, that would be a pity.' At the time the Great Master Wuji had just begun preaching in the Three-Master Hall of the temple. My grandfather took me there to call upon him, and just then Zhao Dazhou was present; at first sight he said, rejoicing: 'This child should be a teacher of men and gods.' Then he stroked me and asked: 'Do you love to be an official, or would you be a Buddha?' I answered at once: 'Be a Buddha.' Mr. Zhao said: 'This child must not be taken lightly; you should teach him well.' When I listened to the preaching, though I did not understand what was said, yet my mind felt a surging, as if there were something I knew but could not express. (Seen a second time by the father, an eighth time by the mother; and once each by the Venerable Xilin, the Great Master Wuji, and Zhao Dazhou. Dazhou, named Zhenji, styled Mengjing, was a man of Neijiang; he held office as Minister of Rites and Grand Secretary of the Wuying Hall, and was posthumously titled Wensu.)

Fuzheng reflects that had Patriarch Han not had this mother, he could not have left home, could not have carried his pure boy's body through to become a Buddha and patriarch; she was truly a Buddha's mother. Again, according to the Record of Buddhist Temples of Jinling: in the Jiajing era the abbot of the Bao'en Temple, Yongning, styled Xilin, kept a horse; whenever he went from the temple to the Ministry of Rites he rode it, and on mounting he would silently recite the Diamond and the Lotus Sutras; upon arriving at the ministry gate he dismounted and the recitation was done. Later, a woman who lived next to the temple was in childbirth, and that very night the horse died; the woman dreamed the horse entered her room and then bore a boy, exceedingly dull, who could only recite the two sutras aloud. Because of this he entered Xilin's temple as a monk, but he could not master any other sutra, and never came to know a single character. Hence the chronicle says the Master's [teacher] held the Diamond Sutra through life, never stopping from it at death.
The thirty-seventh year, the cyclical year Wuwu; the thirty-eighth year, Jiwei

When I was fourteen, the Grandmaster first chose from among his grandsons the learned and virtuous Master Jun to be my teacher. He first taught me the Lotus Sutra, and in three months I could recite it from memory. The other scriptures in circulation I had all already memorized. The Grandmaster said: 'This child is teachable; you must not miss the time with him,' and so he invited a noted teacher to instruct me. (The Great-grandmaster and Grandmaster are both the Venerable Xilin; seen a second time.)
The thirty-ninth year, the cyclical year Gengshen; the fortieth year, Xinyou; the forty-first year, Renxu

When I was seventeen, the Grandmaster again asked a tutor to teach me first the pursuit of the examinations. At the outset I read the Four Books together, then studied the Five Classics, the Masters, the Histories, the ancient prose, verse, and rhapsody. I could at once compose verse, and in the literary society made a rhapsody on the river, the piece 'On the River,' which the whole gathering at the time esteemed. Yet I was often ill, and so I began to wish to set aside the studies I had taken up. (Seen a third time by the Grandmaster.)
The forty-second year, the cyclical year Guihai; the forty-third year, Jiazi

When I was nineteen, because all my fellow students had succeeded, there were those who urged me to go for the examinations. At the time the Great Master Yungu, a man of the right Dharma-eye, dwelt in the mountains at Qixia; the Grandmaster had long supported him, and whenever he came and went always kept him to stay for days or a month. I served him very diligently and often heard his instruction. Just then Master Yungu came out of the mountains, and hearing there were those who urged me on, he feared I might have a mind to leave [the Way]. The Master earnestly opened to me the practice of leaving the world and entering meditation, and the wonder of awakening to the mind-ground. He enumerated the various patriarchs of the Transmission of the Lamp and the Lives of Eminent Monks, and bade me take them and read. I searched my book-satchel and found the Comprehensive Record of Zhongfeng; before I had finished the scroll I was greatly delighted and sighed: 'This is what my heart delights in.' Thereupon I resolved to do the work of leaving the world. I asked my grandfather to shear me, then burned and cast away all that I had studied, and gave my whole attention to a single matter of inquiry. Not yet grasping the essential, I set my mind single-mindedly on Buddha-recitation, day and night without ceasing. Before long, one night in a dream I saw Amitābha Buddha manifest and stand in the sky, where the sun was setting; I saw his face's light and auspicious marks, distinct and clear. I received his feet in worship, clinging with endless sorrow, and again wished to see the two Bodhisattvas Avalokiteshvara and Mahasthamaprapta, who at once showed their half-bodies. From that time on the Three Sages were ever clearly before my eyes, and I gained confidence that the practice of cultivation could be accomplished. That year in winter the meditation hall of my temple built a practice-hall and invited the Great Master Wuji to preach the Prologue to the Avatamsaka. I thereupon received the full precepts from him and followed the lecture; when it reached the Ten Mystery Gates — 'the Sea-Seal's dense grove, the eternal dwelling place' — I suddenly awakened to the meaning of the dharma-realm's perfect and unhindered interpenetration. I earnestly admired the character of Qingliang [Chengguan], and so I named my own style Cheng-yin [Seal of Clarity]. I sought the Master's confirmation, and he said: 'Do you intend to enter this Dharma-gate?' He then spoke of Mount Qingliang, where in winter the ice piles hard and in summer snow still flies, and there is never heat, and that is why it is called Qingliang. From that time, whether walking or staying, the realm of ice and snow was ever before my eyes, and I vowed with all my heart to dwell there. In everything nothing pleased my heart, and the thought of leaving the world I never for a moment forgot. (Seen once by the Great Master Yungu, a second time by the Great Master Wuji, and a fourth time by the Grandmaster.)

Fuzheng's note: Patriarch Han's learning and letters were both already accomplished, and seeing the Buddha-Dharma in decline, he wished to take up the enterprise of [fulfilling] the spiritual and worldly dharma on one shoulder. Hence, at his friends' urging to take the examinations, he too conceived the desire to seize an official rank, so as to fulfill his own vow to spread the great Dharma. But the road of office is dangerous, and with the least carelessness one sinks into it. Fortunately he was warned by the Great Master Yungu, and so he devoted himself single-mindedly to the work of leaving the world, burned his study manuscripts, and begged the Grandmaster to shear him. The karmic occasion of his wholehearted practice and his resolve to awaken all began with Yungu. Yet there are those who single-mindedly recite the Buddha's name, year upon year, who still find it hard to see the Buddha — how could one so soon have the three Sages all manifest, so quickly answering his wish, and again and again have them clearly before his eyes? There are those who, at a practice-hall, listen to the teaching, take the precepts, and pursue inquiry, yet rely wholly on written words — who would attest their body, mind, and life? How could one, upon listening, have his whole body, mind, and life realized, seeing not a single word and phrase? Hearing the ten mystery gates of the Avatamsaka, he could at once awaken to the meaning of the dharma-realm's perfect, unhindered interpenetration, and could at once enter the Qingliang Dharma-gate, seeing ice and snow, and naming himself Cheng-yin. At that time the miraculous power of Wuji and the miraculous power of Patriarch Han were already in the inconceivable. Who would say that with words or without words, a great Dharma-master or a great Chan-master, there are two truths? One must know that one such as Patriarch Han is truly a man come from the West through many kalpas.
The forty-fourth year, the cyclical year Yichou

When I was twenty, on the sixteenth day of the first month, the Grandmaster entered his stilling. The previous year, on the last day [of the year], the Grandmaster gathered all his followers and said: 'I am eighty-three, and whether morning or evening I am going. I have taken on more than eighty disciples, and not one holds to my work.' Then he patted my back and said: 'This child I hoped might come to manhood, but now I cannot. Though he is young, yet he has the view of an older man. After my death, the great and small affairs of the house shall all be decided by him; do not discount them because he is young.' The assembly, choking back tears, received the charge. Seven days into the new year the Grandmaster put on his robes and went the round of the quarters, bidding farewell to each; the whole assembly was astonished. Three days later he spoke of his last affairs, showed a slight ailment, and refused to take medicine. He said: 'I am going; what use are drugs?' Then he gathered the assembly to recite the Buddha's name for five days and nights, holding the prayer-beads, with me held in his arms, and passed away serenely. Because the Grandmaster held the Diamond Sutra all his life, at the end he never stopped. The Grandmaster served as abbot of Bao'en for thirty years, dwelt in the abbacy, and on the eighteenth day of the third month after his passing, the abbacy caught fire, and the whole assembly marveled. That year, in the tenth month, the Great Master Yungu established a meditation session at Tianjie, gathering fifty-three renowned masters of the land to open the Dharma-gate of seated meditation. The Master strongly urged me to go and follow, and at that time the junior master consented, so I was able to take part. At first I did not know the key of applying the mind and suffered much from it. I offered incense and sought instruction, and the Master showed me how to examine earnestly the case of Buddha-recitation. From this I inquired, not swerving for a single thought. Within three months I was as in a dream; I saw not the assembly at all, nor knew that there were the affairs of daily life, so the whole assembly thought me resolute. Before many days had passed, because I used my mind too urgently, a swelling on my back broke out, very red and large; the Master was greatly concerned. I put on my kasaya and prayed with earnest grief before Weituo, saying: 'This must be an old enmity come to demand my life. I vow to recite the Avatamsaka Sutra ten times, and to borrow three months to finish this session, and afterwards will repay it.' Thus, when later in the night I was utterly weary, I went up to the meditation bed and slept deeply; I did not even know when the stilling ended, and when I rose, I had forgotten it. At dawn the Master asked how the ailment was; I said it was gone, and when he looked, it had already healed. The whole assembly was astonished; and so I finished a full session, and coming out I was as though I had never left the meditation seat: walking through the marketplace, I saw not a single person, and people all thought it strange. The founding of the Chan way south of the Yangtze began to flourish with the Great Master Yungu, but of the monks who dwelt in the temple practicing Chan, I alone [did so]. At the time the temple monks' robes all followed the lay fashion, much gaudy in color; I at that time cast aside all the clothes I had worn and sought only a patched robe to wear, and those who saw me thought it strange. (Seen a fifth time by the Grandmaster, once by the junior master, and a second time by the Great Master Yungu.)

Fuzheng observes: the Greatmaster Xilin of Xilin was by no means a common monk. He ended his long life in good fortune, knew his time beforehand, and got a grandson with an eye [of discernment], to whom he entrusted the affairs after death; and [the grandson] was able at last to requite the charge of patting his back, serving both worldly and spiritual dharma — rare indeed. Now everywhere there are meditation sessions, and those who enter to sit find only the comfort of a settled place for their pleasure; who knows the hardship of applying the mind? When Patriarch Han set his mind to Buddha-recitation, he early and often saw Buddhas and Bodhisattvas manifest with light. People content themselves with a little and are satisfied — who would again be willing to seek instruction and earnestly examine the case of Buddha-recitation? Patriarch Han once showed me, saying: 'If one recites the Buddha's name but will not put a death-defying mind to it, but only recites on floating thoughts, then in truth the habitual currents in the alaya-consciousness are entirely unseen; hence in Buddha-recitation one never sees the falling into place of a single thought. If Buddha-recitation is used powerfully, it even surpasses meditating on the cypress tree or a dry shit-stick.' The earnest examination of the case of Buddha-recitation has a basis. And so later when he traveled east and passed Jiahe, he came to Qizhen and paid respects at the stupa of the earlier Great Master Yungu, to make clear his Dharma-milk; and when he dwelt at Wuru, he established a six-period Buddha-recitation practice-hall in place of the meditation session. His prayer to Weituo to be rid of the back-swelling — how extraordinary was its efficacy! Were it not that in the three-month session he was as in a dream, seeing neither the assembly nor the affairs of daily life, and that leaving the meditation seat and walking the marketplace, he still saw no one as in sitting meditation — such earnest use of mind — one must not hope that praying to Weituo would bring such ease.
The forty-fifth year, the cyclical year Bingyin

When I was twenty-one, I came out from the meditation session. In the second month of that year, on the twenty-eighth day, at the hour of noon, the rain poured as from an overturned basin; suddenly a great thunderbolt came down from the stupa, fire broke out in the stupa hall, and in a moment the great hall was burned. By the Shen and You hours, the galleries and painted corridors of the various halls, more than a hundred and forty rooms, were all reduced to ashes. At the time my junior grandfather was abbot; when the matter was memorialized, an edict went down to the judicial office, and eighteen of those concerned in the matter were arrested together. The monks of the whole temple, fearing to be implicated, fled one after another; and there were no temple officers left with whom to consult. I stepped forward and did all I could to save them, personally carrying salt and vegetables to the prison to feed them. The distance from the temple to the Ministry of Justice was twenty li, and I traveled back and forth untiringly for three months; moreover I arranged protection in many ways, and the various parties to the affair finally escaped death. At the time Xuelang Gong, one year older than I, had taken refuge with the Great Master Wuji at the same time as I; we were very close to each other and were at the time regarded as brothers. I at once resolved with Gong on the intention to restore [the temple]. I also said: 'This is a great karmic occasion; it is not easy except for one with great good fortune and wisdom. You and I should throw our lives into practice, nourishing [our strength] to await the right time.' At that time I formed the resolve for a distant journey. Before long, the junior grandfather entered his stilling, and there was none to support the affairs of the great grandfather's household. Earlier, when the Grandmaster entered his stilling he had no savings, and the funeral expenses had all been borrowed, so there were many debts. When the households divided, I knew they could not be kept. Considering the Grandmaster's last charge, I contrived to repay all those borrowings in full; the remainder I divided among the disciples, each taking up his own work, and so the household was preserved. That year in the winter I followed the Great Master Wuji to hear the Lotus Sutra at the Tianjie Temple. Because I aimed at a distant journey, I kept examining the monks of the region to find one who could be my companion; after a long time I found none. One day I saw the rear shelf was spotless, and thought to myself that the keeper of the privy must be no common man; so I sought him out, and when I saw him he was merely a sallow, swollen, sick monk, which made me think him all the more extraordinary. Each morning when I rose, the work was already done, I did not know when he had swept. So I did not sleep, but secretly walked under the eaves to watch him; when the assembly was dismissed [from meditation], he had already finished tidying. Again, some days later I saw a place unclean and saw no one about; I asked the officers, who said: 'The privy keeper is sick in the guest room.' I went to check on him, and his condition was unbearable; I asked the master if he was at ease. He said: 'This karma-laden body is already hard to bear, and the sickness of craving is even harder to endure.' I asked why. He said: 'Whenever I see the alms-food served, I only wish I could let go of everything at once.' I laughed and said: 'This is only a long sickness longing for food,' and so I knew the man for real. I prepared some cakes and fruits and brought them in my sleeve to him, then asked his name. He said: 'Miaofeng,' and he was a man of Puzhou. I thereupon arranged to go abroad together with him. Some days later I looked for him again and did not see him; I knew in my heart that the man, fearing I might be a burden, had gone off secretly. (The junior grandfather, that is, the junior master; seen a second time. Xuelang Gong seen once, the Great Master Wuji a third time, and the privy keeper Miaofeng once.)

Zheng’s note: Master Xuelang was named Hongen; at thirteen he went with his father to hear the Great Master Wuji expound the rules of the Lotus at Baoen Temple. Wuji was a man of Huaiyin who had fully mastered the cardinal tenets of the Xianshou and Cien schools, both nature and characteristics, so that the lecture halls of the time flourished under him. Gong was then a boy with his hair still down; for ten days he listened with all his ears and would not leave, and at last he cut off his own topknot, begging his father to give him up as the Great Master Wuji’s little novice. Hanshan the Patriarch was just twelve and had but lately left home at Xilin; in those fresh years they were close in spirit, as the chronicle earlier records of going to the Tripitaka Hall to hear the teaching. From this point, though in brotherly closeness, the Patriarch had a mind that stood apart and above. At twenty, while he sat in meditation with the Great Master Yungu at Tianjie, Gong saw how withered and still he was and scolded him for not going to hear Wuji’s lectures, saying, “What use is a village-shrine earth-god?” The Patriarch answered, “The ancients said: when one has penetrated the nature through the ancestral school, looking back at words is like opening a door and the pestle dropping into its socket.” Xuelang said, “If that is so, then you are my elder brother.” At that time Baoen was destroyed by fire from heaven, and the two wept for three days, vowing to restore it. Later the Patriarch went from Mt. Tai to the capital; the palace plans for the temple almost came together but never quite aligned, and though he passed through the eastern and southern seas he never for a moment forgot the affair of Baoen. Gong, seeing the pagoda’s finial leaning awry, went from door to door with his bowl among the great houses of the city, and in three years brought the work to completion. Ah, both of them may be called men who did not fail their word. Zibo in his heart made light of Gong and from time to time spoke slightingly of him, but when the Patriarch told him the circumstances of Gong’s leaving home, he was startled and said he must be Kuiji reborn. Much of the above I heard from Master Yiyu.
O

Master Miaofeng of Puzhou, named Fudeng, went to Putuo on behalf of the Prince of Shanyin to offer incense. Returning through Jianye, the northerner, unaccustomed to the south, took a damp chill and broke out in sores, so he went to the Tianjie monastery and asked for the work-post of latrine-cleaner, meaning only to rest. The Patriarch recognized him from among the clean latrine floor and the bright, spotless latrine lamp, and they pledged a friendship of life and death, vowing to live on the mountain and go on pilgrimage together. Master Miao said, “If you have this resolve, on pilgrimage I will carry your straw sandals, and if we dwell on a mountain I will supply the water and firewood.” Soon after, his sores healed and he left; six years later, when they sought each other out in the capital, it was clear that at that time his official business was unfinished and the karmic occasion still awaited, and so he had shaken out his robe and gone. The chronicle passes over it with the words “for fear of hindering his secret journey.” In the end, with Master Miao, that one word “truth” is enough to cover a hundred thousand buddhas and patriarchs.
O
In Pinggu county of Shuntian prefecture there is a mountain called Miaofeng, and he took his name from the mountain.
Longqing, first year, dīngmǎo ●

When I was twenty-two I especially proposed the Venerable Yungu of Zhonggong as abbot of the temple, to save it from ruin. This was the matter of the fire; the community’s debts came to nearly a thousand in gold, all of them handled by me. The assembly could think of no way to settle them, so I devised a plan and fixed a limit of three years, and paid them all. That year, by a ministry dispatch, this temple established a charity school to teach the monks; they asked me to be the teacher, and the novices who received instruction numbered nearly two hundred, and so I again took up my old studies of the Zuo Commentary and the other masters. (First meeting with the Venerable Yungu of Zhonggong.)

Zheng’s note: this act not only settled the entanglements of one branch of the family, it settled the entanglements of the abbot of the whole temple; worldly dharma and Buddha-dharma together, one great stroke of strategy. He is called the Venerable Zhong to distinguish him from the Great Master Yungu.
Second year, wùchén ●
When I was twenty-three, that year I gave up the temple school and taught again at Gaozuo Temple, because of the burden of my branch of the family.
Third year, jǐsì ● Fourth year, gēngwǔ ●
When I was twenty-five, in both years I answered the invitation to teach at Jinshan.
Fifth year, xīnwèi ●

When I was twenty-six, I traveled with my elder brother in the Dharma, Xuelang En, to Mount Lu. Reaching Nankang, we heard the mountains were much troubled by tigers, and did not dare climb. So we took the wind and went on to Ji’an, and visited Qingyuan; seeing the temple in ruin and the monks all wearing their hair long, I was moved to the resolve to restore it. So I spoke to the authorities, and chose those under forty years of age and shaved them all, gaining more than forty men. In summer, returning from Qingyuan, I set in order my master’s affairs and settled them well. In the eleventh month of winter I set out on a long journey with a single bowl. As I was about to go north, Xuelang stopped me then, fearing I could not endure the bitter cold, and urged me for the time being to keep to Wu and Yue, where there are many fine mountains and waters to delight the eye. I said: “We people cling with habit to soft warmth; only in a place where it cannot be applied is it easily mastered. Wu and Yue are but pillow and mat to me.” So with a single bowl I went far away. (Second meeting with my elder brother in the Dharma, Xuelang En.)

Zheng feels that the Patriarch had earlier made the contemplation of cool ice and snow; suddenly going north, he roused great valor, cast his body into the trial, and had long since seized both man and environment, so that empty space itself dissolved and fell away.
O
The above closes the case of the branch of the family at the temple.
Sixth year, rénshēn ●

When I was twenty-seven, I first came to Yangzhou; heavy snow blocked the way, and sickness came on me. After a long while, begging food in the market, I could not get in at any door. I asked myself why, and quickly examined myself, saying: “It is only that I have two coins of silver in my waist-wrap to rely on.” So when I saw monks and Daoists who had begged in the snow and gotten nothing, I at once invited them all to an eating-house and threw down the silver, and it was all spent in one meal. The next day, going out into the street, I entered one or two doors and was able to call out, and so got food. Then I rejoiced, saying: “My strength is enough to make light of ten thousand bushels.” I inscribed my bowl: “The vessel that makes light of ten thousand bushels,” and named my robe: “The robe that makes light of the whole world.” Then I made an inscription for them, saying: You entrust me with form, I entrust you with mind. So it is that this one body is made sufficient by it, and all things are in truth made light by it. Now I shall trail the sleeve of the long wind and wear the lapel of white clouds. In rising, like the wings of the swan; in idling, like the scales of the hidden dragon. Roaming free through the cosmos, leaving or resting in mountain and forest. Why then display the brilliance of crimson and purple? I take only what frost and snow cannot invade.

Zheng ponders that one passage of the scene where he first set out begging and entered people’s doors — truly it cannot be spoken, it cannot be conceived. Master Yiyu said that the Patriarch was resolved on the northern journey and Gong tried hard to keep him; the Patriarch put him off by going into the city, and then set out through the heavy snow. Gong returned to the temple and wept bitterly for a long time; this is why there should be a poem recalling his elder brother in the Western Hills. Bianrong and Xiaoyan, the two Masters, both spoke words of deep accord. Xiaoyan was a man of Yan, and built a hermitage in Willow Lane of the western city of Yanjing. He was born in rénshēn of Zhengde, so that when the Patriarch met him at twenty-seven, Master Xiao was already sixty-two. He has a Record of Moon-Mind, in two fascicles of the southern collection and two of the northern, a rarity among Chan records. These words of their meeting are line by line the sealing and transmitting of the matter that goes beyond.
O
In that year the karmic occasion of Mt. Tai began.

In the seventh month of autumn that year I reached the capital, with nowhere to set my foot. Begging, I went a whole day without food; toward evening I came to the tea-shed at the Western Peace Granary, where I got one meal, and I put up for the night at the Yijiao Temple by the canal. The next day the Left Cavalry General Lord Wang Boyu, learning that I had come, invited me to stay, because of his friendship with his younger brother, the second Lord Wang Zhongyan. So I was able to lodge there for ten days, and then waited upon the Venerable Zhong, Master Mahākāśyapa, and went with him to the Western Hills to hear the Commentary on the Profound Meaning of the Śūraṅgama, and there were verses written in the Western Hills recalling my elder brother. When the lecture period ended, Mahākāśyapa kept me through the winter to hear the Lotus and the Consciousness-Only, and asked the Venerable An, Master of Dharma, to explain for me the three-part syllogism of Buddhist logic. In the eleventh month Master Miaofeng came to see me. The Master had grown a long beard and wore coarse hempen robes. He first announced himself, saying, “A salt merchant has come to call.” When he entered the door the Master at once asked, “Do you still recognize me?” I looked at him closely and, seeing his two eyes, suddenly remembered him as the latrine-cleaner I had known at Tianjie when he was ill, and said: “I recognize you.” The Master said: “I have changed my head and swapped my face.” I said: “The original face is at ease of itself.” We smiled at each other, with no leisure for anything else. He only asked where I was staying, and I said: “Longhua.” The next day he came to greet me, and as we sat at night he asked why his appearance was like this. The Master said: “Because I have long dwelt in the mountains, my hair has grown and is uncut. Just now a donor, His Highness the Prince of Shanyin, is building a Brahma-palace and has commanded me to beg the inner canon, and so I have come.” He asked after me, and I said: “I have come especially to seek the Master, and also to see the capital and pay one visit to a teacher, to cut off the idle thoughts of other days.” The Master said: “Since we parted I have thought of you without a moment’s break, and supposed there was no karmic link between us. Now that you are here by good fortune, I would gladly accompany you begging, and be your outrider to drive off the dogs.” We talked the whole night through; at daybreak, with a smile, we parted. I then went to consult the Great Master Bianrong and bowed to him, begging the Master to give me instruction; the Master said nothing, only gazing straight at me. I consulted Master Xiaoyan, and the Master asked where I had come from. I said: “From the south.” The Master said: “Do you remember the road you came by?” I said: “Once past, and it is done.” The Master said: “Then your coming-place is clear enough.” I bowed, stood in attendance, and begged for instruction, and the Master opened to me a few words on the matter of going beyond. (The Left Cavalry General Lord Wang Boyu and his younger brother Zhongyan; the Venerable Zhong, Master Mahākāśyapa; the Venerable An, Master of Dharma — one meeting each. Third meeting with my elder brother in the Dharma, Xuelang En; second meeting with Master Miaofeng; one meeting with His Highness the Prince of Shanyin; one meeting each with the Great Master Bianrong and Master Xiaoyan. Boyu, named Daokun, styled Nanming, a man of Xin’an, author of the Taihan Collection; his younger brother Zhongyan, named Daoguan, a noted scholar.)

Zheng reflects that on that day the Patriarch came to know Boyu through Zhongyan, and of the two Wangs it was the elder brother who excelled; and came to know Linzhou through Fengzhou, and of the two Wangs it was the younger brother who excelled — in this world how rare are brothers so evenly matched. At the stare and not a single word, where did he place Fengzhou? At the knee and worshipping the old monk, he granted Nanming his place in heaven. Great Lord Wang’s truly great eye and great vow-power brought to fulfillment the great karmic occasion of Mt. Tai and its great merit — a great man indeed. He set out a vegetarian feast and invited both Masters; one seat’s talk was all words of suchness and no word of deceit, words piercing to the very home, words of the world and beyond the world. With whole heart he urged them on the road, adding more and never ceasing; working through mud and water for others, with no thought for himself — for a thousand ages, would any buddha or patriarch not be moved and give thanks? The two Masters set out for Mt. Tai with their faculties pointed at each other, their footing tested and matched. How then the begging and the slow going, the thanks given and the boarding of the carriage — all because Nanming saw it first. The two men were one road; traveling together or going alone, meeting and parting at their own will, none out of order, and everywhere gazing on ancient traces, and by the river’s edge overtaking and sharing one boat. Treading through straw sandals, faster than the post-relay. Their radiant verses, swifter than the odes. King Wu might well review his troops; why should Boyi and Shuqi not block the horses’ path? If he did not meet the Venerable Darun of the Great Thousand, he had already met the First Patriarch of Shaolin. How fine, how startling — the whirlwind laying low the mountains, sealing from afar Caoxi’s non-movement; night and day, birth and death, awakening to the non-duality of Buddha and Confucius. Only a Buddha knows a Buddha, only a patriarch knows a patriarch. Was it Master Miao who sang it forth, and Nanming who drummed it abroad? Wuji, Yungu, Mahākāśyapa, Bianrong, and the Silent One — those five guiding masters, were they not the first voices that roused the spirit and shook awakening? Xiaoyan and Faguang, were they not the stones from other mountains that polished this jade? Entering Shaolin and paying respects to the First Patriarch — was that not the first cause of the robe and bowl that came from the West? Garrisoning at Caoxi and reviving the Sixth Patriarch — was that not the fruit of the flesh-body taking the seat? The Prince of Shanyin offered two hundred in gold, firmly declined and turned over to Master Guang of Funiu — was it to keep him there, or was it for confirmation? Turning over the gold and departing at once — was it for the old promise made to Master Miaofeng at Mt. Tai, or was it the lion and the hidden dragon, refusing the halter and bridle, to make known the workings of the school? The disciple Fuzheng, reading to this point, joins his palms and praises, saying: Rare indeed is the World-Honored One; the Bodhisattva Inexhaustible Intention, unloosing the pearl-and-jade necklace from his neck, gave it to Avalokiteśvara — that was the yielding of the gold to Master Guang. Prince Nata tore out his bones to return them to his father and flayed his flesh to return it to his mother — that was the taking leave of provision and the declining of support. A mother may cast her son into the river; a son may disregard the care of his parents; yet those with clear eyes call this the ultimate kindness and the ultimate filial piety of a hundred thousand million kalpas.

Seventh month of autumn: hearing that the court was sending someone to Mt. Lao to investigate, the people were all terrified. Before the imperial envoy came, I had earlier gone to the eastern sea to await him, and so it was settled. The envoy said: “The holy will is exceedingly angered; I fear it will be hard to resolve.” I said: “Whether it is hard or easy, all depends on you, the envoy.” At first, because the people of the east had long been without a place of refuge, and because the temple had newly been built, they were all unsettled; now the holy will was angered over the matter of the inner treasury, and the people were all the more alarmed. The envoy then questioned me about the “inner treasury,” and I answered that it was the Sage Mother’s personal provision. The envoy said: “If it is the Sage Mother’s personal provision, then all the more is the crime of having wasted it grave.” Thereupon he memorialized the matter, and the Sage Mother, hearing it, was pleased. Soon after, the envoy took his leave and returned north; I saw him off at the edge of the sea, and he bade me farewell with tears.
O
In Shuntian prefecture, in Ji prefecture, several peaks rise sheer and cut off; it is called Panshan, and also Panlong Mountain. At the summit there is a great rock which moves when it is shaken.

When I was twenty-eight, in the first month of spring I went to visit Wutai, first seeking out the Clear and Cool Record and traveling to trace its sites. Reaching the North Peak, I saw something about Hanshan that was very fine, and so asked where that mountain was; the monk pointed it out, and I delighted in its rare beauty, and silently took it as my name, writing a poem to record it, with the lines “Let others go as they will; / Here for now I shall rest the workings.” Because I could not bear the bitter cold of ice and snow, I could not stay. I went again to the capital and traveled east begging, until I reached Thousand-Image Peak in Panshan, where I saw a monk who did not speak; I too asked nothing, and at once joined him in gathering firewood and drawing water, begging and passing the summer. Sima Wang sent a letter to seek me, saying: “I fear you have become a starveling of the eastern suburbs.” When autumn came, because Ouzhenbo of Lingnan — who several years before had sent me a letter without our ever meeting, and was now a court scholar — was eager to see me, I therefore returned. (One meeting with the Silent Monk; second meeting with Sima Wang Boyu; one meeting with Ouzhenbo of Lingnan, court scholar.)

Zheng, reading the Record of the Famous Mountains, finds that at the Dragon Gate of Wutai there is a mountain which the First Emperor of Qin, when he whipped the stones into a bridge to cross the sea in search of immortals, whipped without moving it, and so it was called Hanshan. Unable to bear the bitter cold of ice and snow — this exactly looks back to the former state of clear cool ice and snow, and to the words with Xuelang about being unable to bear the bitter cold, secretly lodging his meaning there. As for the affair of the Silent Monk, the biography made by Lord Zhuan records it in particular detail. It says: the Master and Miaofeng met again at the Yan capital and agreed to go up to Mt. Wutai together to dwell in stillness. At that time Master Miao had not yet set out to beg the canon for the Prince of Shanyin, and the Master was lodging in the private home of Sima Wang Nanming. After a long while, he went to visit Panshan, and climbing to the summit, beside a stone crag, there was a recluse within, ashen-faced and earth-soiled. The Master bowed, and the man did not respond at all; he asked questions, and the man did not speak. The Master knew him to be no ordinary man, and likewise sat silent with him. After a little, the recluse boiled tea and took only one cup and drank it himself; the Master too took one cup and drank. When the tea was done, the recluse returned the tea-things to their place and sat upright as before; the Master did the same. After a short while, the recluse cooked rice; when the rice was done he set it before the seat, and took only one bowl and one pair of chopsticks and ate; the Master too took one bowl and one pair of chopsticks and ate with him. When the meal was over, again he sat upright as before, and the Master likewise. In the night the recluse went out beyond the crag to walk in meditation, and the Master followed him, only pacing east and west separately. The next day the Master knew to brew tea at tea-time and cook rice at meal-time; the recluse drank and ate with the Master, and at nightfall walked in meditation likewise. So it went for one seven-day period, and only then did the recluse ask the Master: “Where does the benevolent one come from?” The Master said: “From the south.” The recluse said: “What has he come here for?” The Master said: “Especially to seek the recluse.” The recluse said: “The recluse’s face is just so; there is nothing extraordinary.” The Master said: “From the moment I entered the door I had already seen through you.” The recluse laughed and said: “I have dwelt at this crag for more than thirty years, and today for the first time I meet one of the same wind.” He asked the Master to stay, and the Master forgot to return. One night, as the Master walked in meditation, suddenly there came a sound at the crown of his head, a crash like a thunderclap, and mountains, rivers, and the great earth, body, mind, and world, were suddenly and utterly void, a state not to be compared with the ordinary emptiness before one’s eyes. In that emptiness-concentration he remained for about the length of five inches of incense; then he gradually felt body and mind again, gradually felt his feet treading solid ground, and opening his eyes gradually saw mountains, rivers, and the great earth, and all the appearances of environment, return as before. Body and mind were light and quick, and the bliss was beyond all comparison. Lifting his foot as lightly as wind, he returned to the crag, and the recluse said: “Why were you so long at your walking tonight?” The Master told him fully the state he had attained. The recluse said: “That is a state of the form aggregate; it is not the original possession. I have dwelt at this crag for more than thirty years, and except in rain, wind, and snow, every night I walk in meditation in that state; but if one does not cling to it, it will not obscure the original possession.” The Master deeply assented to his words, bowed, and thanked him for the teaching. The Master stayed at Panshan a long while. When Master Miao set out with the canon, he asked Lord Wang where the Master had gone, and the Lord at once sent a messenger up to the summit of Panshan to find him; asking, he was told the Master was in the crag; the messenger saw the Master and told him how eagerly his host Master Miao awaited him. The Master then took his leave of the recluse, and could not bear to part; but what could he do against the old agreement? The recluse saw him off, his tears flying like pearls, and turned back only halfway down the mountain. The Master returned to the capital, and Master Miao and Lord Wang welcomed him, laughing: “Why did you come back so late?” The Master told them fully the karmic occasion at the crag. The Lord said: “If that is so, then our Master’s dwelling on the mountain is already complete.” The Master said: “It is still only a state on the roadside.” The Lord and Master Miao looked at each other and laughed aloud. Ah, such extraordinary manifestations — how many the Patriarch met in his life, beyond the telling of brush and tongue. Even what Lord Zhuan records, the true record of Panshan, runs to six hundred words, and may be called a karmic occasion of the greatest size. The chronicle dismisses it with a single phrase: at Thousand-Image Peak in Panshan a monk did not speak, and they gathered firewood and drew water together, begging and passing the summer — it looks like no more than an ordinary meal of home tea and rice. A wondrous state may be loved, yet he let it go and went on; though it was because of Master Miao’s old agreement, he was also unwilling to be a follower of the Two Vehicles, a man who saves only himself. The merit of Lord Zhuan’s making the biography lies most of all in this one case.

When I was twenty-nine, in spring I traveled in the Western Hills of the capital. At that time the famous men of the age — the two Wangs, the two Wangs, Ouzhenbo of Nanhai — were all gathered at once in the capital, all of them men I had long admired. One day I visited the elder Lord Wang Fengzhou; when we met, because I was young, he made light of me. I bore myself proudly as host and guest, and he at once earnestly instructed me in the method of composing poetry; I stared at him wide-eyed and in the end took my leave without a single word. The Lord was displeased, and spoke of it to his younger brother Linzhou. The next day Linzhou came to visit; at first sight he said: “Last night my elder brother lost one eye.” I said: “Has the Lord got his one eye?” The Lord clasped his hands and said: “The young man has already seen me,” and we laughed aloud together. Returning, he said to his brother: “Elder brother, you have lost to Vimalakīrti.” And so he gave me a poem, with the lines “One may know that Wang Yishao / Yielded to Master Zhi in matters of principle.” One day the second Lord Wang was living with me and we were reading the Zuo Commentary, and he said to me: “Your natural endowment is uncommonly keen, and you have the spirit and bearing of great letters; my elder brother is the literary patriarch of the age — why not take him as your master and make a name for one school?” I laughed and spat, saying: “Save your elder brother’s knee; one day he will bow to this old monk and receive the meaning that came from the West.” The second Lord was much displeased, and going home told the Sima Lord, who said: “It is true; I observe that Master Yin has the bones of the Way, and one day he will enter the chamber of Dahui and Zhongfeng — would he be willing to make so little of himself for the sake of mere letters? I only fear that idle wandering will be his undoing.” One day, seeing a poem I had written on a fan with the second Lord, with the lines “Body and world, the mayfly’s two wings; / Heaven and earth, one hair of a horse,” he showed it to the second Lord and said: “Is this a monk of letters?” Another day he made a special vegetarian feast and invited me and Master Miao to come together. In the midst of the seat, the Lord said to me: “The Chan gate is desolate and fallen, and it is a great grief. I, a young man, hold it earnestly in mind. I observe your bearing: your future attainments will not be small — why waste yourself in idle wandering?” I said: “I, poor in the Way, have come out especially for the sake of the great matter, to visit teachers and friends, and so I go on pilgrimage. Only now I am looking over the men of the age, to be done with the idle thoughts of other days; it is not idle wandering. And I am about to set out.” The Lord said: “That is true. I observe that in these times there is no one fit to be your teacher; and were it not for Miaofeng, you would have no friend.” I said: “Long ago I singled him out from among the crowd and made a pact as fellow practitioners; and so I have come seeking him, and met him here by chance.” The Lord said: “How strange! If you two truly go, I would gladly provide your crossing.” At that time Master Miao had brought back the canon, and so the Sima Lord gave him two sets of travel documents, and also wrote a piece to see me off. One day the Lord hurried me to come, and asked: “Miaofeng has gone; why did you not see him off?” I said: “Let him go slowly.” The Lord said: “I know you do not wish to turn on another’s heel. Yet it is greatly otherwise. The ancients were not ashamed of small matters, but ashamed that their fame should not be spread through the world. I only wish that one day you may accomplish a work of light for the Dharma-gate; why then fuss over so small a matter of going or staying?” I was moved and thanked him, and so resolved to go. At once I went to see Master Miao, who had already loaded the carriage; seeing me arrive, he asked: “Are you going?” I said: “I am going,” and at once mounted the carriage, and without taking leave of a single person I departed. In the eighth month of autumn I crossed the Meng Ferry and saw the place where King Wu reviewed his troops, and there was a poem lamenting it: “A slab of stone, a ruined stele, leaning at the river’s head; / Here in that year the feudal lords once gathered. / The kingly net should reach as far as heaven and earth; / It should flow on unbroken with the Yellow River.” Passing the place where Boyi and Shuqi held back the horses, I lamented: “To cast away the state and leave its glory — the meaning was already deep; / In vain there remains the ancient shrine, its cypresses dense and dark. / The color of Mount Shouyang is as clear as this; / It is still the heart that held back the horses in that year.” Then I entered Shaolin and paid respects to the First Patriarch. At the time the Venerable Master Darun had just entered the temple, and I visited him but did not meet him. Coming out from the mountain, I saw the old city of Luoyang, the Sutra-Burning Terrace, and the White Horse Temple. Then I pursued Master Miao, and in the ninth month reached Hedong, where I met the Prince of Shanyin, and so stayed to pass the winter. At that time the Prefect Lord Chen, with Master Miao and me, was very earnest, and had the Zhongwu Collected Explanations of the Zhao Lun carved; I collated it. Earlier, in the Treatise on the Immutability of Things, the meaning of “the whirlwind lays low the mountains” was not clear to me, and I had long cherished the doubt; now that I came to it, it was still obscure. But when it came to the brahmacharin who left home and returned white-haired, and the neighbor who saw him said, “Is the man of former days still here?” and the brahmacharin said, “I resemble the man of former days, but am not the man of former days” — then I was suddenly and clearly awakened, saying: “Truly, all dharmas are without coming or going.” At once I came down from the meditation platform to bow to the Buddha, and there was no appearance of arising or moving; I lifted the curtain and stood before the steps, and suddenly the wind shook the courtyard trees and flying leaves filled the sky, and there was no appearance of movement at all, and I said: “This is the whirlwind laying low the mountains and yet ever still.” Afterward, going out, I saw the flowing water, and there was no appearance of flowing, and I said: “This is the rivers rushing onward and yet not flowing.” Thereupon the doubt of a lifetime about birth and death melted away like ice. And there was a verse: “Birth and death, day and night; / Water flows, flowers fall. / Today at last I know / The nostrils point downward.” The next day Master Miao saw me and said with delight: “What have you attained?” I said: “Last night I saw two iron oxen by the river fighting and going into the water; to this day there is no news of them.” The Master laughed and said: “I am glad you have the capital to dwell on the mountain.” Before long Shanyin invited the Chan Master Faguang of Niushan to come; I had long admired him, and when we met I was delighted to have him to sit in practice with, and in talk our minds met. I begged instruction, and he opened to me the practice of investigating apart from mind-consciousness and learning beyond the paths of sage and ordinary; I deeply grasped his purport. Whenever I heard the Master discourse, his voice came forth like the sound of a heavenly drum. At that time I knew that one who has awakened and understood the mind-ground indeed speaks and breathes differently, and I deeply submitted to him.
