One day he searched out my poems from my bag and read them, and sighed: “Such fine lines — where did you get them?” Then he laughed: “Fine they are, but that one opening is still not through.” I said: “Is the Master’s one opening through or not?” The Master said: “Thirty years catching dragons and seizing tigers, and today a rabbit runs out of the grass and gives me a start.” I said: “The Master is no dragon-catching, tiger-seizing hand.” The Master picked up his staff and would have struck me; I at once held it fast, and stroking his beard with my hand said: “You call it a rabbit, when it is plainly a frog.” The Master laughed and let it drop. One day the Master said: “You need not go elsewhere; I would have you dwell with me at Old Funiu — that is my hope.” I said: “Judging by the Master’s Dharma-wit and eloquence, he is not less than Dahui; yet in daily life he seems always to have a madman’s manner, humming and mumbling without a moment’s pause. Why is that?” The Master said: “That is my Chan illness. When I first awakened, verses poured from me like a stream, day and night without cease, and I could not stop them myself, and so it became an illness.” I said: “When this illness first arose, how should it have been treated?” The Master said: “When this illness breaks out, if one cannot see through it oneself, one needs a man of great eye and hand to give one a sound beating and make one sleep soundly; on waking it naturally vanishes. My only regret is that I have no poison hand.” The Master knew that I was to leave for Wutai at the new year, and so sent me off with a poem, with the lines “The lion in the clouds, ride it here to see; / The hidden dragon in the cave, let it go and rest.” He asked: “Do you know?” I said: “I do not.” The Master said: “I would have you not grasp at a dead snake.” I nodded. For long there had been no master-craftsman in the Chan way, and only on meeting Master Guang did I know that the school still has its workings. The Prince of Shanyin, learning that my two parents were living, gave me two hundred in gold as provision for their care in old age. I thanked him, saying: “I, poor in the Way, have only begun my pilgrimage and cannot yet save myself; how should I dare involve my two parents?” I firmly declined and turned it over to Master Guang. (Second meeting with Ouzhenbo of Nanhai; one meeting each with the elder Lord Wang Fengzhou and the second Lord Linzhou. Third meeting with Sima Wang Boyu; second meeting with the second Lord Zhongyan; third meeting with Master Miaofeng; one meeting with the Venerable Master Darun; second meeting with the Prince of Shanyin; one meeting with the Prefect Lord Chen; one meeting with Chan Master Faguang. Fengzhou, named Shizhen, a man of Taicang, an official to the rank of Junior Sima; his younger brother Linzhou, named Shimao, an official to the rank of Grand Minister of Ceremonies.)
O

Zheng further notes that the biography made by Lord Zhuan says: Master Miao accompanied the Master to fetch the sutras, and going from Henan they turned into Shanxi and reached Puzhou. The Prince of Shanyin, hearing that the canon was about to arrive, led all the clan lords with banners, canopies, music, and incense and flowers to welcome the sutras into the palace. Master Miao told the Prince: “The Master Cheng-yin of whom I spoke has also come.” The Prince, hearing it, was overjoyed; he first invited the Master to meet him, and only afterward had the canon enshrined. He kept the Master to dwell in the palace, sitting face to face with him at every hour, searching out the cardinal purport of the Śūraṅgama. The Prince asked Master Miao to request the Master to lecture on the Śūraṅgama Sutra; the Master wept and firmly declined, saying: “I came to dwell on the mountain, not to lecture on sutras,” and at once wished to flee. The Prince, knowing his resolve could not be turned, bowed low and pressed him to stay two or three months, and then charged Master Miao to accompany the Master to dwell on the mountain. Alas, the Patriarch had long since known Master Miao at Tianjie, and Master Miao had long since commended the Patriarch to Shanyin; hence meeting all at once, at first sight they were as old friends. The excellent affair of discoursing on the sutras ended when it should. What is called “in the knowing between people, what is valued is knowing the heart” is just this.
Third year, yǐhài ●

When I was thirty, in the first month I went up to Wutai with Master Miao from Hedong, passing through Pingyang, which was the Master’s home country. The Master, poor from youth, had met a year of famine; his father and mother died, and there were no grave-clothes for burial. At this time Shanyin and one or two of the authorities helped him, and I divined a high, open site for their joint burial, and composed the grave-inscription. The Master’s secular surname was Xu, and his family lived in the eastern quarter of Pingyang, being, it is said, descendants of Xu Juju of the Spring and Autumn period. At that time the Prefect Lord Hu, styled Shun’an, a man of Donglai, heard that I had come and lodged outside the city, wishing to see me once but unable; and when I set out, he sent me post-station credentials. I said: “A man of the Way on pilgrimage has his straw sandals; what use has he for these?” After I had gone, he pursued me and only caught up at Lingshi, and we went together to the provincial capital, where he kept me in talk for several days and sent servants to escort me to Mt. Tai. On the fifteenth day of the second month I lodged at the Tayuan Temple; the host Dafang divined me a dwelling at the Dragon Gate of the North Peak, the most secluded and precipitous place of all. On the third day of the third month, from out of a snowdrift I cleared several rooms of an old house and dwelt there. At the time I saw ten thousand mountains of ice and snow, exactly the realm I had long admired; my body and mind were washed clean, as though I had entered the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Before long Master Miao went off to visit the Night Terrace, and I dwelt here alone, raising one thought only; when people came I did not speak, but only looked at them. After a long time I looked on people as on stumps, until I reached the place of not knowing a single character. At first, when the great wind rose from time to time, ten thousand openings roared with rage; the ice melted and the torrents of the ravines rushed and surged like thunder; and in the stillness I heard sounds like a thousand armies and ten thousand horses marching out — I took it as very noisy and disturbing, and so asked Master Miao. The Master said: “The environment arises from the mind; it does not come from outside.” I heard that an ancient said: “Hear the sound of water for thirty years without turning the root of mind, and you will attest Avalokiteśvara’s perfect penetration.” So, at a single-plank bridge over the stream, I sat or stood on it every day; at first the sound of the water was distinct, and after long practice the sound was heard when a thought stirred and not heard when none stirred. One day, sitting on the bridge, I suddenly forgot my body, and the sound was utterly still; from then on all noises were still and no longer disturbed me. What I ate each day was only bran mixed with wild greens, and a soup of a little rice to send it down. At first people gave me three pecks of rice, and after half a year there was still some left. One day, after the gruel, as I walked in meditation, I suddenly stood fixed, and saw neither body nor mind, only one great treasury of light, perfect and profoundly still, like a great perfect mirror, in which mountains, rivers, and the great earth appeared as reflections; and when I came to, all was clear, and though I sought body and mind I could not find them at all. Then I spoke a verse: A single startled thought, and the mad mind rests; Inside and out, sense-roots and dust are all pierced through. Turning over, I shatter the great empty space; The myriad forms, dense and manifold, arise and cease with it. From then on, inside and out were utterly clear, and sounds, forms, and appearances no longer obstructed me; all my former doubts dissolved at once. When I looked at my cooking-pot, it had already grown dusty, and because I was alone with no companion, I did not know how long it had been. That summer Xuelang came north and made a point of seeing me; when he reached Mt. Tai and sat in my room, he could not keep back his grief, and after two nights he took his leave. In winter I built a plank hut to dwell in. (Fourth meeting with Master Miaofeng; third meeting with the Prince of Shanyin; one meeting each with Hu Shun’an, Prefect of Pingyang, and the host Dafang; fourth meeting with Xuelang. Shun’an is the later Grand Censor Hu.)

Zheng, at the Zongjing Hall of the Jingci Temple, heard from the Patriarch’s eminent disciples Zhiwei, Xuzhong, and Xiuliu, the three Masters, that the Great Master and Master Miao were at the Dragon Gate of Mt. Tai, sitting on the Dragon-Flipping Stone listening to the boiling spring; for a whole year, until the sound of the spring was unbroken and yet unheard, he was able to enter concentration. Master Miao, knowing the Great Master was about to enter concentration, made a separate hut at the wooden-tile beam; and when the Great Master entered concentration, no one knew how many days passed before he came out. From this one knows that the dust on the cooking-pot was the affair of his solitary dwelling in concentration. So one knows that without a man of awakening, none can enter concentration; and without a man of austerities, none can awaken. The ancient venerable ones said that great awakening comes eighteen times over, and small awakenings beyond counting. To say that one awakening means no further awakening is a great error. In those years the vow-power took ice and snow and coolness as its contemplation; here the karmic occasion came to fulfillment, and through ice and snow and coolness he gained power. This is what is meant by the fuel exhausted and the fire passed on, what is meant by the transmission of the lamp. The patch-robed monks of today who transmit the lamp are transmitting only the fuel.
O

A few words in direct record of Gong still carry the meaning of that year’s pleading against the bitter cold, never forgetting the bond of shared birth and friendship. Gong’s biography relates that on that day he sought out where the Master Han was, and passing Song and Shao and Funiu, went up to the Dragon Gate of Wutai and found him in the drifts of ice and snow, with his waist-wallet and his bowl of rice, vowing to share life and death. The Master said to him: “Each person has his own resolve, and each his own karmic occasion. Your karmic occasion lies in practicing the Dharma to continue the wisdom-life; you should not grow old in withered stillness. This Way has long been buried in Jiangnan; you should carry on the Dharma-seat of your own master Wuji, shoulder the entrustment, and be the eye for gods and humans, so as not to fail the karmic occasion of leaving the world.” Gong nodded his assent, and so they parted with grave ceremony. Afterward he traveled with his staff through the several commanderies of the Three Wu, and taught the Dharma for thirty years, surrounded by great assemblies, so that the lecture seats of the southeast flourished exceedingly.
O

In Wutai county of Taiyuan prefecture, Shanxi, there is Mount Wutai, whose five peaks rise above the clouds; their tops and backs can all be climbed, and so they are called terraces. It is the dwelling of Mañjuśrī, and is called the Clear and Cool Mountain. Indeed, the Patriarch’s karmic occasion of coolness and ice and snow ran from first to last. That the Tathagata cultivated the Way in the Snow Mountains, and that the patriarchs stood in the snow to receive the transmission — now I believe it.
Fourth year, bǐngzǐ ●

When I was thirty-one, after my awakening, having no one to ask for increase, I opened the Śūraṅgama to seal and confirm it. At first I had never heard this sutra expounded and did not understand its meaning at all, so now I simply illumined it with direct perception. If a thought of mind-consciousness stirred even slightly, I allowed no deliberation. So for eight months, and the purport of the whole sutra was clear beyond doubt. In the third month of spring Master Lianchi visited Wutai and came to call; he stayed ten days, and by night we talked heart to heart with deep accord. In the seventh month of autumn Lord Hu, Prefect of Pingyang, transferred to the Yanping military commission, came into the mountains to visit me; in the quiet room we ate only oats

and wild-herb pickles. At that time it was just then fiercely hot, and his outriders went into the mountain ravine and broke ice to chew; the Lord saw it and said: “This is another world; since I came here, my worldly thoughts have been as cool as this ice.” In the tenth month of winter that year the host of the Tayuan Temple, Dafang, was falsely accused and sued before the circuit office, and it was proposed to send him into exile and return him to lay life, so that the monastery was all but ruined. At that time Master Chekong of Mount Lu came and dwelt with me, and happening to see this affair, found it too bitter. I said: “No harm,” and went myself to Lord Hu, going through heavy snow. When we met, Lord Hu said with delight: “I was just thinking how the heavy snow in the mountains could not be borne, and had written a letter and was about to send someone to welcome you; your coming now is truly a response to my feeling.” Yet in the end he released the host, and the sanctuary was preserved whole. He firmly kept me to pass the winter, questioning the Way morning and evening, and I spoke for him the Xuyan. At that time Lord Gao, the Regional Commander, had been moved to garrison Dai commandery, and hearing I was in the office, he said to Lord Hu: “My family has a garden pavilion with many inscriptions and poems; I would seek one poem from a man of high attainment.” Lord Hu agreed, and spoke to me of it. I said: “There is not a single character in my breast; how can I make a poem?” and firmly refused. Lord Gao pressed again and again, and Lord Hu had no way out and begged me hard; so he took collections of ancient and modern poems and set them on the desk to stir my thoughts. I happened to open one, and while I was framing a thought, suddenly the mechanism stirred, and phrases came swift and fast, not to be held back. When Lord Hu came back from the hall, I had already set down twenty or thirty pieces. I suddenly became aware and said: “This is the demon of literary habit,” and at once stopped, taking only one piece to put off the matter, not daring to send out the rest. Yet the mechanism could not be stopped, and before I knew it all the poetry, books, and rhapsodies I had studied before, every one that had ever entered my eyes, appeared at once before me and filled the whole of space, so that even if my whole body were a mouth I could not utter it, and I no longer knew what my own body and mind were. Silently I looked at myself, in a state as if about to fly up, and there was nothing to be done. The next day, after Lord Hu had seen Lord Gao off, I thought alone: “This is exactly what Chan Master Faguang called the Chan illness. Now that I am in the midst of it, who can cure it for me? There is no other way; only sleep can dissolve it. If I can sleep peacefully, that will be my good fortune.” So I shut the door and forced myself to lie down. At first I could not at all; after a long while, I suddenly sat forgetting, as in sleep; the boy knocked at the door and it did not open, and when he pounded on it there was no answer. Lord Hu returned and urgently asked after me; learning this, he had the window broken and entered, and saw me sitting upright wrapped in my robe, and called me with no answer, and shook me without moving me. Earlier, in the study, a Buddha had been enshrined, and on the offering table there was a small bell. Lord Hu picked it up and asked: “What is this used for?” I had said: “When a monk of the Western Regions enters concentration and cannot awake, one sounds this and he wakes — I once heard such a saying.” The Lord suddenly remembered it and said: “Has the Master entered concentration?” and quickly took the bell and sounded it at my ear several dozen times; then I gradually and faintly came to, and opening my eyes and looking around, did not know where my body was. The Lord said: “I went away, and the Master at once shut the door and sat; it is now five days. How is it with you?” I said: “I do not know; it was only one breath.” When I had spoken, I sat silent and examined closely, and in the end did not know what place this was, nor how I had entered it. Then I looked back on the mountain, and on all my former pilgrimage, and each thing was a matter of dream, sought and not found. And all that former clamor that filled the sky was like rain scattered and clouds gathered up, the vast sky as if washed, all still and without a trace of image. Mind empty and environment still, its joy beyond all comparison. Then I said: “When stillness is utmost, light penetrates; / In still illumination, the void is contained. / Turning back to look upon the world, / It is like a matter in a dream” — the Buddha’s words truly did not deceive me. I planned to return to the mountain at the new year, and so told Lord Hu that the forests of Mt. Tai were being bitterly cut by wicked merchants, and that the bodhisattva’s sanctuary would soon be bare and without a blade of grass. The Lord prepared a memorial requesting a strict prohibition. After that, when the state built and repaired the various monasteries, they all relied on this protected timber; otherwise there would have been no wood to take. (One meeting with Master Lianchi; second meetings with Lord Hu Shun’an and Dafang; one meeting each with Master Chekong and Lord Gao, the Regional Commander.)

Zheng has heard that the First Patriarch sealed the mind with the four fascicles of the Laṅkāvatāra, and now the Patriarch Hanshan sealed the mind with the whole of the Śūraṅgama; the sage before and the sage after, their measure is one. Master Lianchi was a man of Renhe in Hangzhou, of the Shen clan, a great family, and a noted scholar of the county school. At thirty-two he went to the Venerable Tianli and had his head shaved, receiving the Dharma-name Zhuhong and the style Fohui. He then received full ordination from the Vinaya Master Wuchen Yu. Because the mourning for his mother was not yet ended, he carried her wooden tablet with him as he traveled, and wherever he dwelt he made offering, and at every meal he made offering. He visited teachers everywhere: going north to Wutai, he moved Mañjuśrī to emit light; reaching Funiu, he trained in the demon-marrow with the assembly; entering the capital, he consulted the two great elders Bianrong and Xiaoyan, and from both received opening. Passing through Dongchang, he suddenly had an awakening and made a verse: “The matter of twenty years ago was doubtful; / Three thousand li away, what strange encounter. / Burning incense, casting spears — all a dream; / Demon and Buddha strive in vain over right and wrong.” Returning south, he sat five Chan periods, and to the end never knew the name of the man on the neighbouring seat. In xīnwèi of Longqing he begged food at Fancun, and gradually brought the excellent karmic occasion of Yunqi to fulfillment, opening wide the one gate of the Pure Land and embracing all three capacities to the end. His works are the Commentary on the Amitābha Sutra and Admonitions to Advance Through the Chan Gate; the Patriarch Hanshan praised these two works as revealing the dual cultivation of Chan and Pure Land, both issuing from the one mind, and as exceedingly subtle in their power to transform. From his leaving the world to its end there was nothing at all to criticize; he may be called one who in the Dharma-gate attained the Buddha’s whole substance and great function. In dīngsì, when I traveled east, I carried a text from Nanyue to make sacrifice, and complying with the request of his black- and white-robed disciples, composed his stupa-inscription, and also wrote seven portrait praises. The disciples of Yunqi painted a portrait of the Patriarch and left it hanging in the mountains, and he himself made a praise for it — all this was because of the karmic occasion of that one night’s heart-to-heart talk when he visited Mt. Tai in bǐngzǐ. Master Chekong first dwelt at Huanglong Pool on Mount Kuang; this time he came to dwell with me at the Dragon Gate, from the tenth month of winter to the fourth month of spring, when he returned to Mount Kuang, lodging at Mt. Tai for more than half a year. This was because the Patriarch was kept by Lord Hu of Yanping, and Master Che acted for him in the affairs about the cooking-pot. Earlier I heard that the false accusation of Dafang was just the doing of the wicked timber merchants who cut wood in the mountains, and that the various mountain communities begged the Patriarch to go and settle it with Lord Hu. Thus he began by settling Dafang’s difficulty and ended by prohibiting the cutting of Mt. Tai’s timber, and for a time all the mountain communities were moved by it — truly the non-duality of worldly dharma and Buddha-dharma. The Xuyan spoken in Lord Hu’s hall was set down from the mouth and from the hand, and was completed in a full month. Lord Hu had men record it into fascicles and at once gave it to the printer, asking that it be named Xuyan and sent out; it was in truth his first work. Its structure of chapters and sentences somewhat imitates the Laozi, but its cardinal purport is that the three teachings are one. Fourteen years later, at Mt. Lao, he wrote the Essay on the Influence of Laozi and Zhuangzi, so that the earlier and later works mutually illumine each other. I respectfully record three passages of the Xuyan to give an example of the rest. It says: He who is dense in affairs is sparse in mind; he who is dense in mind is penetrating in affairs. Hence the denser the affairs, the sparser the mind; the denser the mind, the more penetrating the affairs. One whose mind is not washed can have no way to be dense — this is why the sage values washing the mind and withdrawing to hide in the secret. It also says: The eye contains heaven and earth, yet a speck of dust can rob it of its clarity. The mind embraces the great void, yet a single thought can block its vastness. From this one knows that a single thought is the root of birth and death and the source of calamity and disaster; hence knowing the subtle and knowing the incipient, the sage keeps his guard. It also says: When a thought exists, things exist; when the mind is empty, dharmas are empty. Therefore if a thought is melted away, one is at ease in every karmic occasion; if the mind is like a round mirror, coming and going are ever at leisure. One who excels in this does not go beyond the ordinary, yet sits securely in the wondrous realm. Indeed the way of letters and the way of Chan are always one way; the demon of letters and the demon of Chan are always one demon. When the Way is a thousand feet high, the demon is a thousand feet high. Hence it is said: when the demon comes and the Buddha comes, if the Chan illness has not gone, then flying up or sitting in forgetting — how can one enter concentration? Do those in this world who style themselves men of Chan concentration understand this case of the small bell? Hu Shun’an, deep in karmic bond and earnest in feeling, for no reason stirred and asked about the small bell, and in the turning of an eye the subtle omen was fulfilled — how could this be anything a man can contrive? When I attended at the Zongjing Hall, what I saw morning and evening was this: when he sat, his legs were crossed; when he closed his eyes he entered concentration, when he opened them he came out of it; his two eyes would open like lightning, and he would answer a thousand words like an echo. That five-day concentration of his seems now no more than the affair of first entering the gate.

The transmission of Elder Zhuan records that in that year snow fell in heavy flurries for ten full days, and the snow of every terrace summit was swept into one pile, burying the hermitage of the Dragon Gate to a depth of more than a hundred feet. The Master and Master Che shut their doors and sat motionless, stirring up the fire but once a day to warm their tea and rice. The congregations of North Terrace, White Horse Temple, and Central Terrace, two or three hundred souls in all, devoted themselves to taking up hoes, mattocks, baskets, and brooms, and lowered probing poles down the terrace heights to seek the road to the Dragon Gate. They probed and dug as they came, going and returning; the congregation labored so bravely that only after two full days of probing did they at last reach the hermitage. They shouted for joy, entered the door, and all declared: 'That after such a calamity amid these mountains a fire should still stand — this is the protection of the Buddhas and of Heaven.' The Master and Master Che gave thanks, then said: 'Yet one must pass through it before one gains it.' Thereupon they melted snow into a warm broth and joyfully served the whole congregation. The next day the mountain monasteries, hearing that the two masters were safe, came bearing rice, flour, fruit, and sweetmeats until there was scarcely room to set a foot. Later it was also heard that, dwelling once together with Master Miao, he too had met this great snow and dissolved it by entering samādhi. Snow and ice of the Dragon Gate came to be regarded as nothing out of the ordinary, and so the chronicle for the most part does not record them.
The fifth year, dīngchǒu ●

At thirty-two years of age, in spring, I returned from Yanmen. Because I reflected that I could never repay the boundless kindness of my parents, and also because I felt myself beset by many obstacles in the Dharma, I read the Vow Text of Master Si of Nanyue and resolved to pierce my tongue, to mix my blood with gold-dust, and to write out one copy of the Avatamsaka Sūtra — above, to bind the excellent karmic conditions with prajñā; below, to repay the boundless kindness of my parents — and in this year the project first sprang up. Earlier, the Compassionate Sage Mother, for the protection of the state, had chosen monks to chant sūtras, and I had presumptuously been set down among them. When now the emperor learned of the sūtra-copying, he straightway bestowed gold and paper to assist it. In the fourth month of the next year the copying was begun. At that time Master Chekong returned to Mount Kuang, and I composed ten poems to see him off. (The Compassionate Sage Mother is the Empress Dowager Li — a first appearance. Master Chekong — a second appearance.)

[Piercing the tongue and writing the Avatamsaka Sūtra in blood and gold] Piercing the tongue to draw blood, and blending it with gold-dust, to write out one Avatamsaka Sūtra. Master Yinguang says: 'When Master Hanshan copied the sūtra, it was the Empress Dowager who supplied the paper and the gold. The paper for gold writing must be blue for it to show; on white paper it does not show.
...as when Hanshan, at the Miaode Nunnery on Wutai, pierced his tongue, ground gold with his blood, and wrote out the Avatamsaka Sūtra.' (From the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang
Letter in Reply to Master Hongyi, No. 1)

Zheng's note: That he wrote the Avatamsaka in blood is precisely what later is spoken of when, sharing Master Miao's vow, he established the unhindered assembly and placed the sūtra in the pagoda treasury. The vow had not yet been written when a spiritual response was already felt. The 'the emperor heard and bestowed gold and paper' refers to the fact that, because his name had been placed on the roster of sūtra-chanters, the Sage Mother heard of it and bestowed it — it does not mean the Wanli emperor. The bestowing of the writing gold and paper for the Bao'en Temple, and this matter, are the beginning of the Sage Mother's karmic conditions emerging into the world.

The Compassionate Sage, Empress Dowager Li, was the Wanli emperor's legal mother. She believed in the Buddha with great ardor and gave alms with great fullness, and the people of the capital called her the Old Lady of the Buddha and the Taoists.
The sixth year, wùyín ●

At thirty-three years of age, I bent my whole mind to copying the sūtra; whether the stroke was large or small, with each falling brush I uttered a recitation of the Buddha's name. Whatever monks or laymen from the roaming mountains came, I always had the attendant announce them. Though my hand never ceased from the writing, yet I did not fail in responding to them; whoever came to ask after me I would exchange a few words with. The eminent and my old friends I would invite to take a seat on the meditation couch, converse face to face without missing anything, and still without hindering the writing; when they compared against the master copy on the table, not one stroke was misplaced. Each day I was as always, without the slightest trace of agitation. The old masters of the neighboring districts, secretly thinking it strange, one day led a crowd to test me, deliberately making a disturbance; and when the writing was done and read through, they truly believed. They asked Master Miao, 'How can Master Yin be capable of this?' Master Miao said, 'My friend has but entered this samādhi until it is thoroughly ripe.' Since I took to the mountains, up to the copying of the sūtra, I repeatedly had auspicious dreams. On the first night I dreamed I entered the Vajra Grotto, with the Great Prajñā Monastery beside the stone gate; when I went in I found it vast as empty space, its halls and towers solemn and lovely beyond compare. In the main hall there was only a great couch, and I saw Master Qingliang [Chengguan] leaning reclined upon it, with Master Miao standing in attendance on the left. I hurried to bow, took my place on the right, and heard the Master give instruction: first he set forth the vision of the perfect and interpenetrating realm of the dharmadhātu — that Buddha-lands enter into one another, that lord and retinue intermingle, in the motion of coming and going without movement. Even as he spoke, that realm appeared before my eyes. I knew of myself that body and mind were interpenetrating and at ease. When the instruction ended, Master Miao asked, 'What realm is this?' The Master smiled and said, 'A realm of no realm.' When I awoke, I saw that mind and realm had fused together, with no further doubt or obstruction. On another night I dreamed that I trod in the void and ascended, higher and higher, with no limit above; then I fell, and saw that the ten directions were utterly devoid of anything — only the ground was level as a mirror, clear as lapis lazuli. Looking far off I saw only a vast tower, no smaller than the sky. Within it were gathered all the people and affairs of the world — down to the meanest traffic of the market-streets — all contained within it, and none going beyond. In the tower a high seat was set, of a purple-gold flame-color, and to my mind it was the adamant jewel throne. The tower was so solemn and exquisite as to be beyond thought. I was overjoyed and wished to draw near, but thought within myself, 'How, within the realm of purity and coolness, can there be this defilement?' The instant this thought arose, the tower grew distant. Then I thought again, 'Purity and defilement are but born of my own mind,' and the tower drew near. Presently I saw, arrayed before the seat, a congregation of monks, tallest of body and most dignified beyond compare. Suddenly a monk came forth from behind the seat, holding an opened scroll of sūtra, and handed it me, saying, 'The Master has just declared this sūtra and specially sends word to bestow it on you.' I received it, unrolled it, and saw it was written in gold in Sanskrit characters, which I could not read, so I tucked it away; then I asked who the Master was. He said, 'Maitreya.' I rejoiced, and followed the monk upward until I reached the stair of the tower, where I closed my eyes, gathered my thoughts, and stood. Suddenly I heard the sound of a chime; I opened my eyes and saw that Maitreya had already taken his seat. I straightway gazed in reverence, and looking up beheld his face, dazzling with purple-gold radiance, such as nothing in the world could match. When the bowing was done, I thought, 'Now he has spoken for my sake, so I am the one addressed.' Then I knelt long, unrolled the scroll, and heard him say: 'Discrimination is consciousness-knowledge; non-discrimination is prajñā. Through consciousness one is defiled; through prajñā one is pure. In defilement there is birth and death; in purity there is no Buddha.' At that point body and mind suddenly became void; I only heard within the sky a sound, distinctly and clearly — and when I awoke, the words seemed still ringing in my ears. From this, the distinction between consciousness and prajñā was clear in my heart and eyes, and I knew that where I had been was the Tuṣita heaven, the tower of Maitreya Buddha. On yet another night I dreamed a monk came to tell me that on the summit of North Terrace Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva was preparing a bath and inviting me. I went with him and entered a vast, pure, and bright hall, filled with fragrance. The attendants were all Indian monks; they led me to the bath-house, where I undressed and entered the pool, and saw that one person was already in it. On looking, it was a woman. My mind revolted and I would not enter, but the one in the pool deliberately expanded her form, showing her to be a man. Then I went in and bathed with him. He scooped water in his hand to wash me, pouring it over me from the head down into my very viscera, as if scraping out a tub of flesh; the five organs were washed clean one by one, leaving only a skin like a cage of lapis lazuli, wholly translucent. Then the one in the pool called for tea, and I saw an Indian monk holding half a skull, split like a melon; looking at it, the marrow was dripping wet, and my mind revolted at it. The monk then picked this out with his finger and showed it me, saying, 'Is this not unclean?' and put it in his mouth and ate it. Thus he scooped and ate; it was sweet as honey. When the brain was all eaten there remained only blood and water, and the one in the pool said, 'Give it to him.' The monk then handed it to me, and I took it and drank, and its taste was like sweet dew. I drank it down, and it went through the pores of my whole body, trickling out from every one. When the drinking was done the Indian monk rubbed my back, and with a great slap of his palm I woke. My whole body was drenched in sweat like water, and my viscera were wholly transparent. From then on body and mind were as if washed clean, in a lightness beyond words. Dreams such as these were more often auspicious than not. In sum, they were all my communing with the saints — and once, hearing the Buddha's words that one in such a state has many good dreams, I believed it. (Master Miaofeng — a fifth appearance.)

Zheng, serving by his side in attendance, had often seen the works of the Hanshan Master's calligraphy, both regular and running, of twin excellence, all grounded in the standards of the two Wangs, passing in and out with transformation. While copying the Avatamsaka in blood, he did not stop his brush, and did not refuse visitors; every stroke he wrote was accompanied by a recitation of the Buddha's name; though a worthy sat in converse, still the writing did not stop. Comparing against the master copy on the table, not one character was misplaced. Without a great samādhi and great spiritual power, how could there be not the slightest misplacement? If I lay out the great dream-samādhi he tells: in one dream he saw Master Qingliang face to face, in the Vajra Grotto, leaning on the couch to bestow the prophecy, and straightway the realm came present before him, body and mind without obstruction. In each of these he never once forgot Qingliang, never forgot the karmic bond with Master Miao. Again he dreamed of going to the Tuṣita heaven, to Maitreya's tower, where he saw in person the solemn jewel throne, and Maitreya Buddha commanded a monk to bestow the sūtra; on mounting the seat he saw before him and heard the teaching on defilement and purity, clear in his ears, and so gained the distinction of consciousness and prajñā, transparent in heart and eye. A third dream took him in person to the bath that Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva prepared on the summit of North Terrace — a foul woman, expanding to man — which is but the Hanshan Master's youth-body manifesting, one mind unconfused, originally pure, with not the slightest taint, so that he could enter the sea of fragrant water and shed his skin and change his bone. Again there appeared in strange mutation the good and the foul, the pure and the defiled, the startled loathing and the clinging love — all manner of forms wholly transformed, and all five colors without a master. In the end it was like Fotucheng, who before the water split open his breast and thoroughly washed his stomach and intestines, his body translucent as lapis lazuli. In the end it was like Huangbo and Linji, one blow leaving a mark, one slap drawing blood. In the end it was like Confucius who saw in person King Wen and Duke Zhou, in length and shortness, black and white. With the eyes shut or open, there is nothing that is not a true dream. Clear in his own person, his will and spirit like spirit — the true is the dream-true, the dream is the true-dream; therefore it is said the perfect man has no dreams. Even so, had he not abandoned body and life, sinking deep into that pile of snow and ice, buried alive for six years, and died the great death several times over — how could he come alive out of death, thrust his head from the great dream, wrap heaven and earth, blaze through ancient and modern, and become a measureless great man? And if he had not, today in this body of flesh, sitting upright, manifesting at Caoxi, sealing Qingliang in the north and serving Master Lü in the south, from the head of Dayu ridge where the robe and bowl were seized, dying and living again, three turns and nine bends, renewing two temples — then in the Hanshan Dharma-cloud, on the tip of a single hair was raised the jewel-king's realm; and on the day he took up pen and paper to narrate his own chronicle, he would have been no more than a single hard-working old man of the world, turning his heart to the honored elders. The Chan monks of all quarters, who saw the record of the three dreams during his lifetime, must surely laugh at it as idle talk; those who heard of the three dreams after his death will even revile it as a realm of demons. Only the Hanshan Master himself had confidence to the full; and in all the world, now and hereafter, there is not one who can attain equal confidence. Now I know that Maitreya's bestowal of the scroll wholly certifies the coming age to be as the beginningless age; and that Mañjuśrī's bath was to bathe the body of skin and flesh into the body of the adamantine stage. As Zheng marshals his commentary to this point, in a daze he dreams his way into Caoxi; and within the unspeakable, the unspeakable, the inconceivable, he folds his palms and says: 'Rare is the World-Honored One.'
The seventh year, jǐmǎo ●

At thirty-four years of age: in autumn of that year, the building of the Great Compassionate Longevity Temple in the capital was completed. Originally the Sage Mother, to offer the merits to the late emperor and to protect the holy person of the sovereign, wished to rebuild the Sarira Jewel Pagoda at Taya Temple on Wutai. She commanded the ministers, but because the mountain was so far from the capital, they chose an auspicious site near the city and built the Great Compassionate Longevity Temple there. When the works were done and the report returned, the Sage Mother felt that the Wutai vow was still unfulfilled, so she commanded the emperor still to send eunuchs, with three thousand workmen, to the mountain to build. At this time the court had just begun its Buddhist works, and the eunuchs were sent out for the first time; I feared the works could not be completed, and that the Dharma-gate would suffer. At that time I did all in my power to mediate between them, so that from first to last all went well. (The Sage Mother — a third appearance. The late emperor, Longqing — a first appearance. The emperor, Wanli — a first appearance.)

Zheng once, following the crowd, went to the Great Compassionate Longevity Temple built by the Compassionate Sage, Empress Dowager Li, arriving by way of the Tongzhou water route to Zhangjiawan, and entered the temple. It is fifteen li south of Tongzhou city and twenty-five li north to the Haidai Gate of the capital. The locals say the place had long been a ruined shrine, popularly called the Horse House Temple; the Old Lady of the Buddha and the Taoists, on its old site, renewed it in grand style and conferred on it the title of Great Compassionate Longevity. In front they invited the Hanshan Master, and behind they invited Master Daguan, and both dwelt in this temple. The chronicle records in large letters that in the autumn of this year the capital's Great Compassionate Longevity Temple was completed — thus we see that the karmic conditions of his entering the capital to spread the Dharma and bring calamity upon himself began here. Truly one who has attained the Dharma holds a life hanging by a thread; for first he had risen up in righteousness — such is the style of the Spring and Autumn annals.
The eighth year, gēngchén ●

At thirty-five years of age: in that year a special edict ordered a survey of lands and grain throughout the empire, not sparing a single inch. Wutai had never been entered in the register, but a villain of the county, to deceive and conceal, wished to transfer a levy of five hundred measures of grain onto Wutai, repeatedly sending documents to inspect and report the land; and throughout all the mountains' monasteries and hermitages, there was not a single person who could be at ease — from this the mountain became a fox's den. The elders of the mountains told me of it, and I said, 'Be at peace; let the masters have no worry, and I will slowly manage it.' So I bent my effort and found ways and means, laying the matter before the authorities, and in the end won exemption from the survey, without adding so much as a measure. The Wutai sanctuary was thereby preserved entire.
Zheng knows that conditioned meritorious deeds, if regarded as unconditioned meritorious deeds, are naturally accomplished.
The ninth year, xīnsì ●

At thirty-six years of age, I established the unhindered assembly. At first Master Miao had also pierced his blood and written the Avatamsaka Sūtra, sharing with me the vow to build a perfect sanctuary, called the unhindered assembly. Master Miao begged alms, and money and grain were gathered; from the capital were invited of great virtuous and famous monks five hundred. All the arrangements for the sanctuary were complete, when it happened that the emperor issued an edict praying for an heir, sending officials to Wudang; and the Sage Mother sent officials to Wutai, to the very temple. I thought that all the Buddhist rites performed by monks are but to pray for the state and secretly assist the imperial destiny. Now that the prayer for an heir was the very root of the state, nothing was greater. I wished to merge all the work prepared for the sanctuary into the single matter of praying for an heir, and not to do it for the sake of my own little reputation. Master Miao could not understand; and the envoy sent by the emperor also did not understand the matter, but only sought to curry favor. I strongly disagreed and contended against them, opposing them, yet in the end my counsel was followed. But the reputation of opposing the eunuch envoy also got abroad. Presently, when the southern seditious men stirred up trouble in Jiangnan, those who envied me wished to use it to wound me and break up the sanctuary. Yet because the matter was billed as praying for an heir for the state, it was preserved unharmed from first to last. That year the pagoda was completed, and I straightway placed the gold-written Avatamsaka Sūtra in its treasury, with a single scroll of vow-text. I myself begged alms to make the Avatamsaka world revolving-treasure-reel, to be used on setting up the sanctuary; and all the offerings, vessels, utensils, and provisions — everything needed. Master Miao, in the capital, seemed not to know of it; all was managed by me alone, for ninety days and ninety nights without closing my eyes. When the tenth month came, Master Miao led the more than five hundred monks he had invited, all assembled in a single day, a thousand or more within and without; and their lodging, offerings, tea and rice were all in order, without confusion, and no one knew whence it came — the onlookers were all astonished. At the very start was opened a water-land ceremony of seven days and nights; and during those seven days I ate not a single grain, only drinking water. Yet I did not fail in any duty, offering to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, changing five hundred tables of offerings each day, all in due order without loss, and no one knew whence they came. The onlookers thought it a divine operation; I myself knew it was the aid of the Buddhas' power. (The Sage Mother — a third appearance; the emperor — a second appearance; the heir apparent, Taichang — a first appearance; Master Miaofeng — a sixth appearance.)

Zheng was born in the Shenzong reign and knows that the matter of contending for the heir apparent was the greatest. What the Hanshan Master's appearance in the world most concerned was that the heir-apparent matter came first: his merit lay in being the first to advocate it, and in the princes who settled the succession, in order to plan for the spirit of the state, and not in attaching themselves to the later debates over the succession as a means to open the gate of factional calamity. The blood-written sūtra, the unhindered assembly, are the first cause of the prayer for an heir. The emperor sent eunuchs to Wudang, secretly to pray for an heir for Consort Zheng — and the prayer was to the Taoists. The Sage Mother sent eunuchs to Wutai, secretly to pray for an heir for the Consort Wang — and the prayer was to the monks. Each had their own faith and their own petition. The eunuch, spying the emperor's intent and fearing the unpredictable, therefore set his heart on currying favor, and grew of two minds toward the Sage Mother's command, unwilling to merge the blood-completed and unhindered sanctuary that he and Master Miao had made with the prayer for an heir, so as to display a great feat. For the unhindered assembly had been gathered by alms, and had no bearing on the prayer for an heir; and the prayer for an heir was sent within, apart from the unhindered assembly. Thus Master Miao could not understand, so he was looking at the Buddhist level; the Hanshan Master contended with all his strength, fixing his heart on the foundation of the state. The excellent karmic conditions happened to gather, and his single-minded sincerity reached Heaven. Managing alone, he went ninety days and nights without closing his eyes. The whole company of monks assembled, and for seven days he drank water and ate no grain. The minutest tasks were done as by ghosts, and the great offerings operated as by spirits. Without the radiance of samādhi, how could he have drawn the aid of the Buddhas' power so abundantly? Afterwards, when the calamity arose at Mt. Lao, the emperor's words said, 'All the court is for the monks; I alone am for the Taoists' — this distantly binds up the Wudang-Wutai case.
The tenth year, rénwǔ ●

At thirty-seven years of age: in the spring of that year I expounded the Xuántán of the Avatamsaka; for a hundred days the resident monks and the gathered laity from all quarters, day by day not fewer than ten thousand people, ate at one meal as if sitting in a single hall, without mixing or confusion, without a sound of a herald or a knock at the door. All was disposed by me alone, with no one else to give orders, and the wise could not tell how it was done. So of my whole life's energy, here it was nearly exhausted. When the assembly ended I examined what remained in the storehouse — all manner of money and grain, some ten thousand and more — and sealed and consigned it all to the abbot of the temple, to be the enduring property. Then Master Miao and I, with a single bowl, went off light and free. Master Miao went to Luya; I, being ill, went to the Zhangshi Cliff at Zhending to recuperate. I composed a poem containing the lines, 'Sheer cliffs propped against the sky must bar the sun / On the broken cliff there is no road, only a flying ladder.' In the eighth month of that year the crown prince was born, and I went again to the Zhongfeng Temple west of the capital, writing a preface to the re-engraved Zhongfeng Collected Records, and passed the winter in a water-fasting at a stone chamber. (Master Miaofeng — a seventh appearance; the crown prince, Taichang — a second appearance.)

Zheng reckons: in the tenth month of xīnsì, because of praying for the imperial heir, the great unhindered sanctuary was built at the Great Pagoda Temple on Wutai, completing the merits of seven days and nights; and fittingly, in the eighth month of the following year, rénwǔ, the palace concubine Consort Wang bore the heir Taichang. The chronicle writes in large letters: 'In the eighth month of that year the crown prince was born.' Before the heir was yet born, he already wrote of the heir; when the heir had not yet been fixed as crown prince, he wrote straight out 'crown prince' — great indeed is the style of the Spring and Autumn annals! Reckoning the ten months of a human gestation, the immaculate certainty of it plainly shows that this was the Buddha's and the patriarchs' miraculous incarnation and birth. Thus the great treasure was at last mounted, and his benevolence was suddenly spread; though the state's fortune was near its end and the reign changed, it did not perish — and this was well so. Consort Wang, after the succession was fixed, was made Noble Consort Gong, and died in the thirty-seventh year. When Guangzong ascended the throne, she was posthumously titled Empress Xiaojing. At her death it was kept secret and not reported abroad, and only after four days, at the petition of the ministers, was it announced. At that time the envoy Shen Youze submitted a memorial asking for increased rites, but it was not answered. The affairs of the inner palace are hard to speak of. From this, Master Miao parted from the Hanshan Master; two years later they went together to the capital to receive the imperial bounty, and it seems they never saw each other again. The Hanshan Master, having completed eight years passing in and out of Wutai, now went off: a great cultivation, a great realization, a great sanctuary, a great working of his powers, a great spiritual response, sealing up a handful of treasury and ten-thousand-some of money and grain, and with a single bowl went lightly off. Before this, the Dragon Gate of Wutai made a great conclusion, a great scattering, 'Sheer cliffs propped against the sky must bar the sun / On the broken cliff there is no road, only a flying ladder.' After this, Mt. Lao and Caoxi made a great prophecy, a great transformation. The clear-eyed can themselves grasp it.
Here ends the matter of the ascetic practice and Tao-completion at Wutai.
The eleventh year, guīwèi ●

At thirty-eight years of age, in the first month of spring, the water-fast was finished. Yet because of the empty reputation of Wutai — thinking that under a great name it is hard to dwell long — I took to the Eastern Sea, and here first changed my name to Hanshan; from this moment I no longer knew myself as Chengyin. At first, when the temple was burned down, my resolve was to restore it; so I did the ascetic practice while awaiting the conditions. But having dwelt eight years at Wutai with some opportunities, I feared that to wait longer would lose the time, and so I hid at the Eastern Sea — this was my true resolve. On the eighth day of the fourth month of summer I reached Mt. Lao. When Master Miao first parted from me, thinking I could not go alone, he assigned the Dharma-companion Dezong to be my attendant, and he followed me. I had earlier read the Avatamsaka Commentary, in the chapter on the abodes of the Bodhisattvas, which says, 'In the Eastern Sea there is a place called the Nārayaṇa Grotto, where since of old the hosts of Bodhisattvas have dwelt.' The Qingliang Commentary says, 'In Sanskrit, nārayaṇa means enduring and firm — this is the Mt. Lao of the Eastern Sea.' In the Tribute of Yu, this is the Dengzhou-Laizhou region, and the grotto exists to this day. Because I admired it, I made a special visit, and on reaching Mt. Lao indeed found the place; but it was not livable. I then explored the deepest recess of the mountain's south side, backing upon a multitude of peaks and facing the swallowing sea, utterly exquisite and strange, truly not a place of the human world. The place was called the Avalokiteshvara Hermitage — an old shrine, but only its ruined foundations remained. On investigation, in the early Yuan, the Seven Perfect Ones had come forth in the East and, borrowing the prestige of Shizu, seized many Buddhist temples and turned them into Taoist abbacies. When Shizu returned from his western campaigns and the monks pleaded, many were ordered restored. Only Mt. Lao, hidden on the sea, had not been reached, and so all was in ruins. I delighted in its seclusion — a place truly to flee humankind and quit the world — and resolved to dwell there. At first I spread a single mat under a tree; after seven months, I won the layman Zhang Daxin, a man of the district, to cut brush and raise a hut for me to live in. A full year passed with no one coming or going, and my heart was greatly at ease. At that time the Guifeng Dharma-master of the Ling Mountain Temple in Jimo — a very eye of the region — was delighted to be acquainted. (Dezong, the Dharma-companion of Master Miao; the layman Zhang Daxin; and the Dharma-master Guifeng — a first appearance for each.)

Zheng knows that the reason for the great name of Wutai was that the unhindered sanctuary of the time was too flourishing, and the name of gaining an heir by praying for one in the palace was too manifest; and the words of opposing the eunuch envoy had gotten abroad within — the matter was all the greater, and the name all the less livable. This is why he could not return to Wutai, and could not settle at another mountain, and so went far off to the Eastern Sea and hid himself at Mt. Lao. At first, going from Bao'en to the capital was a resolve to restore; and from Wutai to the capital was also a looking for the conditions of restoration. From the capital to hide at Mt. Lao, and from Mt. Lao to beg the canon and return to his temple, and again to beg for accumulated reserves — these were only the vow to repair the temple at Wutai, whence he says 'this was my true resolve.' Mt. Lao, in Jimo district of Laizhou prefecture, by the sea, is also called Laoshang. It is where King Wu of Wu climbed and obtained the Lingbao Duren Scripture; the Han recluse Feng Meng also hid here; and the place is the most desolate and remote. Yet he went, not a thousand li, but rather he left the familiar for the new, left the ripe for the raw, left the north for the east, left the mountain for the sea, left the ice for the sun, left the Chinese for the foreign — as if there were no alternative. It was chiefly because the report of his contending against the eunuch envoy was known, and he knew the difficulty and withdrew. In the end the great catastrophe arose from this, and the great catastrophe was also resolved from this — the season and the karmic conditions, the Buddha and the patriarchs cannot dodge them.
The twelfth year, jiǎshēn ●

At thirty-nine years of age, in the ninth month of autumn, the Sage Mother, for the merit of the Wutai prayer for an heir, sought out the three administrators of the work, namely Dafang, Miaofeng, and me. The two masters had already come and received the bounty, but I alone could not be found, and so her request was urgent. She commanded the old abbot, the abbot Duan'an of the Longhua Temple, to go in person to seek me. He knew I was at the sea, so he came with his staff and made known her gracious command. I declined and said, 'If I am vouchsafed the grace of the emperor to live out an old age on the mountain, I have received the bounty in plenty; what else should I seek?' He reported back, and the holy will was not to be stopped; soon a site was chosen west of the capital to build a temple, and a eunuch envoy was sent, with a set time for me to come. I declined and would not go. When the envoy returned and reported my resolve to lie fast on the mountain, the holy will took pity, and — since I had no dwelling — straightway sent three thousand in gold, dispatching the same envoy to bring it, that I might build a hermitage. When it arrived, I made all haste to stop it, saying, 'My few thatched rooms give me abundant joy; what need for more?' and would not accept. The envoy pressed me, not daring to return without the completing of the mission. I said, 'The ancients could forge a decree to relieve famine. Now the harvest of Shandong has failed; why not extend the holy grace to the famine-stricken people?' Thereupon I bade the monk bring the envoy, and scattered the gifts among the monks, Taoists, orphans, and prisoners of the various prefectures. Each took its tally of the offices concerned and returned the receipts. The holy heart was greatly delighted, with sighs of admiration. When later I was in trouble, brought down to the garrison and interrogated on how much of the imperial treasury I had used, I answered, 'Pray to have the issuing-register of the inner treasury examined.' The emperor had it checked, and it was but this one matter of relieving the famine; not a hair's breadth more. The emperor's suspicion thereupon dissolved. (The Sage Mother — a fourth appearance; the emperor — a third appearance; the Longhua abbot Duan'an — a first appearance.)

Zheng argues: this 'inner treasury' is not the emperor's purse of expenditure, but the Empress Dowager's own kitchen-grant for her sustenance. To economize in giving alms is an excellent karmic cause of filial piety and compassion — why then should there be an issue of investigation? May it not be that, because of the establishing of the heir, a rift arose in the palace and spread to this? If he had not thrice declined the alms of faith, one would fear that the Sea-Seal Temple was built up and at the mercy of chance, whereas the Western Mountain temple could not be abandoned but also could not be raised. Because of the matter of delivering the famine, great compassion lay before his eyes and great spiritual power turned in the blink of an eye: excellent, excellent!
Whenever it says 'the holy', it refers to the Sage Mother, not the emperor. This particular 'the emperor' is the emperor himself.
The thirteenth year, yǐyǒu ●

At forty years of age: the people of the east had never known monks. When I dwelt on the mountain, the Huang clan was the greatest there, and its sons gradually drew near. The so-called heretic Luo Qing of the present age was a man of Chengyang below the mountain, and the birthplace of that heresy; hence its teaching ran throughout the east, and they knew utterly nothing of the Three Jewels. I dwelt here to teach and transform them; in time, all who were teachers and elders among them led their disciples to take refuge, and from this they first became aware of the Buddha Dharma — this was the beginning of my opening the work.

Zheng knows that when there are the karmic conditions, one can transform heretics; when there are none, one cannot transform Taoists. The heretics took refuge because they saw the coming and going of the eunuch envoys. The Taoists stirred up trouble because they heard and suspected the rift-building within the palace. Hence it is said the Buddha Dharma is committed to kings and great ministers.
The fourteenth year, bǐngxū ●

At forty-one years of age: in that year the canon was bestowed. At the start of the dynasty, when the canon was first carved, there were scriptures composed within this land that had not been placed in the canon; now the emperor and the Sage Mother ordered them engraved. When it was done, the emperor decreed the conferral of fifteen canons, to be scattered and given to the famed mountains of the world, first with four sets set at the four borders: the Eastern Sea at Mt. Lao, the Southern Sea at Putuo, the Western Shu at Emei, and the northern at Luya. At the time, the Sage Mother, because of the Wutai karmic conditions, and because she had repeatedly summoned me without my coming and bestowed gifts without my accepting, gave the first canon to the Eastern Sea. At first I did not know of it. When it arrived, the empty mountain had no place to house it, and the governor of the province had the local office enshrine and offer to it. Seeing there was an imperial edict, I went to the capital to return thanks. In that time, by the gracious command, the palace women and consorts each gave alms to build a temple and enshrine it, asking that it be named the Sea-Seal Temple. While I was in the capital, I happened to hear that Master Daguan was visiting me at the sea; so I set off home, chasing after him at full speed. When I reached the foot of the mountain, he was coming out of it; soon we returned together, lingering for twenty days. He gave me a poem with the lines, 'In idle rest one dwells upon the sea / The fame by chance has fallen on the East.' In the eleventh month of that winter, because since xīnsì I had been much wearied with labor and had not had rest, I was often tired. Now that the meditation chamber was newly finished, I could at last dwell in peace, and set my body and mind down — a joy beyond words. One night I sat still and, rising in the night, saw the sea bright and the sky clearly empty, an entire great treasury of light, with not a single object. Then I spoke a verse: 'The sea is bright, the sky empty, moonlight and snow / In this, the worldly and the saint hide all their traces / The adamant eye suddenly bursts, the hollow flowers fall / The whole great earth returns to the realm of extinction.' Returning to the chamber, I found the Śūraṅgama Sūtra on my desk suddenly opened, and at once saw that your mind and body, and even the mountains, rivers, void, and great earth, are all objects within the wonderful bright true mind. Then the whole realm of contemplation of the sūtra was clear before my heart and eyes. I straightway took up the pen to set down a Śūraṅgama Mirror of Contemplation in one volume; it was done with only half a candle. The meditation hall had just opened its sitting, so I called the rector into the chamber to read it to me, and I myself was as if hearing the words of a dream. (The emperor — a fourth appearance; the Sage Mother — a fifth appearance; Master Daguan — a first appearance.)

Zheng observes: of the famed mountains of the world, only fifteen canons were conferred, and the first four sets were placed at the four borders; and among the borders the first conferred was the Eastern Sea at Mt. Lao, because the Hanshan Master first dwelt there. Master Miaofeng first went to worship at Putuo, then later went to Wutai and dwelt at Luya; so the conferral on Putuo and Luya was likewise because of Master Miao. Mt. Lao and Luya were not great famed mountains yet received the first grant of the new canon — though-by imperial edict, it was in truth the Sage Mother's intent, fixed on the merit of the Wutai prayer for an heir. After parting from Miaofeng, the one the Hanshan Master called his deep Dharma-friend was none other than Daguan: years of longing, and a thousand li to bring his carriage to see them face to face; a pointed confrontation and this day's meeting. Had he not raced to overtake him, how would he have avoided a disappointed return? This one meeting at Mt. Lao is enough for a friendship of a thousand ages. The Hanshan Master's Extra Records say, 'All is illusion — everyone knows it; but one must have a master of the illusory operation, so as not to be turned by illusion.' While at Sea-Seal he happened to think of the case of Master Lü by whose door some man came in the night to ask for his head; he wished to learn such meditative strength, and every night opening his door he practiced contemplation, thinking, 'If someone comes to borrow this head, I will gladly give it.' Tonight so, tomorrow night so; for a long time he felt there was a fixed power of insight. Suddenly one night he was told thieves had entered. I said, 'Just call them in. Light the candle and sit upright, without a frightened heart.' The man reached the door and then crawled, not daring to enter — he was a great tall fellow. I called to him, 'There is nothing here,' and bade them take two hundred cash from the storehouse and give it him. If I had not had a fixed master, I would have been in panic and at a loss. On another night, sitting, he entered a realm where body and world were both empty, and the Sea-Seal radiance sent forth light, and the mountains and rivers shook — a realm he attained in responding wisdom. After a while he penetrated the crucial point of the Śūraṅgama, dimly before his eyes; he hastily lit a candle and wrote, his wrist not able to keep up, until the fifth watch of the night, and then the Śūraṅgama Mirror was finished. When the attendant came out to wait on him and saw the remnant candle on the desk, he was astonished. Alas, all such things are the affairs of the treasury of light; they are not to be sought and measured by busy intention. When the later matters match up, word and brush are both exquisite — read them together, and one can awaken to the Way, and also awaken to literature. What should be noted in these two accounts is that it was Master Lü acting as me, not I acting as Master Lü; and the Śūraṅgama sealing me, not I sealing the Śūraṅgama. This is the intent of the sincere recording.
The fifteenth year, dīnghài ●

At forty-two years of age: in that year I built the halls, and first opened a hall to give the precepts to the assembly. From this, monks from the four quarters came daily in greater numbers. For the lay faithful I explained the Direct Explanation of the Heart Sūtra. In the eighth month of autumn, Vice Censor-in-Chief Hu, having begged leave to return home, brought his own son, sent him out of the household as an attendant, and named him Fushan. (Vice Censor-in-Chief Hu — a third appearance; Fushan — a first appearance. He is the former Prefect Shun'an of Pinyang.)

Zheng, when the Hanshan Master made his eastern journey, met the secretary-attendant Good Master Zhiwei. At the Jingci Mirror-House he met him morning and evening, conversing, and together they explored the deep mystery. The master aided the abbot in his brush-and-ink affairs, and in the end produced the Eastern Journey Collection. Of the Hanshan Master's eminent disciples of the time, none surpassed Master Zhiwei. Through hardship and peril there was nowhere he did not follow, and the entire records of the collection came from his hand. His father, Lord Hu Shun'an, was a man of Donglai, and because of the past karmic bond with his native place, sent him out of the household at the Sea-Seal Temple of Mt. Lao. Later he was committed to the abbot's chamber of the Five Breasts Hermitage, presided over the Dharma-Cloud Temple of Mount Kuang, and at seventy years passed away sitting.
The sixteenth year, wùzǐ ●

At forty-three years of age: at that time a fellow student read my Mirror of Contemplation and asked, 'This sūtra's contemplation of mind is fully illuminated, but the words are not wholly dissolved, so I fear later students will not easily enter. I beg that character by character it be resolved and brought back to the contemplation of mind — then it would be a Dharma-gift beyond all others.' I here first conceived the idea of the Comprehensive Discussion, already set forth its great purport, but it was not yet committed to writing.
The seventeenth year, jǐchǒu ●

At forty-four years of age: in that year I read through the canon and expounded the Lotus Sūtra and the Awakening of Faith to the assembly. Since parting from Wutai I had felt a desire to go home and see my parents, but feared to fall into worldly talk. So I put it to test; one night, sitting still, I chanced to have a verse: 'The misty waves bathe the cold sky day by day / Fishes and birds swim together in one mirror / Last night suddenly sank the moon beyond the heavens / The lonely brightness should of itself mingle with the black dragon.' Then I called to my attendant and said, 'I am now able to go home; I shall see my two parents.' Earlier, for the Bao'en Temple I had begged one copy of the great canon; in the tenth month of winter I went to the capital to receive it, and the emperor straightway commanded it be sent. I took it and went; in the eleventh month I reached Longjiang, where the temple's jewel-pagoda radiated light for days running. On the day of receiving the sūtra the pagoda's light formed a bridge facing north, and the monks receiving the sūtra walked within the light. When the sūtra was enshrined and the sanctuary set up, the light-phenomenon never ceased day by day, and those who came to gaze were more than ten thousand each day, counting it a rare auspicious sign. At the time, my old mother, hearing I had arrived, first sent someone to ask what day I would come home. I said, 'I have come for the court's affair, not for my family. If my old mother can meet me happy as when we last parted, I can stay one night; otherwise I will not return.' My mother, hearing this, said, 'To see each other reborn, joy cannot be exhausted; how could there be grief? A single meeting is enough, let alone two nights?' When I returned and my mother met me, she was overjoyed and quite beside herself, and I thought this very strange. And when I sat at night, an elder of the clan asked me whether I had come by boat or by land. My mother answered offhand, 'Why ask whether by boat or by land?' The questioner said, 'From where, then?' My mother said, 'From the sky.' I was startled and said, 'No wonder that old woman could bear to give me up.' I asked my mother, 'After we parted, did you think of me?' She said, 'How could I not.' I said, 'How did you console yourself?' She said, 'At first I did not know; later, knowing you were at Wutai, I asked the master where Wutai was. He said it lies beneath the Northern Dipper — that is where my son is. From then on, every night I bowed to the Dipper and named the Bodhisattva, and so no longer thought of you. If I thought you were dead, I would not bow, and would have cut off all thought. Now I see you — it is as though you came in an incarnation.' The next day I made offerings at the ancestral graves and chose a burial site for my two parents. When I found it, my father was already eighty. I jested, 'Today I bury the old man alive, so as to spare him coming again another day,' and took up my mattock to dig. My mother snatched it from me, saying, 'The old woman will bury him herself; why trouble another?' And she swung it more than a dozen times. On the third day, taking leave, my mother was joyful as before, without ever knitting her brows; only then did I know my mother was no ordinary woman. In Jimo there was a scholar Huang Nashan, styled Ziguang, the younger brother of the present great Minister of War Huang. When I first came to the sea he was nineteen, and straightway took refuge and asked for instruction. I gave him the Śūraṅgama, and in two months he could recite it. From then he ate no meat; though his parents reproved him, his heart did not waver. He firmly resolved to meditate, never letting his ribs touch the mat. When I came south, Ziguang thought privately, 'I was born in a border land, and for long aeons never heard the name of the Three Jewels; now I have met a great good friend, an uninvited teacher. If he does not return, we are left without a refuge.' So before the great bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara he cut the skin of his arm, lit a lamp and offered it, praying that Avalokiteshvara protect me and bring me home early. From then the burn festered and pained; night and day he sat upright and held fast to the name of Avalokiteshvara, and after three months it healed. When it healed, the scar had formed into an image of the bodhisattva — brows, eyes, body and robe, as if painted; even his own mother and wife did not know it. He constantly begged to leave the household, but I absolutely would not let him. Then he said, 'If the disciple turns a somersault and comes back, teacher, can you stop me then?' From this I knew that in the land of the mlecchas the Buddha-seed had never been cut off. At first, because I was to repair this temple, I dwelt at Wutai; the matter had already found its opening, but it involved a cost of several hundred thousand, not lightly spoken of, so I awaited the time at the sea. Now, when the moment was ripe, I made use of the karmic condition of escorting the great canon to go back to the southern capital, and set out the whole history of the temple. On my return I made my report, laying it before the Sage Mother, and said, 'The work is great and the cost enormous, not lightly to be undertaken. I beg the Sage Mother to reduce your daily fare by one hundred taels, that in three years the matter may be undertaken, and in ten years the work completed.' The holy heart was greatly delighted, and straightway commanded that the accumulation begin in the twelfth month of that year. (The Sage Mother — a sixth appearance; my father — a third appearance; my mother — a ninth appearance. Huang Ziguang Nashan, younger brother of the great Minister of War of Jimo — a first appearance.)

Zheng's note: the chronicle records that the Hanshan Master, from twenty-six when he went north, to forty-four when he returned south and saw his two parents, passed through eighteen years. The Wutai awakening, the successful prayer for the heir, the instruction at Mt. Lao, the manifestation of the Sea-Seal realm, the memorial and the edict bestowing the canon, the pagoda's emission of light, the whole city flocking to worship, the temple buildings stirred to radiance — and furthermore, his two parents well, his clan not orphaned, the ancestral graves still standing, the burial site chosen and dug by himself: in the world and beyond the world, of those who take the empty mind and pass their examination on returning home, how many are there? Those who return to their home village in brocade, even emperors, kings, generals and ministers, are they worthy of envy? And moreover Old Lady Pang revealed the form, the old mountain-mother showed her wonders, the whole household sat in a circle speaking of the birthless — one question, one answer, one coming, one going — nothing but weeping and laughing, such that one cannot tell whether it is kindness or resentment. Ah, a great piece of mischief indeed! And who is Huang Ziguang? He burned his arm in longing for his teacher, bore the Buddha's image in his scar, harbored the old vow of Huangmei, came back with a somersault, and after yet a few years passed away sitting. Ah, this too is no small piece of mischief! This chronicle's saying 'the emperor straightway commanded it be sent' and 'on my return I made my report' both refer to the Sage Mother, not the emperor. The later command to accumulate reserves was, when the calamity fell, done away with because the emperor was asked to examine the inner issuing-register. The Caoxi karmic conditions were completed; the Bao'en karmic conditions were not — was this to trade that for this? The sūtra sent amidst the light had long since consoled the vow of his one life to leave the household for the temple.
The Eighteenth Year, Gengyin ●

I was forty-five. That spring I wrote out the Lotus Sutra in gratitude to the Sacred Mother. At that time certain men who coveted our practice site suborned a Daoist priest from beyond the pale, falsely claiming that he held that temple, and gathered a crowd to lodge a suit at the governor's yamen. Lord Li, the provincial governor, had already learned the whole affair and bitterly hated it; he sent it down to Laizhou prefecture for a thorough investigation. I attended the hearing in person and did my utmost to save them. Several hundred of those ruffians raised an uproar in the prefectural city, surrounding us as the men of Kuang once surrounded Confucius. I had two attendants with me; I sent them off by another road and walked slowly on alone. The leader among them came capering at me with a blade, meaning to kill me. I looked at him with a smile and said: 'If you kill a man, how will you answer for yourself?' His spirit failed him, he put up his sword, and they escorted me about two li beyond the city wall. When we were about to part, the mad crowd suspected their leader of having been won over to my side and wanted to beat him. I reckoned silently: if that crowd once rouses itself, the man is lost. What was to be done? I hesitated. At the parting I drew the madman with me to my lodging, shut the door, took off my robe, sat at ease, laughed and talked as usual, and shared melons and fruit with him. Meanwhile the whole market was crying that a Daoist had killed a monk. The prefect heard it and at once sent many runners to arrest them all. The crowd was terrified and all knocked their heads on the ground, begging to be let off. I said: 'Do not be afraid; only hear what I have to say, that is all.' When they arrived, the prefect asked: 'Did the mad ruffians kill the monk?' I said: 'Not at all. When the arrest came, the monk was eating melons and fruit together with their leader.' The prefect said: 'Why did they raise the uproar?' I said: 'It was mere market noise.' The prefect wanted to put them in the cangue. I said: 'You wish to disperse them; the cangue would only hold them fast.' The prefect understood, and ordered the local officers to drive them all out. Within three days the whole mad crowd had dispersed, and so the matter was quieted. That year I wrote A Treatise on the Influence of Laozi and Zhuangzi. (The Sacred Mother appeared seven times; Lord Li the provincial governor and the Laizhou prefect, once each.)

Zheng observes: in this affair of strife, every step is the art of war and every step a Chan device. Were it so, there would be no difficult affair under heaven and no man hard to deal with. Among the eight essays of A Treatise on the Influence of Laozi and Zhuangzi, only the essay On the Dharma of Mind is short in written extent yet comprehensive in its treatment of the Three Teachings; I append it here to preserve its general outline. On the Dharma of Mind it says: In youth I took Confucius as my teacher and did not know Confucius; I took Laozi as my teacher and did not know Laozi. Then I withdrew into the deep mountains and great marshes, practicing stillness and contemplating the mind.
