When I left, the gentry of the prefecture had pressed me hard to stay, but I would not remain; had I not gone, I too would have been dust. At the time people thought it strange. So it was that I crossed the sea by moonlight and saw the finest prospects of Qiong, which I took to be a fairy capital, one of the ten isles. In the fourth month of summer the governor directed me by writ to return to Wuyang. In the seventh month of autumn I reached Caoxi. When I left, the Patriarch’s Hall had already been pulled down for rebuilding and the work was not yet stopped; on my return, six or seven tenths were complete. The debt for materials and labour came to nearly a thousand pieces of gold, with no means of meeting it. I converted the two palace eunuchs to give, and paid it all; I also repaired the Changchun Hut at Qingmen in Wuyang, to be an administration court of Caoxi and a place for making offerings on behalf of the Sixth Patriarch. (Lord Dai of the governor’s office, a third time. The two palace eunuchs are the former mining commissioners Lord Li and his colleagues, a second time.)

Fuzheng wonders: the two palace eunuchs were the mining commissioners who were able to prove loyal to the Sacred Mother; hence, on the writ returning me to the garrison, they were able to give at once and pay off the thousand pieces of gold owed for the Patriarch’s Hall, material and labour. How could this have been easily brought about by begging for alms? The eunuchs’ gift was also a karmic fruit of the Sacred Mother’s former fame. To look at the air and know a calamity, like Confucius’s shangyang bird that knows the rain, or the halo round the moon that foretells fair weather, is of itself an ordinary matter for a man of clear understanding who sees the first signs; it is not to be called strange talk. In the spring of the third month of the yisi year before, the Mingchang Pagoda of Qiongzhou city fell and crushed the upper storey in which he lodged to pieces, yet Master Hanshan happened to have left, and he said he had escaped being ground to powder; people thought it strange. Twelve years later, in the summer of the bingchen year, on the twenty-eighth day of the sixth month, in the Chunshu Lane of the north city of Jiaxing, the five-roomed hall and upper storey in which Fuzheng lodged collapsed entirely, and Fuzheng was crushed beneath it; three great beams fell astride and propped it up. Bricks and tiles more than a foot across struck his body like the paper goods used in funerary offerings; he felt no pain and was not hurt at all. He came out from among the piled rubble like a clay figure, and after bathing a while was clean, feeling no difference whatever in his movements. The whole city was astonished, taking it for a rare thing even among those born twice. At that time Fuzheng had long believed in the Buddha-Dharma, and when the building gave way with a great crash, the whole household heard a single “Namo Guanyin Bodhisattva” filling the air. On the first of the seventh month he entered Mount Jing and paid his respects to Chan Master Xueqiao, telling him of it; Xue was calm and did not think it strange. Then on the first of the eleventh month, at Mount Jing, he met the Patriarch Hanshan and told him of it; the Patriarch looked startled and did not treat it as ordinary. He therefore gave him the name Fuzheng and the courtesy name Liangsheng, and showed him a verse. Now, reading in the chronicle the words about the broken building in Qiong city, he remembers the former affair. The Patriarch, knowing the first signs with a spirit-like clarity, crossed the sea and escaped being ground to powder, and people thought it strange; Fuzheng, holding that life and death are fated, escaped powder among the powder, and his heart never forgot it. Moved by this, he appends a note of it.
The Thirty-Fourth Year, Bingwu ●

I was sixty-one. In the third month of spring I crossed the ridge to Nanzhou to wait upon Ding Youwu and to thank the Grand Minister Zhang Hongyang. When I was in trouble, the Lord was then assistant minister and knew the whole course of my case most thoroughly; he and others joined forces to rescue me at the time, and my heart was grateful. Now that the Lord was living at home, I went to thank him. He received me joyfully, spoke of old times, gathered his sons, and entertained me at a vegetarian feast in the Xianyun Tower on the river. In the midst of the gathering the Lord said: “People all know that Master Hanshan is a great good teacher, but they do not know that he has done great hidden service for the altars of state.” When the company heard this they were awed, and asked the Lord, who told them the outline; the whole table was stirred, and there were six poems at the time. On my way back I passed Wenjiang and visited the remonstrating censor Zou, staying several days. At Zhanggong, General Chen Ershi kept me in his headquarters; I was ill for a month, and wrote twelve poems on lying ill, then returned to Caoxi. In the eighth month of autumn the imperial eldest grandson was born, and there was a gracious amnesty: all those garrisoned who were old or sick, and all who had been implicated by error, were allowed to have their cases examined and to be released; I was among them. So I went to inform the military gate, and permission was given for an investigation. I went on to the Leizhou circuit, where the case was examined and found to warrant pardon; the surveillance commission made up the list and awaited the memorial, and so I was released from the ranks. (Ding Youwu, a fourth time. Grand Minister Zhang Hongyang, once. The remonstrating censor Zou, a second time. General Chen Ershi, once. The imperial eldest grandson, once. Hongyang was named Wei, a man of Xinjian in Jiangxi; he led the proposal to settle the succession under Taichang, and with Grand Minister Shen Li and the Master of Rites Guo Zhengyu did great service.)

Fuzheng observes: what Lord Hongyang called his great hidden service to the altars of state, and the outline of it that stirred the whole table, was nothing other than praying for an heir and obtaining one, protecting the heir and establishing him, and thereby courting taboo and disaster in matters within and without the palace that may not be spoken of. Hence his words were half revealed, half concealed, and in the end could not be transmitted. The Patriarch Hanshan began his garrison life with this and ended it with this pardon; therefore he writes it large and writes it twice: “In the eighth month of autumn the imperial eldest grandson was born.” Following the precedent of the earlier renwu entry, where “in the eighth month the crown prince was born” is also written with the special brush of the Spring and Autumn, this is why the Heart-Method of the Zuo Commentary came to be written. Who is the crown prince? The posthumous title given after Taichang had already ascended. Who is the imperial eldest grandson? The designation used at his birth in the early Tianqi reign. Tianqi too was born of the Talented Lady Wang of Taichang, afterwards honoured as Empress Xiaoduan. Thus two Talented Ladies of the Wang family in succession bore two emperors. Though the Patriarch Hanshan was himself within the gracious amnesty, his meaning is not solely about the amnesty; his brush ties straight back to the time of the karmic origin of the prayer for an heir at Mount Tai. The great juncture and great public case of half his life lies in the four words “the imperial eldest grandson was born.” Hence one knows that the whole course of the chronicle, from first to last, is the Heart-Method of the Zuo Commentary.
The Thirty-Fifth Year, Dingwei ●

I was sixty-two. In the third month of spring I petitioned to return to my native place, and the governor directed the prefecture of Shaozhou by writ to settle me at Caoxi. While I dwelt in the mountain I was able to preach the Dharma for my disciples. In my youth I had read Laozi, and because the text is ancient and the meaning deep, and I found it hard and knotty, I searched its purport to the utmost and gained something. My lay disciples asked me to make a commentary on it. I had set my mind on it from the renchen year, and only when I had investigated a point thoroughly did I set brush to paper; if a single word was doubtful and did not come clear, I would never lightly let it pass. Thus I laboured fifteen years, carrying it with me in the army, and only now was it finished. (Lord Dai of the governor’s office, a fourth time.)

Fuzheng observes: the Outer Chronicle of the Patriarch Hanshan says that the commentary on the one classic of the Dao and its Virtue took thirteen years before the draft was free of his hand. As for the purport of the Supreme One’s words, he must have tried them on himself before he saw them; they cannot be called stale words on paper without true savour. Whenever I write on a scripture, I must gather my spirit and enter contemplation, and only when I have realized accord with the Buddha’s mind and the opening suddenly bursts forth of itself do I commit it to paper. If it smacks of thought and deliberation, it is of no use.
The Thirty-Sixth Year, Wushen ●

I was sixty-three. We discussed repairing the great hall of Caoxi. In the second month of spring Lord Feng Yuancheng, a man of Wuzhong, took up the post of circuit intendant of Lingxi. He came into the mountain to visit me and stayed the night, and dreamed that a great bodhisattva appeared; moved by it, at dawn he entered the hall to worship the Buddha, and coming before the three great bodhisattvas he saw that two of the pillars were rotten and crumbling. Startled, he said to me: “Why do you not repair this?” I said: “The work is great and the cost heavy; my strength does not reach to it.” He asked: “How much would it cost?” I answered with a certain sum. The Lord said: “There is no difficulty; I will try to do it.” On returning he told the governor Lord Dai, who said: “How perilous! When one sees a child about to fall into a well, one must crawl to save it; how much more when the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas stand in such peril — not to be moved is not to be a man.” Then he asked the cost, and Feng told him my words. The Lord said: “That is not enough. Send at once to the Nan-Shao circuit to survey and estimate, and let me invite Hanshan to discuss it.” I went and saw the Lord, and he was eager to build it himself at his own charge. I told him: “If you spend the public funds, I fear it will not be fitting; only if we follow the old practice of the Dharma gate will it do.” The Lord said: “What then?” I asked that it be done by collecting contributions from the many. The Lord charged the Lingxi circuit to make twelve subscription books, and the three offices, the circuits, and the prefectures each kept a fan, giving as they pleased, all gathered at the prefecture and remitted as one sum, not passing through the monks’ hands. In this way it was no burden and was easily collected. The Lord followed it, and in less than a month nearly a thousand pieces of gold were gathered. I went myself to western Guangdong to select great timbers, and when I reached Duanzhou the governor kept me to repair the Baoyue Terrace, and appointed other officials to buy the timber. In winter the Baoyue Terrace was completed and I wrote a record of it; the timbers were all piled on the bank of the Duan River and transported one after another. At the beginning of the eleventh month of winter, Annamese bandits breached Qinzhou; Lord Dai asked for the imperial troops to punish them at a distance, and on that account he was impeached and dismissed. (Feng Yuancheng of the Lingxi circuit, once. Lord Dai of the governor’s office, a fifth time. Yuancheng was named Shike, sobriquet Wensuo, a man of Huating, a presented scholar of the xinwei year of Longqing, and served as assistant administration commissioner of Zhejiang.)

At the Zongjing Hall Fuzheng heard from an attendant: Lord Dai Yao of the governor’s office held the staff of office in Guangdong for nine years; bandits and rebels on the hills and seas stirred several times, and his long tenure without mishap was wholly owing to the Patriarch Hanshan’s strength. Therefore he gave generously to Caoxi, and the hundred ruined works were all set afoot; only the great hall was not built, for which iron-pear wood was to be used for the beams, all brought from western Guangdong, to the value of three thousand pieces of gold. Had Lord Dai remained one year longer in office, the work at Caoxi would have been accomplished beyond thought. On the eve of his dismissal he kept the Master to repair the Baoyue Hall. At that time the Yao and Zhuang of Annam had breached Qinzhou, and the affair was already in ruin; when the Emperor heard of it, he was nearly arrested. The Master, by reason of his great name, entered the cave with banners and precious canopies and talked the bandits into surrender. When the bandits withdrew, order was restored and a million lives in Qinzhou were saved. Then Lord Dai submitted a memorial asking for imperial troops to punish them, to cover the former failure; and so he was only impeached and dismissed, and escaped arrest and interrogation. The Master’s requital of Lord Dai’s merit in restoring Caoxi was indeed great. Yet he did not boast his own merit nor expose Dai’s fault; with a mere dozen characters he closed the whole case of the governor’s removal from office — which is also the heart-method of the Spring and Autumn in concealing the faults of the worthy, and the utmost righteousness of loyalty and forbearance. At that time there was a book, The Qimen Zhizhang, or Palm-Guide to the Qimen, which he wrote at Lord Dai’s request.
The Thirty-Seventh Year, Jiyou ●

I was sixty-four. In the second month of spring, as I was bringing timber back from Duanzhou, the wind blocked us at the Antelope Gorge; I visited the Duan Stream and wrote A Dream Record of Visiting the Duan Stream. When the timber had been brought to the Meng River I entered the mountain and was just gathering the assembly to set the work going, when several unworthy monks among them did mischief and opposed it, stirring up the crowd to disorder like rebel commoners. Seeing it, I sighed: “This is my own heavy offence against the Buddha’s teaching — the fault of clinging to appearances.” While the crowd was still shouting, I sat alone in the hall, burned incense, and recited the Vajra Prajñāpāramitā; when I came to “the Buddha speaks of four views, which are not four views,” I suddenly had a great awakening, and so wrote the Doubts Resolved on the Diamond Sutra. When the draft was done, the crowd fell silent. As for the unworthy ones, since they did not trust my mind, they were misled by wicked men, grew the more fearful, and brought suit at the censorate, which granted a hearing before the judicial officer. At that time I went lightly out of the mountain to await judgment, living on a boat on the Furong River for two years, until my travelling funds were exhausted. At that time the assistant prefect Lord Xiang Chudong, who held the pass at Hanjiang, invited me to come. On the river we met a wind that wrecked the boat, and when I arrived I fell gravely ill and nearly died; the Lord called physicians and saved me with all his strength. When I returned to the prefecture I lay ill in an inn for nearly a year. (The judicial officer, surname unknown. The assistant prefect Lord Xiang Chudong was named Guifang, a man of Jiaxing, each once.)

Fuzheng had the Doubts Resolved on the Diamond Sutra printed at the Lengyan scripture workshop, in forty-eight leaves. It is not known how, amid all that turmoil and shouting, he could finish the draft in a moment; truly it came from a hand that answered to the mind, and is not to be sought in the words.
The Thirty-Eighth Year, Gengxu ●

I was sixty-five. That year I lived on a boat on the river. In the seventh month of autumn the imperial commissioner came to the prefecture on his circuit and inquired after me; the judicial officer heard of it, for he had just been giving judgment against me. The commissioner strongly disapproved, and rebutted him, saying: “This man has done great service for the Sixth Patriarch. Those who formerly gave for the permanent endowment — now the wicked monks reap the profit, and you turn and condemn him: is this what is called the gate of equal Dharma?” And he ordered the circuit again to investigate strictly. Thereupon the prefectural office came in person to the mountain and examined the monks’ plaint item by item; all was idle talk without substance. They falsely accused me of misappropriating more than eight thousand pieces of gold from the permanent endowment. When I first established the rules for the endowment’s treasury, I had provided numbered receipts. For all income and outlay of money and grain, with the prior and the secretary, every farthing that went in or out was supported by a numbered receipt and not recklessly issued. Now, when the monks who had held office over the years were examined and reckoned before the officials, with the numbered receipts as the standard, not a farthing was found to touch me. Then those above and below, within and without, believed at last that I was not reckless, and the matter was cleared. The authorities were greatly angered at the monks, and I did my utmost to reconcile them. They pressed me again and again to stay in the mountain, but by then my heart was weary, and so I firmly declined. I entrusted the Chan hall to my disciple Huaiyu, and at once drifted away without a care. (The imperial commissioner, surname unknown, once. ○ The Chan hall is the Baolin Hall.)

Fuzheng wonders: Lord Dai of the governor’s office had but just been dismissed, yet those few unworthy monks dared to raise a great storm of trouble. What monks were they? They must have been the old abbots of Caoxi. What money and grain was it that they falsely accused him of misappropriating? It must have been the permanent endowment of many years, which by the old rule of Caoxi was received and paid out before the officials and reckoned before the officials. Ever since the higher authorities invited the Patriarch Hanshan into Caoxi, the old monks could not be masters there, and had long lost the profit of their embezzling; therefore, seizing the moment when the censorate had no friends to turn to, they worked upon the judicial officer to overturn the board. Yet his wisdom saw the first signs and stopped the trouble beforehand, and the mischief of a sudden hour poured out its poison to no avail. Still, two years of living on a boat awaiting judgment meant that in the blink of an eye the hall’s timbers came to nothing: a great loss to the Sixth Patriarch’s karmic affair, and only the Patriarch Hanshan’s far-seeing provision for what came after saved it. Looking back at the earlier affair, when he asked that the inner accounts be examined and the offerings falsely entered without record, the difficulties were great and small, but the solution was one and the same. A place of gruel and rice for a thousand monks, a spotless white ground of one mat, the Chan hall handed over, going and coming in freedom — the public case of Caoxi is closed here, and yet it is precisely not closed. As he was about to set out, he encouraged the disciples of Caoxi in ten verses: “A thousand monks in concord, like Vulture Peak of old; no common thing it is that all take refuge in the fold. Had you not once received the charge the Patriarch gave, how could you ever pass his gate and enter, and be bold? The fleshly body sits before you, living as of old; at dawn and dusk your tea and broth are offered from the heart. The bell and drum sound clearly — that is the Dharma told; no need for painstaking words to play the urging part. Deep must the seeds of merit’s field be sown; cause and effect are like a mirror clearly shown. Though to the jewel mountain you have come full many a time, this time you must not turn again with nothing of your own. Grudge not the toil of work, nor shun the labour sore; remember how of old the stone hung at his waist. When once the breath has stopped, a thousand kalpas wait; if goodness is unsown, your grief is evermore. Let not this life slip by you carelessly, I pray; the arrow-flight of time is truly cause for dread. I fear that when the breath within three inches fades away, you will not know when next you come to this jewel mountain’s head. The garden of merit must never be held light; each step of your heel must be clear and bright. Do not let it fall in disorder and go its own way, lest the blind man walk again in the night. Each inch of beam and tile is made by many a cause; the fat and grease of faithful giving weigh it down. Do not covet the donkey-dung stick he offers you, lightly trading it for both your eyes without pause. The fat and blood of faith outweigh Mount Sumeru; a grain of rice, a stalk of firewood may not be used untrue. Only look at those in fur and horn who pay their debt of old, and suffer in the mud-hell for the karmic debt they owe. Fortunate to be born in the Middle Land, early to leave the dust, wearing the kashaya robe, far from all your kin, enjoying the pure blessings of the Empty Gate — how will you ever repay the Patriarchs’ grace and trust? If from youth you keep the mind set on the upward way, a hair’s-breadth sprout will grow at last a thousand fathoms high. Only when you have endured the bitter frost will you become a timber fit for use, and stand beyond the common sky.” And again, about to go to Nanyue, he took leave of the sons of the Dharma society of Lingnan in ten verses: “Twenty years fallen into the dust of the world; that we meet now, believe, is karma from before. Since first the robe and bowl came southward here, today we take up once more the Chan of pointing straight. The matter is clear enough within yourself alone; no need to ask outside for fortune or for loss. Only turn the light back wherever you may touch, and let not worldly toil besiege and bind you down. The great Way has always been beyond the root and the true; it is mostly by discrimination that we make both far and near. Only when you see through the face your mother bore are you a man outstanding in the dust, and clear. I have drunk the miasmic mists till my teeth are still cold; I do not recall the former hardships of the road. This time I go to the deep and secret midst of the ten thousand hills, to watch the five-hued clouds from within my seat, untold. Twenty years I galloped through the land of miasmic air; this year I have not noticed that my temples are like frost. Now on a single leaf of a boat I go from here, and my traces shall be hidden in the thousand ravines’ host. Long have I roamed the worldly toil and blended with the light, busy only with raising up this one matter of mine. A thousand-foot fishing rod, well-nigh hewn away outright; I turn my head — sea and sky stretch boundless and benign. Since first I took refuge and walked about the Dharma altar, I have ever begged for this heart to be at peace. Say not that we part three thousand li apart; when the bright moon is at mid-heaven, we meet face to face. Sometimes with rod and line I show my simple heart; my bamboo-branch songs are done — how few true listeners stay. The little boat returns on a frosty night apart; bright moon and reed-flowers — where shall I find them, I pray? In the cold sky the wild goose’s call sounds lone and clear; from now my traces fall among the Five Lakes’ shore. Boundless mist and wave carry my thoughts of grief and care; a single sail at the sky’s edge is my way home once more. For the Dharma, how could I decline a distant road? Who says the miasmic sea is the world’s end? Again and again a drop of Caoxi’s water I bestow, to irrigate the five-petal flower that came from the West.”
In the first ten he sets forth the teaching, in the latter ten he sets forth Chan; this in itself is the robe and bowl.
The Thirty-Ninth Year, Xinhai ●

I was sixty-six. In the third month of spring I was living at Dinghu Mountain in Duanzhou, nursing my illness. At first, when I received the pardon and awaited the memorial, there was no reply from the imperial commissioner, and so it was delayed until now; then, having been examined and cleared again, the case was at last cancelled and I was free to go as I pleased. At that time several scholars attached themselves to me and asked for instruction, and so I set forth the Doubts Resolved on the Great Learning.

Fuzheng, reading the chronicle, notes that in the dingyou year he wrote the Direct Pointing at the Doctrine of the Mean; fifteen years later, in the xinhai year, he set forth the Doubts Resolved on the Great Learning. That the Mean came first and the Great Learning after follows the Book of Rites, in which the Mean is the thirty-first chapter and the Great Learning the forty-second. The Master said to Fuzheng face to face at the Zongjing Hall that the Great Learning concludes the meaning of the Mean, and Fuzheng was able to complete the book on that basis.
The Fortieth Year, Renzi ●

I was sixty-seven, dwelling in the Changchun Hut, where I expounded for my disciples the Awakening of Faith, the Eight Consciousnesses, and the Hundred Dharmas, and was asked to set forth a direct exposition. Previously, because the Lotus Sutra’s Beating the Beat had its text and meaning so linked together as not to be divided, so that students found it hard to grasp, I now wrote the Chapter Divisions.
The Forty-First Year, Guichou ●

I was sixty-eight. I kept the summer retreat for my disciples at the Changchun Hut and expounded the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment. Halfway through, a carbuncle broke out on my back and was very grave; the physicians could not cure it, and I was near death. The Great General Lord Wang Hanchong had already made arrangements for my last affairs. At that time a Cantonese named Liang Xingshan, a drinker of wine who had long been famed for treating sores, happened to come; he looked at it and said: “It is grave. A little later and there would be no saving you. Be at ease; there is no harm.” He then gathered only herbs and applied them, and success followed at every turn as if he were juggling balls, the cure taking effect on the appointed day. By winter I was well, and I wrote a text to thank him. This carbuncle had broken out from the time of my first sitting in Chan, and I knew it to be a debt of enmity: whenever I wrote out or recited the Avatamsaka, it would secretly break out, and at my prayer it would stop. Even after coming to Guangdong it had twice threatened without coming to a head; this affliction has been on my body for forty-eight years. At its first rising I happened to forget it and did not know it was a carbuncle, and so it became a grave illness. The requital of that karmic enmity was indeed tested upon my body without fail. In the tenth month, when the illness was cured, I wrote a special letter to Zeng Jinjian, the ministry official of Hengyang, my friend beyond the world, with whom I had long had a pact to retire together in old age at Nanyue; I had written a dozen times without being able to go. Now I sent a special letter, and when my disciple Xuanzhan came to welcome me I set off with my staff, and so left Guangdong. When I first came to Guangdong, several tens of disciples of the Dharma-nature followed me; in time they dwindled, and only Tongjiong and Chaoyi followed me through storm and hardship, trouble and illness, never leaving my side. Tong’an came and went often; now that I was about to leave, none could bear it, and so An and Yi carried their rain-hats with all their strength and followed. I brought with me the attendants Fuhui, Guangyi, and Guangcheng, crossed the ridge, and in the eleventh month of that year reached Hudong, and settled there. Before this my disciple Fushan, with the attendant Shenguang, had gone north to visit his kin; now, within a few days, they too caught up with us. (The Great General Lord Wang Hanchong, the sore-doctor Liang Xingshan, and the ministry official Zeng Jinjian, and the disciples Xuanzhan and Tongjiong, once each. Chaoyi and Tong’an, a second time each. Fuhui, Guangyi, Guangcheng, and Shenguang, once each. Fushan, a fourth time. Jinjian was named Fengyi, courtesy name Shunzheng, a man of Hengyang, who retired as a ministry official of Rites, styled himself the Nanyue Mountain Elder, and wrote the General Understanding of the Surangama in eight fascicles.)

Fuzheng observes: of all the Patriarchs, there is none who does not speak of following the times, and none who does not speak of paying off debts. Can it be that the fixed karma accumulated through lives, even by the great Dharma of the Avatamsaka, may be prayed away and borrowed against, but never escaped? That a body which for forty-eight years suffered again and again from that grudging carbuncle should in the end become an imperishable flesh-body — therein is seen the spiritual efficacy of the great Dharma. The Patriarch Hanshan went back and forth east, west, south, and north; the black-robed and white-robed who took refuge in him cannot be counted even by changing servants. Yet what the chronicle records are as sparse as morning stars. Even the great lords of the time are often not given their names, titles, or native places. In the case of Lord Zeng, the account is somewhat complete, yet even so his name is not given. From entering Guangdong in the yiwei year to this point is eighteen years, and only now does he write the two words “left Guangdong.” In between — his garrison at Leiyang, his entry into Nan-Shao, the restoration of the Nanhua Temple at Caoxi, the Baolin Hall, the pilgrims’ rest hall, and all those great public cases — are all closed with the two words “left Guangdong.” Yet the karmic occasion of Caoxi was in the end neither closed nor gone. Fuzheng further observes: Patriarch Lu, from Huangmei to Caoxi, hid his traces among the hunters’ band for seventeen years before he was shaved beneath the bodhi tree. The Patriarch Hanshan, with hair bound and in the army for six years, preached at Caoxi too with cap and girdle. Patriarch Lu, at the invitation of the prefect of Shaozhou, then sat with the fourfold assembly of one thousand two hundred and preached the Prajñā; from that time his light flowed to the eight borders and his way covered the world. The Patriarch Hanshan, garrisoned in Guangdong, was permitted, at the request of the governor and the various authorities, to move his staff to Caoxi, and at once made the butchers’ doors and wine-shops flourish into a precious monastery; black-robed and white-robed gathered in crowds, and he used the winning and the subduing hand together, so that the seed of Dajian’s way sprang up and was restored. Patriarch Lu’s flesh-body is at Baolin; he passed into cessation in the second year of the Xiantian era of Emperor Zhongzong of Tang. Down to the twenty-fourth year of the Wanli era of Ming, the bingshen year, the Patriarch Hanshan first crossed the ridge and came face to face with Patriarch Lu. Down to the third year of Tianqi his flesh-body passed into cessation at Caoxi, and further down to the sixteenth year of Chongzhen, the guiwei year, he came again from Wuru, crossed the ridge a second time, and opened the reliquary, so that they stood close together face to face — counting in round numbers, exactly a thousand years. Shining on each other before and after, they fit like the two halves of a tally: the sage before and the sage after, their measure is one. As for the tales that circulate in the world, such as those of Chen Yaxian, Master Xiao, and Mao Laizhai, Fuzheng verified their errors from the attendants of the Zongjing Hall. Only the affair of the precepts and wine for the attendant Lingtong he heard in especial detail and verified in especial truth, and it may be recorded. The attendant Lingtong was the crown prince of the kingdom of Champa; his father the king sent five great ministers with the crown prince to Caoxi to invite the Sixth Patriarch to come and receive offerings among them. The Sixth Patriarch would not go, and the crown prince and the five ministers all stood and passed away on the seashore and did not return. The five ministers became spirits and manifested their power in Shaoyang. The people set up a shrine to the lords outside the mountain gate of the Nanhua Temple, and beside it is the Lords’ Bridge. After the crown prince had passed away, he again, by his spiritual nature, appeared in bodily form as an attendant of the Sixth Patriarch, and alone did not abstain from wine; the Sixth Patriarch permitted it, and he received the transmission of the Dharma and departed. One bowl was left behind in the temple, and the monks cast a bronze image of him standing in attendance beside the Sixth Patriarch’s flesh-body. On the image’s head there is a cloth cap. The villagers near the temple would fill the bowl with wine each day and make offering of it, and the wine would turn to water. After the wine was offered, the cap would sit crooked. When the Patriarch Hanshan first entered the mountain and wished to confer the precepts on the assembly, the assembly said: “The attendant Lingtong drinks wine; we are not fit to receive the precepts.” The Master therefore wrote a text and announced it before the Sixth Patriarch’s seat, first giving the attendant Lingtong the precept against wine, and then smashed his bowl. In the announcement he said: “Smash the vessel of wine, to make it a vessel of Dharma. The attendant Lingtong from this time shall not receive wine offerings” — and when wine was offered, the cap did not sit crooked and the wine did not turn to water.

Fuzheng further notes: Lord Zeng Jinjian wrote the General Understanding of the Surangama, in which he says of himself that he was on terms of perfect friendship with Master Hanshan. He first visited him at Mount Lao, and later, when Master Hanshan entered Guangdong and passed through Luochuan, he respectfully entrusted him with the Surangama, and at Leiyang the Master wrote his Notes. Fuzheng has now seen Lord Zeng’s General Understanding, which blends the three translations, and comparing it with the Notes, it seems that the Patriarch Hanshan, when he reached Leiyang, sent the Notes to Jinjian, thereby discharging his former promise. Yet in the earlier chronicle, under the two years bingshen and dingyou, it says that he began to annotate the Surangama, and again that the Surangama Notes were completed. As for its origin, it says that Wang Xinghai of Daxing did reverence by the river and asked for the annotation, which has nothing to do with Jinjian. I do not know what to make of it — could both requests have come at the same time and the work have been finished so quickly?
The above closes the public case of the revival of Caoxi.
The Forty-Second Year, Jiayin ●

I was sixty-nine. When I left Guangdong, those disciples who could not follow me felt their longing grow the keener. At that time the scholar Feng Qinan and others sent letters inviting Fuhui to take my seat in my stead. That year I sent Fushan to escort Hui back to Guangdong. In late spring I travelled to Mount De to pay homage to the Patriarch, and wrote four poems. I visited Lord Feng Yuancheng at Wuling and wrote two poems. I met the assistant commissioner Long Zhuling, received the vegetarian feast of the Prince of Rong, and at the Dashan Temple the assembled monks asked me to expound the precepts. Lord Feng and his fellow followers each contributed funds to build the Tanhua Hut. Returning to Hengyang, I passed Xiangtan by boat and met Bao Yifu. In the fourth month of summer I returned to Huguang, and hearing that the Sacred Mother had passed into heaven, I at once established a bodhimanda of requiting kindness. There was a gracious edict, and so before the spirit tablet I had my head shaved, gave thanks for the grace, and returned to the monastic dress. As for the Surangama Sutra, from the time I was at the Eastern Sea I had resolved to write a General Exposition, and it had long been stored in my heart with no leisure to set it down. In the fifth month of this summer I put brush to paper, and in fifty days the draft was complete. In the eleventh month the hut was finished; there are poems on dwelling in the mountains. At that time my disciples Wuxin and Zhuanyu came to visit me. (The Sacred Mother, an eleventh time. The scholar Feng Qinan, once; Fuhui, a second time. Fushan, a fifth time. Feng Yuancheng, a second time. The assistant commissioner Long Zhuling, the Prince of Rong, Bao Yifu, and the disciples Wuxin and Zhuanyu, once each. Yifu was named Hongkui, a man of Xiushui, a presented scholar, magistrate of Xiangtan, and a lifelong believer in the Buddha.)

Fuzheng observes: that the Guangdong disciples came to invite the attendant Fuhui to take his seat at Baolin — this was the origin of his return to Caoxi. It was before the Sacred Mother’s spirit tablet that he was willing to be shaved, give thanks for grace, and return to the monastic dress. Before this, when the grace of pardon came, when the case was examined and cleared and he was released from the ranks, for eight years he had been unwilling lightly to return of himself to the monastic dress. In the end he had to wait for a bodhimanda of requiting kindness for the Sacred Mother from first to last, requiting the grace of the Sacred Mother’s long life at Mount Tai — and in the karmic cause of the accumulated provisions of the Baoon Temple, there was a doubly close significance. An extraordinary calamity, an extraordinary requital of kindness, an extraordinary gracious edict, an extraordinary shaving — truly an extraordinary juncture of many lives and many ages. The Sacred Mother was the Empress Dowager Cisheng of the Li family, an imperial consort of the Longqing reign, who gave birth to the Shenzong Emperor and the Prince of Lu. Afterwards, as empress dowager, she was faithful and delighted in giving, and everywhere was called the Buddha Old Lady. By Ming regulation, the father of an empress’s kin who bore a crown prince could be enfeoffed as marquis for one generation only, and the sons and younger brothers merely inherited the embroidered-uniform guard position. Only the empress dowager’s father was enfeoffed as Duke of Xuanguo, and her nephew Li Chengming inherited the title of Marquis of Wuqing, continuing for three generations without interruption, with many of the family also passing the examinations, their honour and prosperity without equal; people took this as the reward of the Sacred Mother’s lifelong service to the Buddha. In the twelfth year of Chongzhen, Chengming’s eldest son by a concubine, Guochen, quarrelled with his half-brother over the succession to the title and the family property. The Emperor was angry, saying that hereditary titles for imperial kin were not in the ancestral rules, and moreover disliked their great wealth; an order was discussed to confiscate the estate. Those who carried it out were too hasty, and the Li family could not bear it. Suddenly one day the fifth imperial prince died of illness; after a while he revived and said to the Emperor: “I went and saw the Old Ancestress, who is now accomplishing Buddhahood under the title Bodhisattva Nine Lotuses. She said that the estate of the Marquis of Wuqing was bestowed by me in my lifetime and passed to your father; being guiltless, it may not be confiscated. National calamity is not far off. You go, and I shall come soon.” Having spoken, he soon died. The Emperor, hearing it, was greatly astonished, and so he let the imperial kin settle it among themselves, shelved the former proposal, and built a temple to the Bodhisattva Nine Lotuses north of the palace. This marked the presage of the nation’s fall, and further proved the efficacy of the Buddha-Dharma. I also hear that when the Sacred Mother passed into heaven, she charged the Wanli Emperor, regretting that she had not been able to have Master Daguan and Hanshan establish a bodhimanda, and hearing that Hanshan was still in Guangdong, urged that he be summoned back, and so on. This Fuzheng learned in some detail while serving in the capital at the military supply bureau, where he often worked with the palace eunuchs. The draft of the General Exposition on the Surangama was completed in fifty days, settling the case of twenty-seven years before, the wuzi affair at Haiyin; it too seems to bear closely on the affairs of the Sacred Mother. At that time there was a verse, “Seeing Off Wuxin Rong, Chief Seat, as He Returns to Jingkou”: “In the empty hills I meant to spend my old age’s remnant; who would have thought you would sail east on the Dharma ship? Wait till the lone moon rises over the sea gate; then round off a meditation topic for the old monk.” And one “Inquiring after the Illness of Zhuanyu Heng”: “Long have I watched the four elements as bubbles and shadows; where can the demon of illness hide? The ancients had their own way of resting at ease: it lies only in the single thought of the unborn.” Reading these, one may know the old practice and native capacity of Masters Wu and Zhuan, and may also imagine the karmic bond that led the two of them to travel together to distant provinces.
In that year began the karmic occasion of the Eastern Journey from Nanyue to Mount Kuang.
The Forty-Third Year, Yimao ●

I was seventy. In spring I expounded the General Exposition on the Surangama for the assembly. In the fourth month of summer I wrote the General Exposition on the Lotus Sutra: since, though there were two sections, the full text was not yet thoroughly unified, I expounded it again, and the draft was likewise finished in fifty days. I lectured on the Awakening of Faith and compiled a Brief Commentary on the Awakening of Faith. In the seventh month of autumn I travelled to Nanyue and climbed Zhurong Peak, and wrote poems. On the Double Ninth, Lord Feng, transferred from Wuling to be prefect of Hunan, again invited me to journey with him to Fangguang. Returning to the prefectural city, he and the circuit intendant Lord Wu Shengbai came to visit me at Hudong; when the talk turned to the Surangama, Lord Wu was overjoyed and at once, with his subordinates, contributed funds to have it printed. At the reverence paid to the portraits of the eighty-eight patriarchs, Lord Wu was filled with admiration, and he ordered a painter to copy the small portraits into an album, asking me to write a biography and praise for each. Lord Feng had not long been in office when he invited me to journey to Jiuyi. In the tenth month of winter I reached Lingling and stayed the winter at Yuxi. (Lord Feng Yuancheng, a third time. The circuit intendant Wu Shengbai, once. Shengbai was named Zhongwei, a man of Haiyan, and served as vice-minister of justice.)

Fuzheng observes: this old man of seventy, expounding the Indian scriptures, writing expositions and compiling commentaries, had not a day’s leisure — this is the place in words and letters where the waters run out and the mountains end. Śākyamuni taught for forty-nine years and bequeathed five thousand and forty-eight divisions, yet said he had never spoken a single word. Confucius edited the Odes and Documents, settled the rites and music, praised the Zhou Changes, and compiled the Spring and Autumn Annals, all of it in the years after he was sixty-eight and before he was seventy-three. He forgot food and forgot care, unaware that old age was coming on. In the end he said: “I wish to be without words” — what words has Heaven? As for the First Patriarch’s four fascicles of the Surangama and the Sixth Patriarch’s one fascicle of the Diamond, are these words or no words, a staff or a shout, the same or different? O my Master, my Master! — and hereupon Fuzheng was moved.
The Forty-Fourth Year, Bingchen ●

I was seventy-one. In the first month of spring I returned from Lingling. In the year following Chan Master Daguan’s entry into cessation, my disciple Dayi had asked that his reliquary be brought south, and the black-robed and white-robed disciples had enshrined and honoured it at the Jizhao Hut on Mount Jing — a full twelve years now. I could not forget my obligation in the Dharma gate, and had long wished to go in person to mourn him, and so I had not even sent incense. Now, hearing of the day of burial, I was determined to go. Moreover, there was an invitation from the Eastern Chan Temple at Jinsha, so I set out in high spirits. As I was about to leave, the assembled monks of the Huayao Temple asked me to a feast, to continue the Dharma lineage. I passed by the Meixue Hall and mourned the Chan master Xun’an. In the fourth month of summer I left Hudong, and wrote a poem, Leaving Nanyue: A Self-Mocking Explanation. At the Dragon Boat Festival I reached Wuchang, paid homage to the Great Buddha, visited the Nine Peaks, and did reverence at the stupa of Chan Master Wunian. In the sixth month I reached Xunyang, visited the Eastern Grove, and wrote a poem on the past. I climbed Mount Kuang, mourned Chan Master Chekong, took my summer retreat at Jinzhu Ping, and annotated the Zhao Lun. Seeing how secluded and lovely the mountain was, I had thoughts of retiring there. I viewed all its beauties. In the seventh month I visited Guizong, climbed the Golden Wheel Peak, did reverence at the relic stupa, and wrote poems. It happened that a certain monk offered me the Wuru Peak as a quiet hut. When I climbed up and looked about, I saw that the ground was not broad but the setting was quite secluded, and so I accepted it. At that time the provincial graduate Xing Laici of Jiangzhou wished to be my golden-giving patron, and at once contributed fifty pieces of gold to buy the mountain for me, and so my wish to spend my old age there was fulfilled. It happened that Chen Chishi, assistant administrator of Fuliang, heard I had arrived and came to the mountain to visit me; hearing that I had my mind set on Mount Kuang, he vowed to be a protector of the Dharma. In the eighth month of autumn I left the mountain and came to Huangmei, where I did reverence to the Fourth and Fifth Patriarchs. I visited the Minister of War Wang and entered the Purple Cloud Mountain, staying ten days; Lord Wang was willing to be the patron for the building at Mount Kuang, and he brought along the Prince of Jing and Prefect Yuan and others; then, as the Seven Worthies Society, we parted. At Tongcheng I visited the grand historian Wu Guanwo and the assistant censor Wu Benru, who wished to build a hut to keep me. I visited Mount Fu and wrote a song. I crossed the river and climbed Mount Jiu. At the beginning of the tenth month I reached the Eastern Chan Temple at Jinsha and met the gentlemen Yu, Wang, and Sun. Soon after, leaving Jinsha, I went straight to Shuangjing. Passing Qu’a, the magistrate Lord Wang of Dongli asked me about the Dharma at Guanyin Mountain. The He family of Jiangshu welcomed me to their family villa and kept me several days, then provided a boat to send me on. Passing Liangxi, I visited Mount Hui, where the vice-minister Gao Jingyi and other gentlemen entertained me at the Zou family garden. The provincial graduate Wang of Loudong and the laymen Zhang Jiufu and others welcomed me at the pass, lodged me in their homes, and reverently asked for the essentials of the Dharma. Passing Wujiang, I met the Zhou and Shen gentlemen at the Jiedai Cloister. The layman Yan Shengsheng of Shimen waited to welcome me at Songling and brought me to his home, providing vegetarian provisions to accompany my journey. On the fifteenth of the long-day month I reached the Jizhao Hut. On the nineteenth I performed the cremation rites for Master Daguan. At that time the Master’s disciples, monks and lay, all gathered; I first offered a text in sacrifice. The day had been fixed beforehand and there was no discrepancy. On the twenty-fifth I gathered up the spiritual bones with my own hands and enshrined them at the Mañjuśrī Terrace. My disciple Fakai built the stupa accordingly, and I wrote the inscription upon it, thereby fulfilling to the full my obligation in the Dharma gate of his lifetime. Then I stayed in the mountain to pass the year, giving informal instruction to the patch-robed monks of the Chan hall, which produced the Essentials of Chan Practice. Master Kai asked about the Faxiang school, and I set out for him the General Explanation of Nature and Characteristics. To each who asked for instruction I gave Dharma words, and composed the Song of the Pole-Carrier. The laymen Zhu Baimin and Wang Jie’an of Wumen talked with me morning and evening, taking Dharma joy as their delight. At that time the grand historian Qian Shouzhi of Mount Yu and the secretary Yan Tianchi invited me by letter, and the assistant censor Jin of Wulin and the ministry official Yu, with other gentry, all sent letters to welcome me; but as it was the end of the year I did not accept. (Master Daguan, a seventh time. The disciple Dayi, the Chan master Xun’an, and Chan Master Wunian, once each. Master Chekong, a third time. The provincial graduate Xing Laici and Chen Chishi, assistant administrator of Fuliang, once each. Minister of War Wang, no sobriquet; the Prince of Jing, Prefect Yuan, no sobriquets. Grand Historian Wu Guanwo, Assistant Censor Wu Benru, the Jinsha gentlemen Yu, Wang, and Sun, and the He family of Qu’a, all without sobriquets. Magistrate Wang Dongli, Vice-Minister Gao Jingyi, the provincial graduate Wang of Loudong, without sobriquets; the laymen Zhang Jiufu and the Zhou and Shen gentlemen of Wujiang, all without sobriquets; Yan Shengsheng of Shimen, the Master’s disciple Fakai, the laymen of Wumen Zhu Baimin and Wang Jie’an, Grand Historian Qian Shouzhi of Mount Yu, Secretary Yan Tianchi, Assistant Censor Jin, and Ministry Official Yu, all without sobriquets, once each. Chishi was named Dashou and served as chief equerry. Minister of War Wang, sobriquet Jingfeng, was a man of Huangmei and served as supreme commander of Miyun. Prefect Yuan is the later prefect of Nankang, Lord Yuan Jiuji. Guanwo was named Yingbin, and Benru was named Yongxian, both of Tongcheng. Wang Dongli was named Zhidao, a man of Quanzhou, and served as chief censor. Jingyi was named Panlong, a man of Wuxi, and served as left chief censor. Baimin was named Lu, a man of Suzhou, famed for painting bamboo. Jie’an was named Zaigong, courtesy name Mengsu, a man of Kunshan, who became magistrate as a provincial graduate and soon threw up office and left. Shouzhi was named Qianyi, a man of Changshu, and served as Grand Master of Rites. Tianchi was named Ne, a man of Changshu. Assistant Censor Jin was named Xuezeng, sobriquet Xingwu. Ministry Official Yu was named Chunxi, sobriquet Deyuan, both men of Qiantang. Deyuan wrote the preface to the Eastern Journey Collection.)

Fuzheng observes: in this year, the first half of the chronicle gives the origin of the Fayun Temple on Wuru Peak. The latter half gives the origin of the Eastern Journey Collection: at Jinsha, Qu’a, Wumen, and Wulin, the faithful and Dharma companions of that time, among whom Fuzheng came to take refuge in the Master, was given the name Fuzheng and the courtesy name Liangsheng. In the whole chronicle the great junctures are: first the reverence paid to the First Patriarch, next to the Sixth Patriarch, and now to the Fourth and Fifth Patriarchs — each one following the season’s occasion, face to face seal and attestation, the flesh-body heir of the Patriarchs: marvellous and great indeed. When the Master reached the Jizhao Hut at Shuangjing, Fuzheng was lodging at West Lake in the Liaozhai, reading. Because of the collapse of the great building and the shelter of three beams, and the karmic cause of his rebirth, he hurried to Mount Jing to pay his respects to Chan Master Xueqiao, and in the Qianzhi Hut that had been built before, he was urged to lead in person the worship of the Liang Emperor’s Repentance; when the seven days were done he at once gained ease and lightness of body and mind. He vowed to press on with vigour and did not return home from the mountain, and it happened that at the Jizhao Hut he met the Master, who had come up the mountain to cremate Master Daguan — the very day on which the Master opened the sacrificial text sealed at Nanyue, without a day’s discrepancy. Yan Shengsheng was a man of Tongxiang county living at Shimen, Fuzheng’s fellow graduate, and the father of Kaimei, whose name was Junyan. One evening he had beforehand dreamed of the temple guardian spirit, who bade him welcome Piṇḍola; he saw one seated in the central hall in the place of honour, with attendants seated to either side, all famous elders of the time, masters of Dharma and Vinaya, those he had known in the past — all were there, and he woke with a start. The next day he heard that the Master was coming east, and he ordered a boat to go and welcome him at Songling, and travelled with him through Shuangjing, Yunqi, and the hills about the lake. Wherever they went, he attended the Master longest along with Fuzheng, and was named Fujian. Later, when the Master returned and passed through Shimen, Shengsheng invited him to his home, where there was a troupe of players; the Master ordered them to perform The Pavilion of Moon-Worship, and a great offering was made. Only those attendants who had received full ordination were first chosen and permitted to sit at the feast; all the rest were forbidden. Among those seated at the time were such famous elders as Chaosong, Yiyu, Zhihe, Wengu, Gude, Foshi, Dezong, Xinzong, Xuanjin, and others. In the course of the feast Shengsheng said to Fuzheng: “This is clear and distinct — the very scene of people and setting I saw in my dream of Piṇḍola.” The next day Fuzheng, in the Dharma boat, asked: “Does watching a play hinder the precepts?” The Master sighed and said: “Very hard to say. Another man who does not break the precepts for a day is for that day not breaking the precepts. I who do not break the precepts day after day am day after day breaking the precepts.” Hearing this, Fuzheng felt his heart sink and his courage fail, and to this day the words are still in his ears. The Essentials of Chan Practice and the Song of the Pole-Carrier were both preached for the assembly in the great hall of Mount Jing. It is widely said in various quarters that the Song of the Pole-Carrier was written for Chan Master Xueqiao, but this is a great error. Master Xue stood alone, lofty and steep, and was out of tune with many famous Chan masters; only with our Master was he in unbroken accord. The Master wrote for him the True Praise of the Mountain Master Xueqiao and the Six Wonders Inscription of the Qianzhi Hut. As he was about to leave, he again received from Master Xue the offering of an iron ruyi and wrote an inscription for it; all of this is in the Eastern Journey Collection, and reading it one may know the occasion of their meeting and accord. Therefore I record the Song of the Pole-Carrier here, to resolve the doubts that arise in the Dharma gate.

Song of the Pole-Carrier, with preface: The Dharma cavern of Mount Jing, since Dahui revived the way of Linji, has continued the wisdom-life without a break, and each generation has had its men. Of late the Chan gate has been desolate and its echoes have long ceased. Just now there gathered in the mountain a whole company of students investigating Chan, some of whom, at a single thought, glimpsed the ground and had it appear before them, attaining great freedom. It is a pity that, seated on that pure white ground, they are unwilling to let it go, thinking it extraordinary, not knowing that it becomes a hindrance to the Dharma; in the teachings it is called the obstruction of the knowable. Therefore the ancient worthy said: Even if you can reach the point of a cold pool and bright moon, of the bell-sound in the still night, unimpaired by any knock, undispersed by any wave, it is still a matter on the shore of birth and death. It is as said: In a thicket of thorns it is easy to set foot, but beneath the bright moon’s curtain it is hard to turn the body. This is called clutching the tip of the pole, sitting still in dead water. Even that is not permitted to be dwelt in, much less the case of one who has not yet reached the glimpse of the ground, who has by chance obtained a lightning-flash samādhi and thinks he has attained it, juggling the shadows of the conscious spirit. This is the common ailment of all ages: to be satisfied with a little in Chan. I feared it would fall into the world’s way and spread, misleading many. When someone asked for instruction, I smiled and showed him the Song of the Pole-Carrier. The song says: Pole-carrier, pole-carrier, why so sorely cheated? You want your shoulder light, your stumbling heel unheeded. Though you should bear it back before your birth began, it has long since hidden half of you from man. This board, this cangue upon your neck is hung, and all your flesh and bone to it are bound; if you do not cast it off while it is new, through a hundred thousand kalpas it will prove your foe at last. Sitting, it wearies you; walking, it wearies too. It is plainly a hindrance — why can you not see? Only because at first you took the false for true, a demon breeds within a house of purity. Eyes open, you see it; eyes shut, you see it still; by day the void sprouts lightning in the skies. The Gandharva city rises as a shadow in the air, and the foolish child takes it for paradise. Would you be light? Then you must put it down. What price is a stinking dead toad worth, I pray? Black beans traded in for your own eyes — you must discern the fish-eye from the true alway. There is a road, and it is the best to tread, broad and level as a balance-beam: only do not dally by the flowers and willows, and you shall surely reach the imperial city, I deem. Cast off body and life as if the great earth, nor shun to be ox or horse, camel or ass. If you can truly toss them beyond Sumeru, the sword-tree and the knife-hill are but child’s play. Love it, and by it you shall be undone; its burdens come of all the care you spend. One morning when the crystal flask is broken, the earth and all its hills are shattered to the end. I counsel you: do not carry it at all. The sweat upon a skull dries straight away. Divide your body, scatter your shadow into millions; from now you shall not enter death’s gate, come what may.

Fuzheng further notes: what the Master’s own chronicle records of himself sets down only the outline and has no leisure to set down the details. The commentary that Fuzheng has written likewise obtains only one tenth of what he saw and heard, and omits nine tenths. For instance, in this year’s entry, “he was willing to be the patron for the building at Mount Kuang,” and in the next year’s entry, “Lord Wang, who had already provided the funds to build the quiet hut” — such a faithful patron and official is called only “Minister of War Wang,” with no full name and no native place. Reading it in the past, I supposed it must be the former Minister of War Wang Boyu; but the years are far apart and Chu and She are distant from each other, which was just what I could not explain. Lately, seeing the Master’s Dharma kinsman Master Rongcheng, I learned that it was Lord Jingfeng, who lived at Huangmei and served as supreme commander. So then the omissions among the faithful who took refuge in him are past counting. Again, in that year’s entry, when he reached Jinzhu Ping at Mount Kuang, there are the four words “viewed all its beauties,” which must embrace I know not how many events of the bodhimanda. For example, at Jiujiang there is the bodhimanda of Master Yuan of Shimen, where the Master dwelt for a month and preached, and the man he appointed as abbot there was Master Rongcheng. He had first been a student of Xiuning, of the surname Cheng and the name Keyu; he studied at Shimen with the layman Bi Guanzhi, and at his first sight of the Master he abandoned his home, took refuge, and was shaved, receiving the Dharma name Guangshel, and was then appointed abbot of the Shimen bodhimanda. Later, when the Master was at Wuru, he repeatedly sent handwritten letters charging him to manage the affairs of Shimen, and his instructions were earnest and pressing; this was his closest Dharma heir at the time, yet the chronicle has no leisure to record it. One day Master Rong, with Shao Shisheng, brought various writings in the Master’s own hand to the Ou-xie Dwelling at the Rain-Flower Terrace, burned incense, recited them, and so wrote a note to record it. Another day the master Shaoxuan, whose Dharma name was Ciyi, came from Jiangyin to visit; he was the Dharma grandson of Master Zhiwei and the Dharma heir of Master Cimen. He had once lived at Fayun, later at the One-Bowl Chan Grove in Xunyang, and had also restored the Xiujing Temple at Hongshan in Wuchang. In the chaos of war he buried bones wherever he went and twice established land-and-water rites. He was by birth a son of the Lu family of Jiangyin; after the dynastic change he returned to his village and is now restoring the Wanfo Chan Grove. He says that the disciples he has saved, such as Renda and Liangming, are very many, but that he never had the chance to attend the Master in person. Of the chief disciples whom the Master most approved, none equalled Master Zhiwei, whose name was Fushan. In the beginning he shared good and ill fortune with the Master, appearing six times in the chronicle of the Master’s approaching death; in the end he ran about supporting the reliquary and recorded in detail the karmic circumstances of the Master’s last affairs. He is the true son of Wuru. Again there is Master Xuzhong, whose name was Guangyi: at the Baolin assembly he personally witnessed the nirvāṇa, begged the Master to let down his foot, and transmitted his dying words — all clearly attested; he is the adopted grandson of Caoxi. Now Master Zhiwei’s great-great-grandson Renxi, styled Mingji, studies the Dharma at Changgan; and Master Xuzhong has a disciple Ciren, styled Jianru, who is abbot of Qixia. It was these too whom Fuzheng, after the chaos, met by karmic chance while lodging in the old capital of Nanking, and who brought the chronicle and commentary to completion. Among these, the circumstances of the Master’s last affairs, as heard from Kuanju, whose name was Guangyong, are especially detailed and accurate. The many later accounts are all untrustworthy, and I dare not set them down rashly. I regret that he passed away so suddenly at Qixia, and did not live to see the chronicle and commentary completed. Kuanju was in truth the heir of Zhiwei and the grandfather of Mingji. Again, at one time, going back and forth to the Patriarch’s Hall and the Bao’en Temple, there was one whom Fuzheng met when Master Su of Lingfeng was preaching: Master Huaibai, whose name was Hengdao, who had lived at Fayun for more than two years, attended the Master closely, and received the full precepts from him. And the prior of the Patriarch’s Hall, Zhanchi, whose name was Xiuru, was the grandson of Great Master Xuelang and the direct heir of the revered elder brother whom the Master often remembered. All these gentlemen, together with Master Su of Lingfeng, had deep Dharma bonds, and by rule are recorded here after the Dharma lineage.

From taking refuge in that year onward, in all matters of attending closely on the Master, Fuzheng began to call him “our Master.” At first he enshrined and honoured his Dharma image at the Dragon-Tree Altar of Mount Yao, and later at the Ou-xie Dwelling of the Rain-Flower Terrace — this when the monk Juelang was preaching in the Three Treasures Hall, and he specially led the assembled attendants to do reverence at the feet of the one who presided there. Now that Master Su is again preaching in the Three Treasures Hall, Fuzheng has been able to take counsel with him and bring the excellent work of the chronicle and commentary to completion; the whole origin of it is recorded here.

Master Su was of the Zhong family; in his youth he lived at Sumen and studied the Confucian classics, firmly believing in Confucius, whom he often saw in dreams. At seventeen, reading Master Lian’s writings, he first awakened to the Pure Land. At twenty-two, through Master Xueling Jun’s Key to the Contemplation Hymn he came into accord with our Master, went to Mount Kuang to consult him, and there, offering a stick of incense, asked about the Dharma. The Master showed the layman Zhong a verse: “The West lies only in your own heart’s head; when afflictions are empty, deluded thoughts are stilled. Then you will see Amitābha’s true face: he comes of old, from the sea of suffering, sailing his boat of compassion.” Two years later he relied on Master Xue, abandoned his home, and was shaved. From then until the Master’s passing into cessation there were four occasions of dream-karma. Now he expounds the Tiantai school and points the way to the Pure Land — the Dharma milk that Fuzheng witnessed with his own eyes.
The Forty-Fifth Year, Dingyi ●

I was seventy-two. On the first day of the first month of spring I expounded the precepts for the assembly. I went down from Shuangjing to mourn at Yunqi; more than a thousand black-robed and white-robed disciples had long been waiting in the mountain, and I stayed twenty days. Every night I gave informal instruction and answered questions on the Dharma; each was filled with joy, and I set forth the secret practices of Master Lianchi’s life. Some disciples wept to hear it, saying that I had revealed what others did not know, and they asked me to write his stupa inscription. When I left the mountain, Master Xuanjin and the scholar Tan Mengxun, with the gentry and laymen of the prefecture, invited me to stay at the Zongjing Hall of Jingci; for days thousands of fingers were raised around me as I expounded the great precepts, and I wrote the Record of the Zongjing Hall. At that time all the famous worthies of every quarter gathered about the lake, and with the scholar Tan asked about the Dharma, each pressing his own hard questions; it was called the greatest Dharma assembly of the southeast, such as had never been seen before. Then I visited Lingyin, the Three Zhu, and the Western Hills, and praised the three ponds of releasing life, and so departed. At that time the officials and laymen of the city provided boats to release living creatures and gave me a farewell feast on the lake, and moreover drew up a petition asking me to stay at Yunqi; so there was a promise of three years. Passing Zhili, the vice-minister Yue Shifan and the assistant prefect Xiang Chudong, old acquaintances of mine, met me at the Lengyan Chan Cloister. It happened that Shen Lübo of Linxi welcomed me to his home, and in the midst of the gathering he suddenly asked where the stupa of the former Master Yungu was, saying he did not know its whereabouts. The layman told him at once: “Near, quite near — about a li from Qizhen.” I was overjoyed, and that evening I went to the temple and did reverence at my late master’s stupa. I saw that the temple was most secluded and lovely, while the stupa court was rather desolate; I was sad for a long while. Regretting that my journey was hurried and I could not set it in order, I respectfully asked Mr. Shen to repair it in my stead, and charged him to establish a long-life field to support the incense and lamps. Of all that I passed by on that journey, the writings I made at the time were collected by Master Xuanjin He and the scholar Tan Mengxun into four fascicles and printed under the title Eastern Journey Collection. Returning to Wumen, the two masters Chaosong and Yiyu invited me into Mount Hua and to visit Tianchi, Xuanmu, and Iron Mountain, all famous places. At Cold Mountain the gentlemen Zhao Fanfu, Wen Wenqi, Yao Mengchang, Xu Zhongrong, and Xu Qingzhi asked about the Way at Guanyin Mountain. The two officials Feng Yuancheng and Shen Xuanzhu entertained me at their homes. As I was about to set out, my disciples Dongwen and Hanyue, the grand historian Qian, Wang Jihe, and Qu Wanchu welcomed me to Changshu, and so I came to Mount Yu and lodged two nights. The grand historian of Fushui escorted me to Qu’a, where He Zhiren and his sons and nephews waited at the Sanli Hut at Benniu and asked me to stay in their garden for the summer retreat. I firmly declined and returned to the mountain. The layman He Zhiren gave me the portraits of the eighty-eight patriarchs, painted by the great gentleman Ding Yunpeng, and I accepted them. He escorted me to Jingkou, where I received the vegetarian feast of the black-robed and white-robed of Three Mountains, and in the Dache Hall expounded the precepts for the assembly. When it was done I at once set sail for Mount Kuang, and on the first day of the fifth month passed Baixia, spending a night on the river and seeing one or two old friends. On the fifth I reached Wuhu, where Liu Yushou of the works ministry was supervising the customs barrier and detained me, asking me to write A Discourse on Strange Dreams. The ministry official Cui Helou met me on the river. On the sixteenth day of the fifth month the boat reached Xingzhu, and I arrived at Guizong and lodged there. At that time Minister of War Wang had already provided the funds to build me a quiet hut, and on the fifteenth of the sixth month I ordered my disciple Fushan to begin work at Wuru; by the tenth month one room was finished, and I was able to dwell in peace. (Master Lianchi of Yunqi, Master Xuanjin, the scholar Tan Mengxun, and the assistant prefect Xiang Chudong, a second time each. The vice-minister Yue Shifan and Shen Lübo of Linxi, once each. The monk Yungu, a third time. The two masters Chaosong and Yiyu, and Zhao Fanfu, Wen Wenqi, Yao Mengchang, Xu Zhongrong, and Xu Qingzhi of Cold Mountain, once each. Feng Yuancheng, a fourth time. Shen Xuanzhu, Dongwen, and Hanyue, the two masters, once each. The grand historian Qian Shouzhi, a second time. Wang Jihe, Qu Wanchu, the layman He Zhiren and his sons, the works official Liu Yushou, and the ministry official Cui Helou, once each. Minister of War Wang, the former Jingfeng, a second time. The disciple Fushan, a sixth time. Master Xuanjin was named Dahe, a disciple of Great Master Xuelang, abbot of the Zongjing Hall of Jingci, and a colleague of Fuzheng. Shifan was named Yuansheng, a man of Jiaxing, and served as junior minister of war. Fanfu was named Yiguang, famed for cursive seal script. Wenqi was named Zhenmeng, a first-place graduate who became chief minister. Mengchang was named Ximeng, an official of the palace secretariat. Qingzhi was named Rong, a secretariat drafter. Xuanzhu was named Yongmao and served as chief minister. All the above were men of the city of Suzhou. Jihe was named Yuchun, and Wanchu was named Chunren, both famous scholars of Changshu. Yushou was named Xixuan, a man of Suzhou, and served as assistant administrator.)

Fuzheng observes: in the one age of the Great Ming, the great monks of the Dharma gate who appeared together in the Wanli reign and whose fame overflowed were none other than Lianchi of Yunqi, Daguan Zibo, and Hanshan of Caoxi — the three great elders of the world at that time. He who was the flesh-body heir of the Sixth Patriarch was our Master alone. Our Master, an old veteran of seventy, made one Eastern Journey, and the two stupa inscriptions for Yunqi and Zibo stand as imperishable biographies; the sacrificial texts and likeness-praises fill many leaves with splendour, like the three great elders gathered in conversation. That Fuzheng was able to move among them, staff and sandals, was a rare encounter of his life and a good cause from former lives. In the Eastern Journey Collection that Fuzheng copied out with his own hand, the Essentials of Chan Practice was spoken in the Dharma Hall of Mount Jing, the Essentials of Buddha-Recitation in the Dharma Hall of Yunqi, and the Essentials of Reciting the Cundi in the Zongjing Hall of Jingci. For going west and coming east, and for the various secret gates of mantra-holding, these three instructions leave nothing unstated. Master Da was the first and greatest Dharma friend of our Master’s life; he always regretted that he could not weep face to face for him, and the origin of the Eastern Journey was precisely to settle this first great public case. Master Lian’s accord at Mount Wutai was forty-one years before; Master Yungu’s karmic occasion of sitting in Chan at the Tianjie Temple was fifty-two years before, at the very beginning. These other two great public cases were also settled in the half year of the Eastern Journey. On the day he mourned at Yunqi, more than a thousand black-robed and white-robed pressed him to stay in the mountain. He did not grant their request, but had his portrait painted and left it to be honoured, in expectation of the future, asking that they write a praise themselves. The one who, hearing of Master Lian’s secret practices, wept aloud was Lord Song Huaqing, a disciple of Yunqi. He lingered long at the Zongjing Hall, yet the chronicle omits his surname, for the Dharma occasions of that time were so thronged that its light could not be counted through every crack. And so Fuzheng reflects that in all the chronicle’s course, from Bao’en in Nanking to Jingci by West Lake, the places are so many li apart and the times so many years apart. Of the black-robed and white-robed worthies who took refuge in him in a lifetime, no more than one or two in a thousand are preserved. Yet within its words there is a deep import of its own, which the clear-eyed will be able to fathom for themselves.

That which the chronicle says — that Master Xuanjin and the scholar Tan Mengxun, with the gentry and laymen of the same prefecture, invited him to stay at the Zongjing Hall of Jingci, where for days thousands of fingers were raised around him as he expounded the great precepts, and that he visited Lingyin, the Three Zhu, and the Western Hills and all the famous places — was all a matter of a hundred days. At that time, because the Sacred Mother’s gracious master had been persecuted for spreading the Dharma, and after long garrison duty had returned alive, his fame was truly loud and wide: from the provincial grand coordinators and the regional commanders down to officials great and small of the prefectures and counties, and the faithful of every quarter, officials and laymen, and the elders and younger men of the three gates of Dharma, Vinaya, and Chan, all gathered at Wulin — truly a day worth a thousand years. At that time those who first proposed inviting him from Yunqi and then brought him to Jingci at Nanping were the Renhe magistrate Zhou Jihou, the provincial grand coordinator Jin Xingwu of this region, the ministry official Yu Deyuan, the education commissioner Ge Qizhan, the provincial graduate Wen Qixiang, the official Song Huaqing, the literatus Yan Yinchi, the literatus Zou Mengyang, and other faithful donors. The one who set in order the rules of the cloister and managed the various affairs of providing for the assembly was Master Xuanjin He. At first he put his name to the invitation, and afterwards he followed at his heels to carry out his commands, serving as guest-master and secretary and toiling with the morning lamps: this is indeed a great public case in the whole course of our Master’s Eastern Journey through the three Wu regions. At that time Fuzheng attended him daily, and not a day passed but he trembled as though among dragons, gods, and ghosts. He saw that the Master, as he went about, had never a whisk or a staff; his jade countenance was bright and fair, and in the summer heat he did not sweat; morning and evening when he washed, the water in the vessel was perfectly clear. When he sat he always crossed his legs in full lotus without troubling his hands to arrange them. Closing his eyes he entered samādhi, opening them he left it — by day, by the lamp, walking, standing, sitting, lying. At the least request his eye-light was like lightning, and no speck ever clung to his lids, nor did he trouble his hand to wipe them. After his calamity his feet were slow to walk and he could not stand long; a few paces and he must be supported, a hundred paces and he must be carried. There were four faithful ones who bore him, two from Caoxi and two from Nanyue, who gave up their bodies to serve him over thousands of li and did not leave him for years. From the day in the tenth month of winter of the yiwei year when he received the decree of garrison in Guangdong, the Master let his beard and hair grow, until his long beard was a foot long, and he preached with cap and girdle for twelve years. Down to the eighth month of autumn of the bingwu year, when the imperial eldest grandson had been born and the gracious amnesty released him from the ranks, he had still not been shaved. Nine years more, until he left Guangdong in the jiayin year, and in the fourth month of summer reached Hudong, where he heard that the Sacred Mother had passed into heaven; then he established a bodhimanda of requiting kindness, and in obedience to the gracious edict had his head shaved before the spirit tablet and changed into the monastic dress. Before this he had gone unshaved in Guangdong for fully twenty years. From that shaving to the day in the eleventh month of winter of the bingchen year when he came east to Shuangjing, when Fuzheng first saw the Master’s perfect form, only three years had passed — not long at all. When he ascended the hall to preach, he would open his mouth for thousands of words without swallowing a single one, like a great bell sounding, heard even outside the hall. When he took up the brush to write words of instruction, he did not alter his usual cross-legged posture, and could spread thousands of characters on the paper with no pause in the brush. The attendants who took down his words were worn out running to and fro, with no leisure all day. With his left hand he would turn his bead-string; with his right he would hold a white bamboo folding fan, never out of his hand winter or summer, lifted but not waved, closed but not opened. When some great matter of command arose among men and gods in the three realms, one rap on the desk and none failed to respond. Bamboo clappers and staff, blows and shouts flying — none could match the working of that one fan. It could make demons retire and obey faster than thunder. Of the reaches of his power of the Way and his spiritual penetration that Fuzheng witnessed with his own eyes, he records here a rough account of the greatest. At the Zongjing Hall, one day as he had just ascended the seat, two monks came supporting a third between them up the steps, raving without cease. His two companions begged the Master to rescue him, saying: “This monk has recited the Great Compassion Mantra for five years and has never done a bad deed; we do not know why he has been possessed by a demon to this degree.” The Master said: “This illness can be cured.” At once he ordered an attendant to inquire throughout the hall, and three who had practiced the secret mantra of Ucchuṣma Vajra were found and brought forward. The Master then recited it himself from his seat and had the practitioners pass on the teaching. At first it was not understood; the Master struck the desk with his fan in a display of awe, and as soon as a single phrase was brought up and passed on, the response came like an echo. The practitioners then passed it on phrase by phrase to the end, and the mad monk awakened as from a dream and withdrew after doing reverence.
