The Master sent him to the incense-kitchen dormitory, and he was as though nothing had been wrong. Those seated there that day included Wu Xingke, the provincial administrator of this province, the Renhe magistrate Zhou Jihou, and the education commissioner Ge

zhan and Yinliang, a whole generation who had never deeply believed, and at this they changed countenance, and the whole assembly was moved. Another day a monk came to do reverence, and before he had risen the Master struck his fan and shouted: “Murderous thief, what do you want with me?” The steward hurried him out. The monk went off without a word, and the assembly stared in astonishment, not understanding. The next day it was heard that he had been arrested for robbery. Such spiritual powers cannot be enumerated. In the two months of his flying staff, every day there was a donor who made an offering of a hundred pieces of gold for the great cauldron of Jingci, boiling ten piculs of rice; whether he stayed or journeyed, not a day passed without lighting the fire. On the day he reached Jiaxing the assembly welcomed him into the Chan hall of the Jinming Temple. The Master ordered Fuzheng to summon his old friends: the minister of war Yue Shifan and the assistant prefect Xiang Chudong, and both came to pay their respects. Chudong, when he held the commission of Kuangzhou, had greatly consorted with the Master and attended him with medicine, settling for a time the judicial officer’s case of demonic possession, and the Master was deeply grateful to him. In their correspondence of that time the Dharma words and handwritten notes were the most numerous. Shifan was wont to make playful talk out of his joy in Chan; formerly, when he was in the ministry of rites and the Master was persecuted for spreading the Dharma, he spoke out boldly to save him. Now they met with great joy. They had scarce sat down and the greetings were not yet done when Yue asked: “Just now I am puzzled by the four phrases on ‘su’ — ‘In wealth and honour, act in wealth and honour; in poverty and meanness, act in poverty and meanness.’ How does the Master explain them?” The Master answered: “Su is a blank sheet of paper: draw a gauze cap and it becomes a gauze cap; draw a beggar and it becomes a beggar.” For in the Ming dynasty officials were called gauze caps. He laughed heartily, and after a while took his leave. At that time, when the feast was done, candles were set out and tea was taken in informal instruction, and the hall door was already shut, when suddenly someone with a staff came shouting outside the door. Some recognized him as the runner Qian of the grain yamen, and took him for a drunken madman; they drove him off but he would not go, and his voice grew shriller, mingled with Buddha-words: “Today the living bodhisattva has come down; I should be delivered. Do not block me.” Fuzheng thought his words strange and told the Master. The Master said: “Call him in.” He came in, joined his palms, and did reverence with the full deportment of a son of the Buddha, and all eyes were upon him. He knelt on both knees and made the bow of a Buddhist. The ghost spoke through him, saying that he was possessed by Qian Da, whose name was Zhong and who was called Ren, and who had borrowed the body to seek deliverance. “Your disciple in life kept a long fast and practiced the Pure Land for eight years. Now the term of my death falls on the fifth seventh-day; I have not gone to the underworld but should be born in the Western Heaven. I beg the bodhisattva in compassion to guide me.” He fell to the ground weeping and wailing without cease. The Master called six elders among the attendants who were devoted to Buddha-recitation to stand by, and himself unrolled the bead-string for him. He at once had a bead-string given to him, and he recited the Buddha’s name a thousand times, and the body the ghost possessed could recite it. The whole hall was solemn and silent. When the recitation was done he had the Mengshan Food-Bestowal Text performed, and when it came to “One should contemplate the nature of the Dharma realm: all is made by mind alone,” he raised his fan, struck the desk, and cried aloud: “Be released at once!” The other answered at once: “Released!” Three calls, three answers, quicker than echo or shadow. He rose again with the full deportment of a Buddhist, gave thanks for rebirth in the Pure Land, bowed east and west to the assembly, and said: “Strive each of you; we shall meet at the Dragon-Flower Assembly.” It was already past the first watch, and the assembly had not dispersed; some wept, some sighed, and some even secretly laughed or murmured, but the Master remained perfectly at ease. As was his custom he must mount his carriage and return to the boat; the other followed the carriage to the cliff’s edge, made reverence and gave thanks, then returned to the gate of the Chan hall and, saying “Thank you, old Master Qian, for the deliverance you obtained by borrowing me,” fell to the ground and woke — and was once more the runner Qian in his usual state. Those nearby said that Ren was a scholar of the Zhong family across the river, the father of Wen Shao, who in life had practiced the Pure Land most devoutly, and that such a response was fitting. Fuzheng replied: “That is my friend of the Bibi Scripture Society, Zhong Shengfu.” At once he went with several of the faithful to knock at the door and drew him over to the Dharma boat to give thanks. Then it was learned that on that day the dead man was exactly in the fifth seventh-day of mourning, and that the runner Qian, coming to press for grain, had entered before his spirit seat and in his drunkenness had drawn the soul to deliverance. In the later examination of the xinyou year Shengfu passed the provincial test. That day there was a relative and friend, the layman Xu Taiwei, long a believer in the Buddha, who, seeing the Master’s spiritual response, invited him to his home, where he had set up the spirit seat of his father, the assistant censor, and begged him to preach the Dharma. Every word the Master spoke revealed the secret affairs of his life, and those who heard were awed into submission. Within a day or two the word spread of the living bodhisattva, and recitation and rumour ran through the city; the elders of the prefecture, children, and women craned their necks as if crazed. Fuzheng attended the Master to Qizhen to do reverence at the stupa of the monk Yungu; then, with carriage and canopy and full deportment, he came to the Eastern Stupa so that the thronging crowd who thirsted for him might have one sight of him and do reverence. In a moment black-robed and white-robed gathered in crowds; from the mountain gate to the abbot’s quarters shoulder pressed heel, and the long causeway and broad platform had no room left to set a foot. So he took counsel with Mr. Yue Shifan to lead the Master in front up the steps to the stupa, and then barred the stupa door. The Master’s frame was great, and they could only support him to the southern railing of the second storey; when the fourfold assembly saw him they bowed in rows and did reverence, rising and falling prostrate to the ground, steaming like cloud and smoke, and only dispersed at nightfall. Lamps were lit as he entered the abbot’s quarters and ascended the seat to preach, giving a few words in brief; then came the feast, and when the feast was done he at once went aboard the boat; those who came bearing incense and offerings of fruit pressed the boat down. The master of the Eastern Stupa hall at that time was Master Jingxiu. The next day the Lengyan invited him to a feast, the master of that hall being Master Maolin. He went through the scripture workshop and inquired into all its rules, and thereupon specially charged Fuzheng with the matter of carving the canon, talking on and on without end. That day the men and women of the city who came to share in the joy also filled the place. The day after that the boat crossed to Songling.

The chronicle also says that the famous worthies of every quarter all gathered about the lake and with the scholar Tan asked about the Dharma, and that the splendour of that southeast Dharma assembly had never been seen before. It also says that of whatever writings he made at the time along the way, Master Xuanjin He and the scholar Tan Mengxun collected four fascicles and printed them under the title Eastern Journey Collection. This was because our Master, at the nirvāṇa assembly, let down his foot as a sign and gave his charge earnestly, singling out the one word “with” — attributing the surpassing cause of the Eastern Journey directly to Fuzheng himself; nowhere in the whole chronicle is there a comparable stroke of approval. In his youth Fuzheng, at the bidding of the late assistant equerry Lord Fantong, was given the courtesy name Mengxun. Afterwards, when his own body lay beneath the collapsed hall and he was saved by the shelter of three beams, it happened that in that very year he met our Master, who gave him the Dharma name Liangsheng. Later he styled himself Sao’an, and people no longer knew him as Mengxun. The verse our Master showed Liangsheng says: “The roof-beam fell and crushed the scholar Tan; being crushed, why did the scholar not die? If the beam had reached the body, the body would be shattered; if the body had reached the beam, the beam would not avoid it. Both have reached — why do they not touch? Ask yourself the reason they do not touch. The illusions before you are not to be compared to a beam; why should the scholar Tan first panic so? If you would not panic, watch a dog driven to leap the wall.” This was the instruction given at their first meeting. Afterwards there were earnest Dharma words given him on holding the Cundi and on the awl-piercing, all recorded in the Eastern Journey Collection. And so he recalls those days: from Shuangjing to Yunqi, invited to stay at the Zongjing Hall of Jingci and to open the hall, then journeying about the lake, Lingyin, Tianzhu, and the various mountains, and to Zhili, Jinming, and the Eastern Stupa, where the light shone greatly; then crossing Songling and Wumen, straight to the Eastern Chan Temple at Jinsha, where he did reverence at his feet and took leave. From spring through summer he attended him with the morning lamps, with no idle day. As the boat was about to be loosed, the Master stroked Fuzheng’s back with his hand and said with a smile: “The affairs after my death I entrust to you.” This was a matter of his twenty-seventh year. Fuzheng’s feeling for the Master was no less than an infant’s craving for the breast; the Master’s care for Fuzheng was no different from a tender mother’s rearing of her child. At that time Fuzheng’s father was at court and his mother in attendance, and the Master, seeing the first signs early, foretold to him the unfinished karmic causes of standing in the world and entering society, and firmly stopped him from following him to Wuru; yet in his gazing and leaning, in dream and sleep, he never forgot him for a moment. From that parting to now his years have reached sixty-two; he is old. All along since receiving the prediction he has held the Cundi, four twelve-year cycles as one day. He sent offerings to Fayun, and the letters that went back and forth fill his boxes. At the Stone Lamp bodhimanda in the capital of Yan he mourned in silence and longing. Only now, face to face with the Dharma image, does he expound the chronicle in commentary, drawing out the instructions of former days and the records he was shown, in hope of settling one day the public case of entering the canon and requesting a posthumous title; and only now does he know that the words of the charge about affairs after death belonged to this very day. Alas, our Master loved Fuzheng as though there were no second in his eyes at the time; and Fuzheng’s service of the Master has perhaps answered to him in some small part.
The Forty-Sixth Year, Wuwu ●

I was seventy-three. The laymen of Wuxia contributed funds to build me the Yilao Hut. That year I began to build the Buddha Hall and the Chan hall at Wuru. In the third month Lord Chen Chishi, assistant administrator of Fuliang, came into the mountain, and with Lord Bao Zhongsu, ministry official of Xin’an, and Lord Xia Woqi, ministry official of Xingzi, formed a society of ten friends to help with the cost of building; by the long-day month the halls were complete. (Chen Chishi, a second time. The ministry official Bao Zhongsu and the ministry official Xia Woqi, once each. Zhongsu was named Ying’ao, a man of Huizhou, and served as chief of the court of imperial sacrifices.)

In the fourth month of summer of the dingyi year, when Fuzheng took leave of our Master, he was charged to collect funds to make an image of the three holy ones of the West coming forth from the mountain — that is, Amitābha, Guanyin, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the lords of the six-period Buddha-recitation bodhimanda, in imitation of Master Yuan’s Lotus Society. This image is rare among the world’s temples, and it happened that a master craftsman of Jiangxi had inherited the art, and the sandalwood carving was exquisite and uncommon. It also happened that a single coiled root of a natural seat was obtained, on which the three holy ones were seated in a row; and again that five ancient bronze censers, vases, candlesticks, and offering vessels were found. In that spring it was completed, and the attendant Master Xuzhong Yi, as the Buddha Hall was about to be finished, came to welcome it, and Fuzheng that same day bought a boat and sent it. At the first sight of it our Master was joyful and praised it, and to this day it is honoured and complete. The halls built at Wuru stand in the prefecture of Jiujiang, county of Dehua, on the shady side of Mount Kuang; at first it was called the Wood-and-Stone Hut, and now it is called the Fayun Temple. The abbot was Master Zhizheng; after his passing it now belongs to Master Ciyan, styled Runhong.
The Forty-Seventh Year, Jiwei ●

I was seventy-four. In the first month of spring I began a long term of reciting the Avatamsaka Sutra and expounded the General Exposition on the Lotus Sutra for the assembly. In summer I expounded the Surangama, the Awakening of Faith, the Diamond, the Perfect Enlightenment, and the Consciousness-Only, the sutras and treatises. In the seventh month of autumn I charged Lord Yuan, prefect of Nankang, to write a record, making Wuru a permanent endowment for the support of the aged of the ten directions. On the fifteenth of the eighth month I shut myself in retreat and cut off all ties, imitating Master Yuan’s practice of burning incense at the six periods in place of the water-clock, and gave my mind wholly to the pure work. I often reflected that the Avatamsaka school was about to lose its transmission: men feared that Qingliang’s subcommentary was too vast, and their minds could not reach it, so most in the world set it aside and relied only on the Combined Treatise. But I thought that Qingliang was the ancestor of composition in this land, and that if he were abandoned the school would lose its lineage. I resolved to take only the subcommentary text and set forth its great purport with the brush, so that readers might easily understand it, entitling it the Essentials; and in the retreat I began to read, revise, and cut it.

Fuzheng observes: in the chronicle the Qingliang public case appears five times, and in the end it is closed with the Essentials of the Avatamsaka. Three years later, in the renxu year, the draft was done — and the karmic occasion of Qingliang was accomplished, and the karmic occasion of Caoxi likewise. Can it be that our Master was Qingliang come again? Moreover, at that very time our Master took the burning of incense in place of the water-clock and made the pure work his whole aim, and yet he could again revise the subcommentary of Qingliang and the whole Avatamsaka school into the Essentials and hand it down to later men: this is what is called the Pure Land as mind-only, the ten thousand dharmas returning to one.
The Forty-Eighth Year, Gengshen — the Accession Year of Taichang ●

I was seventy-five. In spring, outside my lessons, the attendant Guangyi asked me to set forth the Perfect Enlightenment and the Awakening of Faith in direct explanation, and to annotate the seven inner chapters of Zhuangzi. In summer I was ill with a foot ailment. In the eighth month of autumn Lord Chen Wuyi, ministry official of Macheng, Lord Xu Mingheng, ministry official of Anyi, Lord Wu Xunshang, ministry official of Xingzi, Lord Lu Jingye, prefect of Jiangzhou, Lord Yuan Jiuji, prefect of Nankang, and Lord Li Zhongda, the judicial officer, came into the mountain to ask about the Way. The former circuit intendant of Hunan, Lord Wu, now transferred to the Guangdong judgeship, entered Caoxi to do reverence to the Patriarch and asked the disciples in the mountain to send him biographies and praises of the Patriarchs. In my illness I compiled more than seventy short biographies, each with a praise attached, and wrote them out with my own hand. It was already eight years since I had left Caoxi for Nanyue and dwelt at Mount Kuang. The monks of Caoxi longed deeply for my return and sent inquiries again and again, wishing to invite me but unable to. It happened that Lord Wu, going to his post, came into the mountain by the way and saw the work of my restoration, and sighed over it a long while. The monks then told him the whole matter — how they longed for my return and could not obtain it. Lord Wu gladly became their protector of the Dharma and at once sent letters to invite me. The whole assembly of the mountain, with the gentry, elders, and scholars of the province, jointly drew up a petition and came to Mount Kuang to beg me with tears. The Guangdong disciple the censor Wang Xingdong came into the mountain in person three times to invite me, but I firmly declined on account of illness. (Guangyi, a second time. Chen Wuyi, ministry official of Macheng, Xu Mingheng, ministry official of Anyi, Wu Xunshang, ministry official of Xingzi, Lu Jingye, prefect of Jiangzhou, Li Zhongda, judicial officer of Nankang, and Wang Xingdong, censor of Guangdong, once each. Yuan Jiuji, that is Lord Yuan, and Lord Wu, that is Wu Shengbai Zhongwei, a second time each. Jingye was named Menglong, a man of Shanyin in Zhejiang, chief examiner of Guangdong, and served as assistant administrator of Guizhou. Zhongda was named Yingsheng, a man of Jiangyin, an official censor, who was arrested and died in the time of the eunuch Wei.)

Fuzheng observes: in the chronicle the first entry is that in the eighth month of autumn of the tenth year of Wanli, the renwu year, the crown prince was born; the second entry, that in the eighth month of autumn of the thirty-fourth year the imperial eldest grandson was born; the third entry, the forty-eighth year, gengshen, which is the change of reign-title to Taichang. For on the twenty-sixth day of the seventh month of that year the Shenzong Emperor died and Taichang ascended, and an edict decreed that the next year should be the first year of Taichang. On the third day of the ninth month of that year the Guangzong Emperor in turn died, and on the sixth day Tianqi ascended. The supervising official Li Ruogui and the investigating censor Zuo Guangdou petitioned that from the first day of the eighth month to the end of the twelfth month the reign-title Wanli be dropped and the days be styled the first year of Taichang, borrowed from the late emperor; in the end it was not approved. This too failed in the meaning of a proper beginning and a proper ending, and came of a moment’s groundless expedient, closing the matter in haste. To borrow from the late emperor and so diminish the calendar years, which is unfilial toward the one who died later, is worse than to borrow from the later emperor and so make plain the first year of sacrifice, which is filial toward the newly ascended. Moreover, to take the first year of Tianqi as the first year of Taichang is precisely to believe that the edict of Taichang’s accession was no borrowing. The second year of Tianqi was in truth the first year of Tianqi. Now the first year of Taichang can only be appended in a side-note under the forty-eighth year of Wanli. Our Master feared that this change of reign-title would be buried, and therefore writes it large and twice under the forty-eighth year, gengshen: “the change of reign-title to Taichang.” These five characters are the greatest instance of the brush-method and heart-method of the Spring and Autumn; how could they have been met with in the chronicles of former Patriarchs? The prayer for an heir at Mount Wutai, the protection of the heir at the Cishou Temple, and even the interrogation at the Zhenfu Office and the garrison service beyond the Dayu Ridge — what Chancellor Zhang Hongyang called his great hidden service to the altars of state — all come to one great conclusion in these five characters. In the intervals of the incense-clock and Buddha-recitation at Wuru, to expound, annotate, and compose, preaching ardently without an empty day — how could that be within the power of an old man of seventy-five, and ill at that? The work of Wuru was unfinished and the work of Caoxi revived: this is what is called “Heaven’s movement is strong; the gentleman strengthens himself without cease.” My friend Wang Jiyan, whose name was Qilong, wrote A Debate on the First Year of Taichang and Doubts Raised, examining back and forth in detail the regulations of reign-changes in ancient and modern times, some two thousand characters with all his strength, and truly he first spoke my own mind. His main point is that a change of reign-title after the year has passed is the constant rule for all ages, and that changing it with the month is the error of a moment — two phrases cover it. He also says that if a year can be divided into two sections, then since Wanli, Taichang, and Tianqi all fall within one year, why can it not be divided into three? That is a forced and disjointed argument, making the Guangzong temple a mere wart. These words open the eyes and pierce the heart still more; my poor view had not reached so far. Moreover, the Guangzong Emperor’s sagely virtue was lofty and generous, and he was a lord not to be produced in a generation: in the month of his accession the Yellow River at Lingong in Shaanxi ran clear for three days. He early stopped the mining taxes by decree, recalled all the tax eunuchs, and sent out treasury gold to reward the frontier to the amount of a million; he summoned back the outspoken officials who had offered advice, as though he had no leisure even to eat — and this is only what the new government accomplished. As for his nurturing of virtue in the Eastern Palace, his benevolence and filial piety were exhaustively devoted, when within there were the forms of flourishing and withering and without the provocations of partisans; to stand in such a place was truly hard. When the Shenzong Emperor was about to die he decreed that the Honoured Consort Zheng be made empress and charged him to carry it out; the court officials disputed it, yet in the end he could not bear to take it from her. These forty days of filial thought and benevolent grace reached to three reigns — the way of Heaven may still be asked about. So, because in the Patriarch Hanshan’s chronicle there stand the five characters “the change of reign-title to Taichang,” Fuzheng was moved and noted it.
In that year there was a letter showing Fuzheng his intention of going to Caoxi, and he wrote beforehand an inscription for the layman Tan, provincial graduate.
The First Year of Tianqi, Xinyou ●

I was seventy-six. In summer, at the request of the assembly, I expounded the Surangama Notes. In the tenth month of winter my disciples, the provincial graduates Liu Qixiang, Chen Dixiang, Chen Dichun, and Liang Sixiang, came to inquire after me. At that time the former observer of Shaoyang, Lord Zhu, now transferred to the Guangdong sea circuit, together with Lord Wu, sent letters and came again to Mount Kuang, and I again declined on account of illness. (Liu Qixiang, Chen Dixiang, Chen Dichun, and Liang Sixiang, once each. Lord Zhu, the former Xingcun, a second time; Lord Wu, the former Shengbai, a third time.)

Lord Zhu Xingcun and Lord Wu Shengbai, two elders of Fuzheng’s own district and both men of Yanguan, were in the end able to bring about the gathering of the flesh-bodies of the Sixth Patriarch and the Patriarch Hanshan — so great a karmic occasion. In this year, though he had not yet returned to Caoxi, the first signs of return had already stirred and the momentum of return was decided. Had he not returned to Caoxi again, then even though his flesh-body came forth from Wuru, without coming face to face with Patriarch Lu there would have been no great marvel.
The above closes the public case of the Fayun Temple at Wuru on Mount Kuang.
The Second Year, Renxu ●

I was seventy-seven. I pressed on with the Essentials of the Avatamsaka, and the draft was done. The assembly asked me to expound the Surangama, the Perfect Enlightenment, the Diamond, the Awakening of Faith, and the Zhao Lun, and the various sutras and treatises. When Lord Wu returned from his audience at court he sent letters again, his meaning the more urgent; and Lord Zhang Sanxing, prefect of Shaoyang, sent a special letter and dispatched the hall master Ben’ang to me. My feelings left me no choice, and I resolved that I must go. On the tenth day of the eleventh month, at the winter solstice of that year, I left Mount Kuang and crossed Lake Peng, and wrote poems. Before long Lord Zou Nangao, the chief of the academy, returning north, sought me in the mountain. By then I had reached Jizhou, and met the grand historian Xiao Zhuoxiu, Ma Jifang, Zeng Yaochen, Liu Shaoye, He Keshang, and Liu Zhuanhua, who asked about the Way at the Ziyan Mountain House. On the eighth day of the twelfth month I crossed the ridge, and on the fifteenth entered Caoxi. (Lord Wu Shengbai, a fourth time. Lord Zhang Sanxing, prefect of Shaoyang, and the hall master Ben’ang, once each. Lord Zou Nangao, chief of the academy, a second time. The grand historian Xiao Zhuoxiu, Ma Jifang, Zeng Yaochen, Liu Shaoye, He Keshang, and Liu Zhuanhua, once each. Sanxing was named Yizhen, a man of Huating in Songjiang, who rose from prefect of Shaozhou to assistant commissioner of Guangxi. Zhuoxiu was named Yunju, styled Xuanpu, registered in Xuanhua of Guangxi, a man of Taihe in Jiangxi, and served as junior minister.)

Fuzheng observes: Lord Nangao and those after him were all men of Jiangxi of firm principle and of the Dharma, noted in the last leaves; they were chosen out of many and only a few taken, and in the end he never gave his approval to any one of them. Confucius at seventy-two, in the tenth month of winter, composed the Spring and Autumn, laying down his brush at the capture of the qilin in the western hunt; the next year, at seventy-three, he dreamed of the offerings and sang his last song. The Patriarch Hanshan at seventy-seven, on the fifteenth of the twelfth month, composed the chronicle, laying down his brush at the crossing of the ridge and his entry into Caoxi; the next year, at seventy-eight, his flesh-body passed into cessation. The sage before and the sage after fit like the two halves of a tally — how should one speak of Confucian and Buddhist appearances? Still more marvellous: our Master, during his former stay in Guangdong, twenty-one years from first to last, was never shaved. Only when he came to Chu did he assume the perfect form and return to the monastic dress. Had he not returned again to Caoxi, then the black-robed and white-robed of Guangdong would never in their lives have seen our Master’s perfect form in monastic dress. Yet whether with hair or without, in monastic or Confucian dress, wherein the sages differ and agree does not lie here at all.

Fuzheng was able to see the works of our Master: the Surangama Notes, the Essentials of the Avatamsaka, the Beating the Beat on the Lotus, the Hanging Mirror on the Surangama, the General Exposition on the Surangama, the General Exposition on the Lotus, the Explanation of the Awakening of Faith, the Explanation of the Consciousness-Only Treatise, the Direct Explanation of the Perfect Enlightenment, the Treatise on the Influence of Laozi and Zhuangzi, the Explanation of the Classic of the Dao and its Virtue, the Explanation of the Seven Inner Chapters of Zhuangzi, the Hanshan Preface, the Direct Pointing at the Doctrine of the Mean, the Doubts Resolved on the Great Learning, the Heart-Method of the Zuo Commentary to the Spring and Autumn Annals, the Palm-Guide to the Qimen, the Dream-Wandering Collection, and the Gazetteer of Caoxi. Those that Fuzheng copied out with his own hand and sent to the block were the Eastern Journey Collection; and printed, the Doubts Resolved on the Diamond. His writings are many more. As he said face to face, there are the Treatise on the Three Teachings, the General Explanation of the Analects, and the Palm-Guide to the Qimen. And as Jianru said, there are the Complete Recorded Sayings in a certain number of fascicles, which after our Master’s passing were stolen and sold elsewhere by the attendant Xinqi and cannot now be seen; these are not recorded in full. What the wisdom-life of the Buddha and the Patriarchs rests upon is the Surangama Notes first and the Essentials of the Avatamsaka last. The school does not depart from the teaching, the Patriarch does not depart from the Buddha: in these it is most manifest and notable. Our Master often said of himself that whatever came from his brush or tongue was always gathered in spirit and entered into contemplation, realizing accord with the Buddha’s mind; if it smacked ever so little of thought and deliberation, it was of no use. And this Essentials of the Avatamsaka, whose draft was completed, belongs to the year before his passing into cessation at seventy-seven, standing in place of Śākyamuni’s last holding up of the flower between the twin trees. His power of samādhi and his spiritual light, vigorous and unceasing, are fully present in the palm-leaf books of the Mahāyāna: how could thought and deliberation reach so far?
In that year began the karmic occasion of his return to Caoxi, leaving unfinished the public case of a Hanshan temple and the flesh-body succession to the Patriarch.
Here ends the Commentary on the Veritable Record of the Old Man of Hanshan’s Own Chronicle.
Appendix
Thirty-Six Praises of the Ancient Buddha in the Flesh Who Restored Caoxi, the Patriarch-Successor Hanshan (with Preface and Titles)

I sigh in secret that the maṇi jewel is priceless, and that one seldom meets a merchant who can tell it. The poor son loses his treasure only because he has long been lost on the road home. That is why students of the Way are as many as the hairs of a cow, while those who awaken the mind are as rare as the horns of a qilin. I was born out of season, to meet the autumn of change and vicissitude; how fortunate am I in body to see the day when the ancient Buddha appears. This udumbara flower of Caoxi bloomed once three thousand years ago; the cause and fruit of the flesh-body meet again after five hundred lives. Dwelling where he should not dwell, he dwells in this body, and the ten thousand things are complete in me. Attaining where there is nothing to attain, he attains his place; and turning back upon himself and becoming sincere, there is no greater joy. Great Master Yongjia has said: “The three bodies and four wisdoms are perfected within the essence; the eight liberations and six penetrations are the seal of the mind-ground.” Now the flesh-body bodhisattva, Great Master Hanshan, with just this mind-seal, seals all once and for all, and there is no other dharma. One gate steps beyond samādhi and dhyāna, one gate enters straight into the wondrous adorned path. No need of clay or wood, of red or blue pigment: the Dharma-body fills the void. Why need of golden terraces and silver pavilions, when his image shines through the Dharma realm? Yet ignorant worldlings still complain that he went about in cangue and chains, driving his stake and pulling his oar. So, reading his chronicle, I set out its titles and made these thirty-six praises, in compliance with the request of Tan, the director of education, of Sao’an.
(A White-Robed Rebirth) ●

Not in the middle, nor within, nor yet without — he leaves the world more thirsting and more devout. The soiled robe, how could he bear to cast it down? I fear that beings will scarcely grasp it, one and all.
(The Knot of Doubt over Birth and Death) ●

Ere he had found the road to serve the King of Emptiness, he already knew to drill for light within the smoke. He burned up the three thousand great thousand worlds, and sought life within death — a marvellous device.
(Requiting Kindness and Attaining Deliverance) ●

Old Lu, who handed on the robe, was then no monk; he smiled at old Cai who trudged the dusty road. To give this body and mind to lands as countless as dust — this, and this alone, is requiting the Buddha’s grace.
(The Vow to Restore) ●
Leaving home, he meant to save all living beings; why then bring disaster on a whole temple of monks? He saved a crowd of men who had nothing to do, and the adorned precious hall is in his own body.
(Going to the Capital to Seek Instruction) ●
Wrongly setting down those words of Yongjia: to seek a master and ask the Way is to investigate Chan. Had he not entered the wave that startles men, how could fish and dragons leap into his boat?
(Meeting the Master in Willow Lane) ●

The black dragon’s pearl he picked up, a jewel for the house; would he let it fall into another’s ten-thousand-fathom pit? Though this land of Zhen is broad, there is no other road; for a while he borrows the feet of sons and grandsons to walk it.
(Meeting a Friend at the Capital Gate) ●
Through you the mind-seal knows its former face; like answers like, with no fine shavings left. The frontier goose was not startled up by men; the wind struck the reed-mist and filled the blue sky.
(Lying in the Snow at Mount Tai) ●

He would test the lotus within the red-hot furnace; fine gold, a hundred times refined, shines the brighter. A ball of snow in his hand, he strikes where it is easy — and only then feels the coolness surpass all talk of Chan.
(Hiding Together in the Western Hills) ●

The Tathagatas of the three ages speak with a single voice; only then one knows how many kalpas he lay as if asleep. In me there is nothing hidden from you; every bit is so — the osmanthus fragrance fills all, and one wonders at so many words.
(Capital for Dwelling in the Mountain) ●

A poor man in the mountain, without a single string of cash; he calls on Heaven again and again in bitter cry. The eighty thousand Dharma gates enter from here — much like a trader who has got his capital at last.
(Reverencing the Patriarch at Shaolin) ●
The blue-eyed barbarian monk came into Han; nine years — why was his mouth so hard to open? Today he has caught and beaten that stinking bearded one, and shapes a fist to smite him in the face.
(Not Meeting Daqian) ●
They said there was a Daqian at Mount Song, and to this day the Shaolin Chan is unbroken. Had he known earlier not to go to Mount Song, he would have spared the beings who lick at wild spittle.
(Joyfully Meeting Faguang) ●
Faguang took up his staff and chased the rabbit; then turned and flung it back to strike the toad. The dead snake he did not cut but let it go, and boasts before men of the Chan school’s play.
(Listening to the Water at Dragon Gate) ●

He did not walk where the people of the time walked, but came to the bridge side to listen to the stream. Suddenly he stamped and cut the road of the stream’s sound: the ear hears nothing, and the eye is blind too.
(Rising from Samādhi, Dust on the Cauldron) ●

How many times the flowers bloomed and their shadows climbed the wall; on the crystal hall there is no news at all. The axe-handle rotted, and he did not know the years; the gibbons cried all night — did they ever cease?
(Protecting Mount Tai) ●
Who can measure the breadth of Mount Tai? Year after year the emperor’s million bushels of grain. How could this matter be explained? One look from Lord Hu, and there was no harm.
(Intercourse with the Holy Assembly) ●
If you do not know the man, look at his friends: Mañjuśrī and Maitreya expose the family’s shame. Dreaming awakening, awakening dreaming — all alike; were I to see it, I would hurry to beat the dog.
(The Birth of an Imperial Heir) ●

Pointing to heaven and earth when the Buddha was first born; the five positions of lord and minister — he is the honoured one. The imperial prince of the Great Ming is like the Buddha: the maṇi pearl appears and sets heaven and earth at rest.
(A Remote Dwelling on Mount Lao) ●

A frontier-sea monk, a subject with nothing he can say; thrice daily fare, and when he is full he rests. Else I should prove ungrateful to my sovereign lord; east, west, north, south — what difference was there e’er?
(Mother and Son Discuss the Profound) ●

With staff in hand one still must reach one’s native place; before a foot was lifted, one saw one’s mother’s face. Long has her living face from her son not been parted: mother and child, hoes in hand, laugh a good laugh together.
(Requiting Grace, the Karmic Cause at Rest) ●

From the first the karmic cause arose, and blessing could revive; ten years of scant fare to thank the imperial grace. When all but done, the Japanese came to the land of Korea: good things are much beset — so it has been heard of old.
(The Stern Punishment of the Garrison Officials) ●

How many times, cut off from all that came after, did he win rebirth again; filial love and piety need not bar one from the historian’s green bamboo. In the end the imperial heart awakened from this; as at the first, mother and son relied upon a true monk.
(Graciously Garrisoned at Leizhou) ●

The imperial grace was vast, and the law took its course with lenience; sent into garrison at Leizhou, he walked with his staff. At the tip of one finger there is no second thing; all heaven and earth throughout are light.
(A Criminal Paying Respect at the General’s Gate) ●

The governor’s awe-inspiring majesty had long been heard of; how much more, in chains and cangue, to pay respects at the general’s gate. Who would have known that at the meeting he would be called a qilin and a phoenix: from this day South Ridge first held a monk in honour.
(Dredging the Source at Caoxi) ●

Why should the Patriarch’s seat be so utterly still and bare? If the source is not dredged, the toil is all in vain. Hitting the crooked straight with the crooked, the sky’s blue runs on unbroken; forgetting shame and forgetting glory, one sees the nature firmly.
(A Hundred Ruined Works All Set Afoot) ●

Doing, one never reaches the place of true emptiness; in the end the Han hound runs chasing the clod. Rat-creep and snake-slither have nothing to do with it; though the lightning rolls and the wind races, it is still not quick.
(A Wicked Monk’s Contrariness) ●
Jambudvīpa, alas, for so many years; morning and night, all in a daze, dragged along by this. How could one escape being dyed by the dust and grime? Come quickly and gather up the old-wife Chan.
(Pardoned and Restored to His First Dress) ●

On the homeward road one may well be an ox in the fire; one leaf has barely fallen and ten thousand lands are in autumn. The moon is white, the waves are still, and there is no other matter: this heart is still there at the tip of the fishing pole.
(The Eastern Journey Wins a Qilin) ●

In the southeast Dharma cavern one rejoices in the many monks; yet none was seen to be a silent Vimalakīrti. Just then came Mr. Liang, seeking blessing and wisdom: among all those horns, you are the qilin.
(The Lotus Opens on Wuru Peak) ●

Nothing in the world excels the lotus flower; it pierces stone and threads sand, utterly without a speck of dust. Its fragrance fills all space, nor blooms nor fades; but fools, clinging to marks, are tangled like hemp.
(Entering Caoxi Once More) ●

Tidings one should know are the same as ever; of the old haunts the meaning is all the longer. The moon in the Caoxi water joins the three realms; seek out a fellow student, the better to take counsel together.
(No Moon at Mid-Autumn) ●

Spring has its hundred flowers, winter has its snow; summer has its cool breeze, autumn has its moon. Tonight, in mid-autumn, one watches only the stars: from of old the Unborn is all the more vast and clear.
(Sitting in Cessation in Worn Robes) ●

Stripped of the very trousers his mother bore, he is still an ordinary man; far removed from coming and going, he shows the blind how to inquire. Alone, aloof, his light before and behind: and still he fears the foolish ape may stir the jade-green pool.
(Building the Stupa at Mount Kuang) ●

When a man of attainment meets one, there is no negotiation; he raises the high banner and puts on his own foolishness. Uncomprehending of what lies within, one can but laugh aloud: welcoming and sending off, he plays the blind man well.
(The Broken Niche Reveals the Buddha) ●

The comings and goings of folding and unfolding are subtle and profound; gods and men in crowds — who among them knows? A single command made Lord Song raise his precious sword; one thunderclap shook the whole of Mount Sumeru.
(The Flesh Body Sits in Mighty Steadfastness) ●

Insentient things preaching the Dharma make occasion for many words; the speechless withered stump is a master seen again. When host and guest meet, it is delusion still; light before and shining behind, the words run coarse and fine.

The Later Affairs of the Revival of Caoxi and of the Flesh-Body Patriarch Hanshan

Fushan, abbot of the Fayun Temple on Wuru Peak and former attendant of the Narayana Cave of the Eastern Sea, records as follows. In the third year of Tianqi, the guihai year, the Master was seventy-eight and dwelling in the Chan Hall of Caoxi. The prefect of Shaoyang, Lord Zhang, together with the officials and gentlemen of the whole prefecture, entered the mountain and asked the Master to preach. In the third month of spring the disciples of the Dharma-nature of Wuyang arrived, and the Master, whose mind was then wholly set on the gift of Dharma, first expounded the great precepts for them, then the Awakening of Faith, the Consciousness-Only, and the Surangama. In the fifth month of summer Ma Jifang, a licentiate of Jizhou, and Wang Weizou, a provincial graduate, came to pay their respects. In the eighth month of autumn, when the assembly of the Patriarch was over, he sent an attendant to take leave of the provincial administrator Lord Wu; as he was about to set out, the Master charged him, saying: “In the Buddha’s and the Patriarchs’ spreading of the teaching, what matters is the season and the karmic occasion. When the occasion runs counter to the time, to what shall the teaching be entrusted? The business of one period is done; I am about to return.” The assembly was wholly at a loss, and all took this for words of his wish to go back to Mount Kuang. He composed a poem, “Thoughts on the Mid-Autumn Moon,” one piece. After the Double Ninth, he wrote out for the attendant Shenguang the poem on dwelling in the mountains, appending the note: “Though this old man is lazy with brush and ink, I fear that if a breath does not return, I shall again be a debtor to a future life. Yet if you look at them as poetry and calligraphy, then you greatly wrong my intent.” On the first day of the tenth month of winter his disciple Tongjiong arrived from Mount Kuang, and asked after the resident assembly of Wuru and the elders of the various monasteries in the mountain; the Master’s heart was greatly gladdened. At that time his disciple Jingtai asked him to compose a self-praise, which set forth the whole purport of his life. On the third day the Junior Minister Lord Xiao Xuanpu entered the mountain to visit him, and they talked deeply for three days and nights, greatly delighted. He asked for the essentials of the Dharma, and the Master accordingly composed two Dharma words and three poems and gave them to him. On the sixth day, when Lord Xiao was leaving the mountain, the Master charged him: “You are looked up to by the realm and the common people; take good care of yourself on the road ahead.” Lord Xiao still planned another meeting. The Master said: “This mountain monk is old; the four elements are about to scatter. The karmic bond of another meeting with you must wait for the Dragon-Flower Assembly.” So they parted, and he returned to the abbot’s quarters. On the eighth day he showed a slight illness. When the assembly inquired after him, he said only that the old man was weary, not ill. On the ninth day, when the medicine was brought, he would not take it, saying: “I am going; what use is medicine?” The attendant Guangyi, hearing these words, asked in alarm: “Should the Master, alas, pass beyond, what charge have you to leave?” The Master rebuked him: “You have attended this old man for years — how can you hold such a view? You should all bear in mind that the matter of birth and death is great and impermanence swift, and recite the Buddha’s name in earnest.” Guangyi said again: “If the Master will not show us a single word, how shall we know how to conduct ourselves?” The Master said: “What the golden mouth proclaimed has become old paper; of what use are my words?” And so he showed not a single word. The twelfth day was the Master’s birthday, and black-robed and white-robed disciples gathered like clouds. Lord Zhang Sanxing, prefect of Shaoyang, entered the mountain and brought a purple silk Chan robe to congratulate the Master on his longevity, and they sat talking together the whole day. When evening came Lord Zhang withdrew; that very night the Master three times called for water to bathe. The next morning he called for the Chan robe Lord Zhang had brought, put it on, and took his leave of Lord Zhang. Lord Zhang came again to the side of his couch, and the Master said: “This mountain monk is going. Many thanks for the great protector’s abundant heart.” Lord Zhang said: “The Master’s Dharma body is without ill; unworthy as I am, I am the lord of this land, and all things rest with me.” The Master smiled, joined his palms, and thanked him. At noon Lord Zhang took his leave and departed; the Master at once called an attendant to fetch pure water to rinse his mouth, saying: “Today I cut off the tangled vine.” Again he called for hot water to bathe and change his robes, and the assembly gathered about him reciting the Buddha’s name. He charged them: “You must not be alarmed. Follow the Buddha’s rule: you may not wear hemp or mourning garments, and you may not weep and wail; with one mind recite the Buddha’s name.” At the third watch of the afternoon he sat upright and passed away. That night a ray of light illumined the heavens, flocks of birds cried mournfully, and black-robed and white-robed lamented aloud, their voices shaking the mountain valley. After his transformation he sat upright for three days, his face fair, his lips red, his hands and feet soft, as though entered into Chan concentration. Word was sent to Lord Zhang, who at once dispatched officials to offer condolences and seal the shrine. At that time Lord Xiao had been gone but five days and was still at Xiongzhou; hearing the news of the Master, he grieved the whole day. But when he further heard the circumstances of his transformation, he rejoiced, saying: “The Master is a man of the holy ranks. Had he not seen through the juncture of birth and death, how could this have been?” He at once composed an elegy and sent condolences, and further donated a hundred pieces of silver, composing a text and charging the prefects of Nan and Shao to build a shadow hall for him. When the Dharma kin of Wuru on Mount Kuang heard the news, the disciples Fushan and the rest, obeying the Master’s dying command, went at once to Caoxi and bore the Master’s reliquary back to Wuru, building a stupa at the place the Master himself had chosen. By then the shadow hall there was already finished, and the monks pressed hard to keep it. Fushan and the others again reported to the grand historian Wu, the assistant censor Wu, the provincial administrator Sheng, Wang Mengsu, Miao Mutai, and the other officials of the society, and wrote to the authorities concerned to petition; and so the Supreme Commander Lord He of Wuwo and Lord Wang, the chief administrator of this province, a man of excellent virtue, sent an official dispatch to the prefecture to escort the reliquary back to Mount Kuang, issuing a warrant and travelling funds. On the twenty-first day of the first month of the yichou year it set out, and on the twenty-eighth day of the second month it reached the Fayun Temple on Wuru Peak of Mount Kuang.

The Master’s Dharma lineage consists of forty characters, with a verse that runs: Great is the virtue, deep and wide the blessing; kind and benevolent, his measure is universal and equal. Cultivating and upholding, he transcends the Dharma-realm; awakening in accord, the wondrous mind blends. Still and tranquil, he awakens to constant joy; perfect and bright, the essence of his nature penetrates. The light of wisdom shines on forever; the transformation of the Way long prospers and flourishes. (The character “De” is the Patriarch Hanshan’s Dharma taboo-name; “Da” is the Dharma taboo-name of the Empress Dowager Cisheng of the Li family. He commanded that his disciples’ names begin with the generation of “Fu.”)

Zhang Yizhen, prefect of Shaoyang, styled Sanxing, also styled the Daoist of Suchness, wrote the preface to the chronicle, saying: The chronicle of the Great Master Hanshan — his Dharma heir Xinqi came and asked that a plan be made to give it to the block-carvers. For in former days, when I was prefect of Shaoshi, I welcomed the Master from Wuru to dwell at Caoxi; and when the Master showed his cessation, I went again to take leave of him — it seems there was a concurrence of former causes. I recall that in the past I sent the monk Ben’ang to welcome the Master. Earlier the Master had shut himself in retreat for eight months; on the day the welcoming company arrived, he opened the retreat and said to them: “I was going; you should have sounded the bell and drum early and waited.” The assembly of Wuru gathered around him weeping and pressing him to stay. The Master said: “Caoxi is my own wish; the season and the karmic occasion — how dare I not accord with them? If I may beg the spirit of the Sixth Patriarch to let me entrust my bones there, that would be fortune indeed.” So he set off swiftly with his staff and bowl. Crossing the ridge, he sang: One look at the five clouds and I enter Nan’an; ten thousand folds, a thousand turns, the sixty-six rapids. When I come to where the water ends and the mountains run out, plum blossoms beyond counting are seen at the ridge-top. That the Master’s mind was set on ending at Caoxi is a sign already plain enough. In the twelfth month of the renxu year he reached Caoxi; in the winter of the next year, at the face-to-face charge of the Master of Rites Lord Xiao, I made contributions in many quarters and divined a site on the sunny side of the mountain, where I built the burial stupa and roofed the shadow hall, relying on the strength of many hands to finish the work. Then the Master showed his cessation, and I forthwith arranged his burial; of the Master’s wishes it seemed that none was unfulfilled. Not long after, I was transferred from Shao, and the Dharma heirs of Wuru, borrowing the great power of those in authority, moved the remains to Mount Lu, leaving hair and nails behind at Caoxi; and the stupa and hall I had built were also unharmed. Now all dharmas are empty of marks and have neither going nor abiding; Caoxi and Wuru are alike a hall of blessing. To abide or to go — both return to dream and illusion; what mind could the Master have had in it? The Master met the world with an empty heart and saved the world with a compassionate heart; above he illumined the sage’s virtue, below he pitied the people’s suffering; he took refuge in the Patriarch’s court and kept the Chan lineage flowing; in hardship and in ease he was one and the same, from first to last unchanging; a guide for gods and men, a dragon-elephant of the Dharma gate. These things stand out clearly, item by item, in the chronicle; how should I presume to add a single word of embellishing praise? Because his heir came to ask me, I have set down a rough outline of him, and that is all.

Fuzheng notes: Zhang Sanxing, Lord Zhang, knew the Master, welcomed him to Caoxi a second time, personally escorted him at his cessation, and arranged his burial; his wishes were all fulfilled. His power of the Way and his former causes were assuredly no small matter. And when, borrowing great power, the reliquary was moved, the stupa and hall happily remained unharmed; on the day the stupa was moved to Wuru, reading those words about going and abiding as dream and illusion, how could his heart not have been stirred with longing? When our Master returned once more to Caoxi and his flesh body appeared, it must have greatly comforted Lord Zhang’s heart’s wish; whether Lord Zhang lived to see or hear of it, I do not know. If it had not been for those two welcomes and farewells, and for his crossing the Dayu Ridge, where the robe and bowl could not be lifted, and coming back again to the very place divined that day for the burial shadow hall, facing Patriarch Lu, sending forth a great light to shine through the kalpas — how could one see that our Master’s vow-power truly suffices to cut off all streams and to embrace heaven and earth? The one song sung as he crossed the ridge can still be struck against metal and stone to this day; that he knew the subtle signs and was godlike in it must be seen at the juncture of birth and death. I further note that what Master Zhiwei Shan recorded — our Master’s cessation at Caoxi and the return of his reliquary to Wuru — were matters of the single year Tianqi renxu, and were not in time to be included in the chronicle. The preface written by Zhang Sanxing, Lord Zhang, sets forth the beginning and end of that earlier great matter of the going and coming between Caoxi and Wuru, and may be called clear and complete. Our Master’s birthday was the twelfth day of the tenth month, and on the twelfth day of the tenth month of that very year he showed his illness and took leave of the prefect of Shao, Lord Zhang; one day later came the time of his transformation. In going and coming he was wholly his own master: truly a rare thing since the beginningless kalpas. After he reached Wuru he was reburied and given a floating offering, and down to the guiwei year of Chongzhen it was already twenty-two years since the renxu year. Then appeared once more the welcoming of the reliquary to Wuru and the return of the reliquary to Caoxi, the manifestation of the flesh body, and the rivalry with Patriarch Lu — the whole beginning and end of the great matter. Yet of the supplementary chronicle and the various printed records and biographies, not one or two parts in ten are clear. Because Fuzheng was released from his post at the Nanyong Academy, he lodged at Jiangning between the Southern Mountain, the Rain-Flower Terrace, and the treetops; there he was able to follow the disciples who had personally attended and gone to and fro with the Patriarch Hanshan — Masters Rongcheng, Kuanju, Jianru, Mingji, and the rest of the Dharma kin — and to inquire of each the general outline; gathering up the imperishable outlines of the Dharma gate’s pivotal matters, in preparation for another day, after the precedent of the posthumous title Dajian granted to Patriarch Lu, to petition for a posthumous title. This is what I pray for. And so I recall how our Master, at the parting, patted Fuzheng on the shoulder and said with a laugh: “The affairs after I am gone are entrusted to you.” That day I was in the dark and did not know what he meant; now I am able to pour out my heart and set down remembered events at the end of the chronicle — truly this came of the season and the karmic occasion. Thinking back on that face-to-face charge, it is like waking from a dream: that he knew the subtle signs and was godlike in it — in my Master I believe it the more.

The abbot of Fayun Monastery, Miaorong, whose personal name was Guangcheng, and the abbot of Qixia Monastery, Jianru, whose personal name was Ciren, had both been among the dharma-attendants who, on the days when the shrine was welcomed and sent forth, twice traveled back and forth to Caoxi. They told in full how our teacher, in the winter of the renxu year, on the eleventh day of the eleventh month, because the provincial treasurer Wu Shengbo, the Shaozhou governor Zhang Sanxing, and his Guangdong disciple, the licentiate Liu Qixiang, had time and again sent letters to Wuru earnestly inviting him, and had even sent the hall-master of Baolin, Ben’ang, to come and receive him--our teacher then resolved to leave Mount Kuang and enter Caoxi. On that very day he ascended the seat in the Wuru dharma-hall and made it known to hall-master Ang, and likewise took leave of the assembly. He sat cross-legged for a long while, unaware that a great serpent had coiled itself beneath his body, its form pressed flat as a cushion. When he rose and saw it, he took it as an omen and lit a flame to accompany the journey; it also prefigured that, having entered Caoxi, he would remain but a single year and never return to Wuru again. On the day he arrived back at Caoxi, hall-master Ang invited him to ascend the hall and preach. Word by word he broke open the old case of the Sixth Patriarch’s bodily relic and the incense-offerings, and the meaning of how what came before and what came after answer each other; therein one sees the spirit of one who knows beforehand. The dharma-words ran: “Before the Sixth Patriarch came forth into the world, he was only a wood-seller of Xinzhou. Because he had planted the spiritual root in former lives and long nourished his practice, the instant he heard the Diamond Sutra spoken and the line ‘should dwell nowhere,’ he cut off the birth-and-death of eons, awakened to his own mind, and so received the robe and bowl of Huangmei. Is not the Baolin of today come down from the shoulder that bore the firewood and the waist-stone that husked rice? Hence it has such vast and boundless brightness that fills the whole world. Every word, every phrase of the Chan school flows from that firewood-shoulder and that husking waist-stone, and so today the incense and offerings are no different from when he was alive. The flesh-body, firm and unrotting, is no different from one who speaks the Dharma now. Such blessings too come from that firewood-shoulder and that husking waist-stone. This beam of prajñā-light that the Sixth Patriarch awakened to, every person has a share of, lacking not a hair’s breadth. If one can but awaken to one’s own mind, then one may churn the long river into ghee and turn the vast earth into gold; plucking up a single blade of grass, make it a sixteen-foot golden body; and with that sixteen-foot golden body, serve as a single blade of grass. Naturally one then possesses great spiritual powers, transforming freely at will, doing whatever one pleases, nothing impossible.” He further said: “Our teacher, re-entering Caoxi, had it in mind to rebuild the great hall of Caoxi. The many monies he had raised from the three offices and the prefectures went entirely to purchasing iron-pyrus timber in western Guangdong and, as recorded in the chronicle under the wushen year, had already been hauled into Caoxi. The two gentlemen Wu and Zhang, together with hall-master Ang, shared in this vow, and so their pleas for his return were all the more devout. And our teacher, knowing that his hour had come, said, ‘When conditions and the times run contrary, where shall the transformation find a place to lodge?’ And so, in the winter of the guihai year, upon the thirteenth day of the tenth month, he passed away.” There was, moreover, a plot that the vice-minister Xiao Xuanpu had asked the governor Zhang to divine for a shadow-hall, two li south of Nanhua Monastery in Shaozhou, named Tianzi Gang, the Hill of the Son of Heaven. An old prophecy said: “Head above Tianzi Hill, feet treading the Yellow Mud Pond; whoever is buried here, from generation to generation a Dharma-king will arise.” The Guangdong congregation, having taken refuge, therefore raised a stūpa on that spot and there interred his whole body. The Wuru disciple Fushan, styled Zhiwei, together with Shenshen, styled Yihui, Guangyi, styled Xuzhong, and Ciren, styled Jianru, hastened to Guangdong to receive the shrine but could not gain it. So they went about in the Wu-Yue region and, by the teacher’s last command, laid the matter before the many patrons: Wu Benru, He Zhiyue, Wang Jie’an, and Qian Shouzhi. These wrote to the Guangdong judicial commissioner Lu Jingye, who sent a dispatch to Shaozhou; and on the twenty-first day of the first month of the yichou year the shrine was opened and borne back to Mount Kuang. As the land there was dank and damp, Fushan built a stūpa-court and set the shrine floating upon it. The prefectural judge of Nankang, Qian Woxin, whose personal name was Qizhong, chose a place and buried it. Eleven years later, in the yihai year, fierce tigers rose up in the mountains, and Fayun could no longer keep his congregation at peace. Fushan blamed the unquiet spot of the stūpa, and again brought the shrine forth to its floating platform, where he saw that the protecting enclosure had been half eaten by ants, and he dared not divine a tomb. Nine more years passed, and in the ninth month of the guiwei year the Lingnan disciple, the minister Chen Zizhuang, sent a letter with plenty of provisions to greet it. It happened that the Guangdong disciple Liu Qixiang, serving in the penal office of Ruizhou, was auditing the stores of Nankang, and he threw himself into the task of returning the shrine to Caoxi. When they reached Meiling, there was the newly appointed commander-in-chief of Guangdong, Song Zhaoming, named Ji, who ten years earlier, beneath the banner of the Guangdong governor-general, had formed a dharma-affinity with our teacher. Crossing the ridge to take up office, he chanced upon the spiritual shrine and, marveling beyond measure at his fortune, ordered his soldiers to shoulder the shrine and personally escorted it into Caoxi. Months after taking his post he came again to Caoxi, where the shrine-bearing disciples Guangcheng, styled Miaorong, and Cili, styled Jianchi, seeing a crack in the shrine, secretly bored a small opening through it to peep within, and there beheld the master seated upright as though alive. They were debating whether to open the shrine, but no one dared decide. When Song heard this, he at once drew his blade and split the crack open, and they saw the twin cross-legged feet as if alive, the nails and hair both grown long and of a bright red. The robe and shoes were still new, and only when they met the wind did they crumble and fall to pieces, laying bare the five limbs. Suddenly a monk arrived and asked that, following the Indian rite, powdered sandalwood from Hainan be smeared over the body until it was like lacquer; the smearing done, he departed. Long before, in Caoxi, an unmarried girl had vowed to embroider a robe of a thousand Buddhas to offer in homage; fearing that her breath was unclean, she wrapped her mouth in yellow silk as she plied the needle and thread. When the robe was finished, our teacher had already passed on into the shrine, and the robe was left in a chest of the Baolin storehouse. One day the abbot-monk, celebrating a penitential rite, wished to don this robe, but the monks clamored and stopped him. Later, when our teacher’s flesh-body returned to Caoxi and came forth from the shrine, the purple gauze robe was suddenly blown to shreds by the wind, and the countryfolk snatched up the pieces as auspicious tokens. So they took the thousand-Buddha robe the girl had embroidered and clothed him in it; the robe had lain in the chest twenty-two years, yet its luster was as fresh as new. Thereupon it was enshrined at the site of the old stūpa-court, and the monastery was named Hanshan, half a li from the Baolin hall of Nanhua Monastery. The disciples attended him after the manner in which the Sixth Patriarch is attended at Baolin: at dawn they bring a basin of hot fragrant water, steam his face until it sweats, wipe it with a cloth, and set before him food and drink with full reverent offerings, exactly as though he were alive. Once a year they bathe him, and the water of the washing is taken by the countryfolk to drink for the healing of sickness, and it is gone in a moment. Every year the pilgrims of Caoxi, in the second and the eighth months, all the people of the province entering the mountains to pay their respects, would, after offering incense to the Sixth Patriarch, proclaim that they had come to offer incense to the Seventh Patriarch; and so the title “the Seventh Patriarch of Caoxi” arose. For the Guangdong pilgrims, of one accord, had in mind that bodhisattva in flesh, and in a single moment from the Southern Sea to the Northern Sea, all within the realm heard this name and took it as a matter of course. Yet certain critics held that one must not overstep the five lineages and schools, nor yield to a passing word-of-mouth transmission, for fear of giving a handle to those who would later revise the lamp-lineage as a single orthodox succession. Zhen, not measuring his own worth, hastily composed three treatises--on the dharma of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, on the robe and bowl, and on the flesh-body--to lay before the clear-eyed.

Zhen remarks: Above Śākyamuni are called the seven Buddhas; from Śākyamuni’s transmission to Kāśyapa and below, on to Bodhidharma, they are called the twenty-eight patriarchs of the West. From Bodhidharma’s crossing east and below, on to Caoxi, they are called the six patriarchs of the East; they are not called Buddhas, nor are they simply called masters. The Sixth Patriarch transmitted to Huairang and to Xingsi alone, two branches only. Huairang dwelt on Mount Heng, and so his line is called the Nanyue line, and he transmitted to Mazu. Nanyue is not recorded as being called a patriarch, yet Mazu is uniquely honored as patriarch. Is this not to say that Mazu gave the dharma to the many, and did not receive it as a single transmitter of the robe and bowl? Under Mazu came Baizhang, and under Baizhang came Huangbo; these are called great masters or Chan masters, and are never heard called lineage-tutors, for at that time there was yet no teaching of a division into schools. Under Huangbo came Linji, and it is here that the Linji school is first named; the title of a school begins from that time. Before this there were the names of two branches, but no gates of two schools. Under Baizhang there was also Guishan, and under Guishan came Yangshan; and so arose the Guiyang school. Thus one branch of Baizhang gave rise to two schools. Xingsi dwelt at Qingyuan, and so his line is called the Qingyuan line, transmitting to Shitou; under Shitou came Dongshan, and under Dongshan came Caoshan, and by the easy slip of the tongue they were confusedly called the Caodong school. Under Shitou there was also Xuefeng, and under Xuefeng came Yunmen, called the Yunmen school. Later there was also the Fayan school. Thus one branch of Qingyuan gave rise to three schools. Now Huairang and Qingyuan are of one generation, Mazu and Shitou of the next, Baizhang and Xuefeng of yet another--three generations below the Sixth Patriarch--and in none of these do we hear the name of a school. Even Huangbo, of the fourth generation, is not heard to stand with Guishan, Dongshan, and Yunmen of the same generation to contend over the name of a school. This is precisely why Huangbo towers above his fellows and dared to take Mazu to task. Huangbo once said, “Within the great Tang there is no Chan master.” A monk asked, “The venerable ones of all quarters gather the assembly and open the teaching; why then do you say there is no Chan master?” Huangbo said, “I do not say there is no Chan; I say only that there is no master. Do you not see that beneath Master Ma there were eighty-four who sat in the dharma-court, and of those who obtained Master Ma’s true dharma-eye there were only two or three, and among them was the monk Guizong? A man who has left the home-life must know the matter that has been transmitted from above. Thus, even one of the fourth patriarch’s heirs like Niutou, who spoke at length and in breadth, still did not know the pivotal device that points upward. With this eye one can distinguish the true from the false in the schools. But when it touches one’s own present affairs one cannot grasp it; one only knows to recite phrases, to stuff them into the skin-bag, and to go about saying ‘I understand Chan.’ Can that take the place of your birth-and-death? To make light of the elder masters is to fall into hell as swiftly as an arrow flies.” Great indeed are the words of Huangbo! The wisdom-eye and the dharma-eye truly do not deceive me; only the direct grandson of Mazu could carry on so. This is what is meant by “blue comes from indigo yet is deeper than indigo,” and “curdle comes from milk yet is finer than milk.” When Linji made the division into schools, Huangbo gained many sons; and Guiyang, Caodong, Yunmen, and Fayan, following one after another in fame, split the gates and divided the households, and so Mazu, Baizhang, Shitou, and Xuefeng gained many grandsons. One flower and five leaves: we never hear of the flower and the leaves being marked as the root and the trunk. Only because root and trunk are not two does the fruit ripen whole. If one flower can become a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand million flowers, and five leaves can become fifty, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand million leaves, then the more flowers the more leaves; and as the saying goes, “When the leaves are many the flower does not bloom; when the flowers are many the fruit does not set.” Though the words be small, they can illustrate something great. If everyone chases flowers and pursues leaves, where shall one ask after the root and the trunk? Even if fruit can be had, it is only fruit grafted from a flower onto a strange stock; where does the root lie? I am so foolish as not to understand wherein the reality of the schools truly consists. “The ten thousand dharmas return to the One”--this is the teaching. “Where does the One return?”--this is the school. The dharma abides in the hearts of all under heaven, and the heart of the dharma cannot have five. The school abides in the heart of a good and wise teacher; how then should the heart of the school have five? When Bodhidharma came west, those who knew him called it only the Chan school; if the school has five, then the mind has five and Chan has five. I am too dull to see wherein the reality of the five schools truly lies. The five schools are gates; they are titles. The gate of a patriarch is in no wise different from the gate of a Buddha; the title of a patriarch is finally no different from the title of a Buddha. He who can become a patriarch must be able to become a Buddha, and he who cannot become a Buddha must surely not be able to become a patriarch. A patriarch comes from the Buddhas and the bodhisattvas. To give him another title, that is permissible; to give him another gate, I fear it is not. Still more, to take five titles and set up five gates is like the children and grandchildren of a household seizing upon the ancestral estate and scattering the family goods in disorder; this I do not understand. As to the division of titles, it is not only the Buddhas and patriarchs that are divided. Even Śākyamuni has ten titles, and the Buddhas and bodhisattvas have countless and boundless titles; these cannot be held up as equal. As to the union of gates, it is not only the Buddhas and patriarchs that unite. Even the Tiantai dharmanature school, which follows the Lotus and Nāgārjuna’s Madhyamaka; the Xianshou school, which follows the Avataṃsaka and the contemplation of the dharma-realm; the Nanshan Vinaya school; the Cīen Dharmalakṣaṇa school, which illumines the Consciousness-only school; and the Vajraśekhara Yoga three-mystery school--every teaching must have a school; without a school no teaching is established. They cannot be split into two. If they may be divided and made two, they must surely belong to the heretics, the outer paths, and the Lesser Vehicle. Know that the Pure Land is the mind alone; this is the ten thousand dharmas returning to the One. The patriarch can come west; the Buddha can return west. From the west and from the east, from the south and from the north, none who think but submit--this is what is meant by Buddha and Patriarch. The Dharma of the Buddha is equal, with no high and low. That titles differ, how can one hold them to be equal? Yet for rebirth and for the upholding of the Dharma, one must first have the title. The flesh-eye takes refuge wholly in the reverent name. Long ago I saw a Chan worthy whom the vulgar called “Lord”; Yunqi forbade it and it ceased. This is the meaning of Confucius’s rectification of names and the Spring and Autumn’s fixing of ranks. In the present worldly order, unless one has founded a state and carried on a house, one may not be called a patriarch; yet among the hundred crafts and the myriad trades, all may be called master. In the world-transcending order, they are called the twenty-eight patriarchs of the West and the six patriarchs of the East, and are not heard to be called mere masters. Mazu obtained the dharma from Caoxi and Nanyue before the schools were divided; therefore it is fitting to call him patriarch. Hanshan too obtained the dharma from Caoxi, and going to and fro between Nanyue and Qingyuan, in every place, in every moment, did nothing but speak the dharma, practice the dharma, and transmit the dharma. Though he came after the schools were divided, he still returns to the time before they were divided; therefore it is fitting, following the precedent of Mazu, to call him Patriarch Hanshan. Only those who personally attended him may call him our teacher; those who inherit the dharma may call him the master of the house. As for the titles of great master and seventh patriarch, these all go along with the common custom. The Jingzong Record quotes the words of Bodhidharma: “To illumine the mind-school of the Buddha, with no error whatsoever, and to have practice and understanding answer each other--this is called a patriarch.” These words match perfectly the meaning of “Patriarch Hanshan.” If the great master Daguan, in his verse in praise of Master Hanshan that he sent with the image of Master Kang, says that the flesh-Buddha of Caoxi has appeared, he means Patriarch Lu. Patriarch Lu may be called the flesh-Buddha, and Patriarch Hanshan should be no different; so let us call him the flesh-Patriarch of Caoxi. The Chan monks who push themselves forward in the world can truly bear no comparison. In general, only the schools, the dharma, and the vinaya may be called lineage-tutors, dharma-masters, and vinaya-masters; one may not call them lineage-patrims, dharma-patrims, and vinaya-patrims. Only when the three gates are hard to name might one be called patriarch. Thus Patriarch Lu,’ obtaining the school from Huangmei, the dharma from Yinzong, and the vinaya from Zhiguang, is a model for Mazu, for Hanshan, and for those who come again in later ages.

Zhen further notes, in the outline of the life of Patriarch Lu: When the patriarch had received the robe and the dharma from Huangmei, he came to the South Sea and met the dharma-master Yinzong, who, hearing the words about the wind and the banner, invited the patriarch into his room, held the ritual of a disciple, and announced to the four assemblies, “This Layman Lu is a bodhisattva in the flesh.” Gathering the famous worthies, he shaved his head; and further, before the vinaya-master Zhiguang of the Fahsing Monastery, he received the full precepts. That ordination platform had been set up by the Tripitaka master Guṇabhadra in the time of the Liu Song. That master had recorded, “Hereafter a bodhisattva in the flesh shall receive the precepts on this platform.” From this we know that the patriarch who confers the robe and the bodhisattva in the flesh must be one person, while the monk who shaves the head, the master who confers the precepts, and the tutor who confers the dharma must not be one person. This mind is the same, this way is the same, but their meaning is distinct and their rule is distinct. Again, Patriarch Lu said to the four assemblies, “I have unworthily received the robe and the dharma of Master Ren; now I preach the dharma for you, but I do not transmit the robe.” And one day he said to his disciples, “I wish to return to Xinzhou.” The great assembly, mourning, begged the patriarch to remain and said, “Master, when you go from here, will you come back sooner or later?” The patriarch said, “The leaf falls and returns to the root; when I come, I shall have no mouth.” Again they asked, “From whom did the master’s dharma-eye descend?” The patriarch said, “The one who has the Way obtains it; the one who is without a mind penetrates it.” From this we know that the robe and bowl of the patriarchs had long been without vestige since the Xiantian years of the early Tang. As for the robe and bowl now handed down at Caoxi, they did not come from Huangmei but were bestowed in the Shenlong first year of Emperor Zhongzong of Tang, who dispatched the eunuch Xue Jian to invite him; Patriarch Lu, declining on the grounds of illness, did not go, and thus discoursed with Xue Jian, saying that the Way is realized by the mind, and not by sitting in meditation and practicing concentration. His words were very full. Xue Jian, receiving the instruction, was suddenly enlightened, took his leave and returned to court, and memorialized the patriarch’s words. An edict thanked the master and bestowed upon him a kṣāya of worn patches, five hundred bolts of silk, and one bowl. From this we know that the robe and bowl of Caoxi are only the royal offerings, not the token of the Fifth Patriarch. It is Mazu alone who transmitted the dharma the most, and even his disciples had many disagreements; therefore one may speak of his transmission of the dharma, but not of his transmission of the robe and bowl, nor of a transmission of a token, nor of a transmission of a school. To take a material thing as a token of transmission is something the outer paths often have. How could Mazu have so many robes and bowls? The story about the robe and bowl that is handed down is, through a thousand years, mere dust for food and mud for soup; the life of the Buddhas and patriarchs is in no way bound up with it. Only our Hanshan, a patriarch in the flesh, inherits the transmission of one flower and five leaves, so as to reach a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million leaves.
